3846: The petitioner, a woman, filed a petition under section 13(1)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 for dissolution of her marriage with the respondent. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that the petitioner had failed to prove the factum of marriage and that she was not entitled to any relief. Dismissing the special leave petitions, this Court, HELD: (1) The presumption is rebuttable, a heavy burden lies upon the petitioner who seeks to deprive the relationship of legal origin. [829 B] (2) The presumption arises in favour of wedlock only when there are two or more spouses living together as husband and wife. In the instant case, the petitioner has failed to discharge this onus. [830 C D] (3) The presumption does not arise merely because the evidence adduced by the parties is not sufficient to rebut it. It may be that the evidence adduced may have some relevance to the question of law involved in the case but that cannot be made the basis of a presumption. [831 E F] (4) The presumption can be raised only if the evidence adduced is such that it would be impossible to arrive at a conclusion one way or the other that the evidence produced by the parties would be sufficient to sustain its validity. [832 G H] (5) The presumption must be drawn from the facts proved by the party. The evidence adduced must be such that it can reasonably be assumed that the existence of the fact required to be established will be conclusively proved. [833 A B] (6) The presumption should be raised only when the evidence adduced establishes that the factum of the marriage between the parties is admitted. [834 A B]
5810: The petitioners, who were the respondents in the appeal filed by the respondent No. 1, were the appellants before the High Court. The award was made on May 31, 1979. The award is an unreasoned one. The High Court dismissed the petition for special leave to appeal against the said order. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High court has rightly held that the relevant documents had not been taken into consideration. [642C] 1.2. The High Courts have consistently taken the view that the award should be set aside if it is found that the award was vitiated by patent illegality or perversity. [643A B] 2.1. In the instant case, the award was made after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed under section 34(3) of the Act. The award does not indicate that all relevant documents had been taken into account. The High courts have also pointed out that the award itself shows that all relevant papers had not been considered. [644E F] 2.2. It is not desirable, in the interest of justice, to keep this matter pending because some cases are pending here on the question of the validity of unreasoned award per se. [645F G] 3.1. There is no allegation of any violation of principles of natural justice. [646B] 3.2. In the facts and circumstances of the case, there is no error of law apparent on the face of the award or gross mistake of fact resulting in the miscarriage of justice or of equity. [647D] 3.3. The High Cour t has rightly held in favour of the petitioners. [648G H] 4.1. It is true that the award is an unreasonable one. But the award is not liable to be interfered with unless it is shown that the award suffers from manifest injustice or perversities. [649H; 650A] 4.2. A party cannot be permitted to take advantage of a wrong committed by another party. [650B] 4.3. An award which is based on conjectures and surmises is not open to challenge on the ground of irrationality. [664
6169: The petitioner, a member of the State Legislature, was appointed as Chairman of the Advisory Board. He filed an application for being appointed as Chairman. The State Government in its counter affidavit stated that the Board had been set up at the State level and steps were taken to set up the Advisory Boards. The Board was constituted on 1st April, 1985. The Board submitted its report on 30th March, 1986. The State Cabinet took a decision on 29th March, 1987 to constitute the Advisory Board for the State. The Board also recommended that the State Government should constitute a Board consisting of three members. The State Govern ment issued a notification dated 3rd May, 1988 constituting the Advisory Board with three members. In the meantime, the State Government issued another notification dated 4th June, 1988 constituting a Board consisting only of three members, one of whom was a woman member. The State of Nagaland challenged the validity of the notification by filing a writ petition before this Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification dated 3nd May, 1988 was not valid. The State appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State Government has the power to constitute the Board. The Board is constituted within six weeks from today and the State Government shall constitute the Board within six weeks thereafter. The Board shall be set up within six weeks of its constitution and every such Board is directed to send its first proceeding to the Registry of this Court within eight weeks of its Constitution. The State government may make small variations depending upon the requirements of any particular State. The State Govt. should indicate as to who would be the Chairman and Secretary respectively of the Board. Such Committee should be set up at State level and necessary steps are directed to be taken within eight weeks. The State will submit its first proceeding within four weeks of its establishment and the Board shall submit its second proceeding to the State Government within eight weeks thereafter. [355C D] 1.2 The State Government should indicate as how many members have been working in the Board. It should indicate the names of the persons who are working in the State. [354E] 1.3 The State Government must indicate as to what are the conditions which the Board would require to take into consideration while framing
2166: The respondent was prosecuted for an offence under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. He was acquitted by the Magistrate on the ground that he had not been given a certificate as required by sub section (2) of section 13 of the Act. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the sample sent to the Director of the Central Food Laboratory was adulterated and that the report of the Public Analyst showed that the sample contained the result of the analysis. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant could not be convicted for an offence committed under section 16 because the report of Public Analyst did not contain any such finding. [1191 G] 2. The report of the public analyst is conclusive evidence of the fact that the sample was adulterated. It is only when the report of a public analyst contains a finding that it has become absolutely unsafe to act upon it that the court can convict the accused. [1192 H] 3. In the instant case, the report of public analyst does not contain any finding that the sample analysed by him was adulterated or that the result of analysis indicated that the sample did not become absolutely unscientific. The report merely states that the sample had become highly decomposed and no analysis of it was possible. [1193 A B] 4. The report does not show that the sample which had been sent to the Public Analyst had become absolutely unscathed. The report also does not indicate that the result thereof had been communicated to the Public Prosecutor. [1194 C D] 5. The report cannot be regarded as conclusive proof of the fact stated therein. [1190 E] 6. The report in the present case does not contain the result of a scientific analysis of the sample sent for examination. The report is conclusive evidence about the fact that it had become absolutely unfit for human consumption. [1195 F] 7. The report must be regarded as a piece of evidence relating to the facts stated therein. The report may be treated as a piece with some other material which would have been admissible but the report itself does not contain. The report therefore cannot be regarded either as conclusive or binding on the prosecution. [1196 C D] 8.

7131: The appellant assessee, a registered dealer under the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957, filed an appeal before the Karnataka Appellate Tribunal against the assessment order of the assessing authority. The appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal on the ground that unpaid "not disputed" tax was the additional tax which was payable by the appellant. The High Court in revision held that the additional tax levied under Section 613 of the Act had not been paid and that the appellant was entitled to refund of the excess amount. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the additional levy under Section 6B of the Act was a levy distinct from the impost under Section 5 (1) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder including those relating to refund or exemption from tax are applicable only when the tax is leviable under the provisions of the statute. [5G] 2. The provisions relating to refund and exemption from tax apply in relation to the levy, assessment and collection of the additional tax. The expression "tax" has been defined to mean a tax leviable under the provision of the Act, and as such includes the additional tax contemplated under Section 6 B of the Act which has been imposed after the amendment of the Act by the Amendment Act of 1973. [6H; 7A B] 3. The provisions regarding the period of limitation for filing appeals against orders of assessment are contained in section 20(3) of the Karnataka Sales tax Act, 1957. The said section provides that no appeal shall be entertained unless the prescribed period of limitation has expired. The proviso to sub section (3) of Section 20 makes it clear that the period of 30 days specified therein is to be reckoned from the date of receipt of the order appealed against. The proviso does not make any distinction between the time taken in prosecuting the appeal and the time spent in obtaining the certified copy of the order. [7C D] 4. The provisions in regard to the period of appeal have been made applicable to the appellate authorities under the Act. The provisions do not provide for any separate period of limitation. The provisions are intended to enable the appellate authorities to decide the appeal within the period of time prescribed. [7E G
2907: The respondent was a member of a scheduled tribe. He had applied for the grant of quarry lease in respect of a quarry and he was granted a permit to extract stone from the quarry. The appellant refused to accept the tender on the ground that the respondent had not paid the amount due under Rule 10 promulgated in exercise of power under the Regulation. The respondent thereupon filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Divisional Forest Officer, but the High Court dismissed it holding that the amount claimed was not recoverable under the Assam Forest Regulation VII of 1891. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The rule does not give rise to any liability to pay a sum of money. It is true that the rule does not apply to recovery of the amount alleged to be due for failure to carry out the obligations of the tender by proceedings under the Assam forest Regulation, 1891. But the rule does neither give rise to an obligation nor does it confer any right on the person who has been refused to act as such. [901 B D] (ii) The rule applies only where the amount claimed is not recoverable under law or is not payable under the law. It is not applicable where the amount is not recoverable as an arrear of land revenue. [902 E F] (iii) The rule is not applicable to recovery of money due under the Act. [903 G H]
2986: The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal conspiracy under section 120B of the Indian Penal Code. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions Court. On appeal, the High Court acquitted him but set aside the order of committal passed by the Magistrate. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence of abetment of an offence of forgery; (ii) the Magistrate did not examine any witnesses during the committal proceedings but on a perusal of the charge sheet and documents filed before him under sec. 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure he framed charges and committed the case for trial to the Sessions Court; (iii) the Magistrate took cognizance of the offences without applying his mind to the question whether or not the offence of conspiracy was made out against the appellant; (iv) the Magistrate acted in excess of his jurisdiction and therefore, the order of commitment was illegal and void; (v) the Magistrate could not have taken cognizance of the alleged offence without examining the witnesses; (vi) the Magistrate was wrong in taking cognizance of the case without examining the accused; (vii) the Magistrate having taken cognizance of an offence without examining any witness, the order was bad in law; (viii) the Magistrate committed error in proceeding against the appellant without examining the prosecution witnesses; (ix) the Magistrate wrongly assumed the jurisdiction of the Magistrate when he took cognizance of an off ence without examining the complainant and the witnesses; and (x) the Magistrate erred in holding that the Magistrate had jurisdiction to take con sideration of the evidence adduced before him. HELD: (1) The Magistrate took cognizance without examining the complaint and the witnesses as required by sec. 196A(2). [760C] (2) The Magistrate did not consider the question whether the offence of forgery was made out or not. The Magistrate did so because he was satisfied that the offence of cheating was made out. [760D E] (3) The Magistrate had no power to take cognizance at all. The Magistrate had only to see whether the allegations made in the complaint were sufficient to justify the summoning of the accused. 5711: The petitioner company was registered under the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973. It filed returns for all the quarters covered within the period indicated above as prescribed by the Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1973 and the Haryana Act for the quarters of the remained years in question as the Haryana Act came into force with effect from 5th May, 1973. On the receipt of notice relating to assessment years 1968 69, 1969 70, 1970 71, 1971 72, 1972 73 and 1973 74, the petitioner company appeared before the respondent No. 2 and complied with the requirements of such notice by production of documents, books and other papers. While the matter was thus proceeding, the second respondent issued a notice on 24.9.1982 requiring the petitioner company to produce certain further records and documents. The petitioner company appeared and complied with all the formalities. The assessing authority completed the assessment and issued a notice dated 24.9,1982 calling upon the petitioner company for furnishing the required information. The petitioner Company did not appear and did not file any reply. The petitioner also did not produce any evidence that the returns furnished were correct or complete. The petitioner 's appeal against the said order was dismissed by the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax. The petitioner has challenged the validity of the aforesaid notices as also the vires of section 28A of the Haryana Act. The petitioner contends that the provisions of section 28 A are mandatory and non compliance thereof is fatal to the proceedings. The petitioner submits that the impugned notice is bad in law as it does not comply with the requirements contained in section 28A. The petitioner further submits that the first respondent had no jurisdiction to issue the impugned notice as he was not satisfied with the returns submitted by the petitioner. The petitioner therefore prays that the impugned notices be quashed and set aside. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Sub section (1) of section 28 of the Haryana General sales Tax Act,1973 provides that where the assessing authority finds that the return furnished by the dealer is incorrect or incomplete, he shall serve a notice on the dealer requiring him to furnish a return within 15 days of the date of service of the notice. If the return is not filed within the time specified in the notice, the assessing authority may proceed to assess the tax payable on the
886: The appellant was the owner of a piece of land in village Mohammadpur Munirka. He purchased it from Mrs. Sethi and her husband. The sale deed was executed by the vendor in favour of the appellant who was the purchaser. The appellant filed a criminal complaint against the vendor on April 1, 1959, alleging that for several months no further action was taken on the said First Information Report which was hanging like a sword over his head. The Magistrate ordered that the appellant 's complaint should stand adjourned. On July 25, 1959 the appellant moved the Punjab High Court under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceedings initiated by the First Information Report in question. The High Court held that no case had been made out for quashing the proceeding initiated by the first respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court erred in holding that no case was made out for the quashing of the proceedings; (ii) the High court erred in holding the appellant guilty of an offence under section 420 I.P.C., and (iii) the High Courts ' order quashing the proceedings was not justified. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant could be prosecuted only if there was a legal evidence adduced in support of the charge. [504 F] (ii) The High Courts ' orders were not justified on the ground that the appellant had failed to prove the charge. It is well settled that where a party fails to discharge the burden of proving a particular fact the matter must be decided on the basis of the facts proved. [503 C D] (iii) The High court was wrong in holding that there was no legal evidence adduced by the appellant in support of his case. [502 E] (iv) The High courts ' order quashing proceedings cannot be sustained because the appellant has failed to establish any legal evidence. [505 G] (v) The High 'Court was wrong in thinking that the appellant would have liked to add one clause to the deed to the deed. [506 H]
2023: The assessee was a sovereign of India and was assessed to income tax for the year 1950 51. He claimed that he had been assessed to income Tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, in respect of the two years. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee 's income accrued to him during the accounting year and that as he ceased to be a sovereign from January 26, 1950, his income did not accrue to him thereafter. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment. In appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the assessee was exempt from taxation under the International Law. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the assessee could not claim immunity from taxation under International Law because the assessee was not liable to tax under the Income tax Act. HELD: (i) The assessee was not entitled to exemption under International Law. [560 C] (ii) The assessee 's case was covered by the International Law and the assessee was entitled to relief under the International law. [540 D] (iii) The assessee could not be said to have enjoyed immunity from taxation when he ceased to exist. [541 E] (iv) The assessee continued to enjoy immunity from taxation even after the merger. [542 F] (v) The assessee being a sovereign of the country, could not claim exemption under International law. The assessee was therefore not entitled to any exemption under the International Laws. [543 B] (vi) The assessee having regard to International Law was entitled to exemption from taxation under international law. [551 A] (vii) The assessee had no right to claim exemption under the Income Tax Act. [552 B]
5771: The appellant filed an election petition challenging the election of the respondent on the ground that the result of the election was materially affected on account of improper rejection of nomination papers of three candidates. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the appellant had failed to prove that the result was materially affected by the improper rejection of the nomination paper of the respondent. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the nomination paper filed by the respondent was invalid and the returning officer rightly rejected her nomination paper. [979E] 2.1 In view of the clear provisions in section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the High Court was right in holding that the nomination papers of the respondent were improperly accepted. [980B C] 2.2 The High Court was not justified in setting aside the election of respondent on the sole ground that the election was vitiated on account of the improper rejection or improper acceptance of the nomination papers. [981C D] 3.1 The decision of the High Court is based on a misreading of the relevant provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. [982D E] 4.1 The view taken in Sri Babu Ram 's case (supra) has been followed in Narbada Prasad vs Chaggan Lal & Ors., [l983] 4 SCC 328. [984F] 4.2 The view taken by the High Court in Sri Babu Rana Joshi vs Satish Kumar & Ors., A.I.R. 1986 Rajasthan 268; Sri Babu Ram vs Jugal Kishore Gupta, [l985] 4 SCC 311, referred to.
2079: The appellants were convicted under section 353, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to three months rigorous imprisonment. They appealed to the High Court which set aside their conviction and sentence. The High Court held that there was no satisfactory evidence to convict them under sections 143/402, Indian Penal code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the two offences being fundamentally distinct in nature could be separately taken cognizance of; (ii) the two charges having been framed against the appellants for the offence under section 351, Indian Penal Cod e, the trial court had no jurisdiction to try the appellants for that offence, (iii) the charge sheet did not disclose any offence under section 186, Indian Penal, Code, and (iv) the prosecution case was based on circumstantial evidence. HELD: (i) The two offences being a separate one, the trial of the appellants for those offences must be held to have been commenced by reason of the provisions contained in section 195, Criminal Procedure Code. [855 B] (ii) The two charges having not been framed, the trial would be illegal. [856 A] (iii) The two proceedings are independent in character and cannot be equated with each other. [857 D]

They carried on business principals, merchants and dealers in dyes, etc., in various branches of the Indian Income tax Department. In the years ending March 31, 1945, the I.T.O. had to pay commission at rates varying between 7 1/2% and 12 1/2%. The I.Ts. paid by the assessees were not included in the profits of the business. The I. Ts. claimed that they should be allowed a deduction of 5% of their gross profit as against the actual sales made by them. The I Ts. disallowed the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the I. T.O. but the Tribunal held that the I. C. was entitled to a deduction of 10% of the net profits without deducting any excess profits tax or Business Profits Tax. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended (i) that the I Ts, were not liable to pay any income tax; (ii) that the payment of commission was not allowable under section 21(1)(a) of the Excess Profits Tax Act; (iii) that the payments were not deductible under section 21 (3); (iv) that the amount of commission was an expenditure within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Act; (v) that the provisions of section 21(4) of the Income tax Act were not attracted because the I. A.C. had no power to make such a provision. HELD: (i) The payment of commission is not an item of expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business. It is only when the payment is made in pursuance of a contract entered into with another person that the payment can be said to have been made in pursuance or for the purposes of the business of the other person. [511 B] (ii) The payment was made in pursuance to a contract entered with another person and therefore the payment was not an item which could be regarded as expenditure laid out for the purpose. [512 D] (iii) The payment is not an expenditure laid out entirely for the purpose or for the
6517: The respondent No. 1 was the owner of a Petrol Pump which was set up on a site in Dehradun, of which respondent No. 5 was the lessee. Respondent No. 1 had applied for a 'No Objection Certificate ' for conducting a Petrol pump. The District Magistrate granted the 'No Objection Certifi cate ' to the appellant. The District Collector cancelled the 'No objection certificate ' and the 'no objection cer tificate ' granted by the District Magistrate. The Commissioner of the Division set aside the 'No Objections ' and the said order was upheld by the Commissioner. The High Court allowed the writ petition filed by the respondent No.1. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the District Authority under Rule 151 could cancel the 'NoObjection Certificate ' only when the licensee ceased to have any right to use the site for storing petrol; (ii) the District Magistrate under Rule 151 can cancel the 'NOC ' only when he is satisfied that the licensee has ceased to have no right to use site for storing petroleum; (iii) the District Collector under Rule 151 cannot cancel the 'noob obtai nation certificate ' granted to the licensee. [977 G] 2. The District Authorities under Rule 151 are empowered to cancel the 'Nos Objection Certificates ' issued to the licensee after giving him a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The District authorities under Rule 151 do not have any power to cancel the N o Objection Certificates issued to the licensees after giving them a reasonable opportunity. [978 A B] 3. 2366: The appellant was convicted under section 5 (3) (a) of the Explosives Rules, 1940. He was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and also to pay a fine of Rs. 2,000 in default to undergo rigorous sentence for six months. The High Court held that the three minor boys were employed in the manufacture of fireworks and that they could not be held guilty under section 304A, I.P.C. The High court did not find the two other accused persons, Abdul. The prosecution case was that the appellant had allowed minors to enter the premises licensed under the Rules for manufacture of explosives on April 28, 1960. The High 'Court accepted the finding of the trial court that the three minors were actually employed in the manufacturing process on April 28. 1960. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court should have found that the three major boys were actually employed by the appellant in the manufacture and that the High 'Court should have given its own reasons for coming to the conclusion that the three adult boys were actually engaged in the manufacture. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The High Courts decision is correct. [611B] 1.2. The High courts judgment does not suffer from any infirmity. [612E] 1.3. The High has rightly relied upon the evidence of the three minor girls who were admittedly employed in the factory. [613F] 1.4. The High would have been justified in convicting the appellant if the three minor children were actually employed on the date of occurrence. [614D] 1.5. The High should have considered whether the three minor women were actually employed or not in the manufacture or in the process of manufacture. [615G] 1.6. The High ought to have considered whether there was any material to show that the three young boys were actually working in the manufacture, or in the processes of manufacture. The High could have gone into the question as to whether the three young girls were actually employed. [616H; 617A] 1.7. The High was right in holding that the three small boys were actually employe d in the manufacture process. [618A] 1:8.
6753: The appellant, a Sagar Mahila Vidyalaya was incorporated by a registered deed of trust dated 17th November, 1933. The said trusts were registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The appellant filed an application for revival of the execution proceedings on the ground that the judgment debtor had defaulted in carrying out the directions of the revisional court and as such the order passed by the D.I.T., Sagar on 20th August, 1942 was illegal. The D.I..T. rejected the application. The appellant 's revision applications against the aforesaid orders were dismissed by the Second Additional District Judge, Sagar. The High Court allowed the revision petitions filed by the appellant and set aside the orders of the D. I.T. The appellant appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the judgment debtors had committed default in carrying out their directions and as such they could not be proceeded with further. HELD: (i) The judgment debtor had failed to comply with the direction of the DI.T. In the circumstances it would be difficult to hold that the judgment creditor had committed any default in carrying on the directions of his revisional court. [912 E] (ii) The judgment creditor had no right to proceed against the judgment debtor under section 31(2)(a) of the U.P. Debt Relief Act, 1947. The judgment debtor was not a member of the society. He was merely a member of a society. The judgment creditor was not a person who could have been proceeded against under section 31 of the Act. [913 F G] (iii) The judgment creditors had no right or authority to proceed against them under section 31 (1) of the Act because the judgment debtor was a member of an association which was registered under the U. P. Co operative Societies Act, 1965. The judgment debtors had no right, title or interest in the property. [914 H; 915 A B] (iv) The judgment debtors were not members of the society and were not entitled to proceed against their properties under section 31. [916 C]
2511: The appellant was charged with offences under section 120B of the Indian Penal Code read with section 135 of the New Act and sections 23(IA) and 23 B of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947. He was tried by a Magistrate for the alleged offence under section 120 B of the Indian penal code read with section 5(2) of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000. In appeal the High Court acquitted him but confirmed his conviction and sentence. The appellant came up in appeal to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the statements recorded by the Customs authorities under the provisions of the old Act were admissible in evidence at the trial of persons accused of offences, inter alia, under the , and that the statements so recorded were inadmissible under section 161 read with section 162 of the Code. HELD: (i) Section 25 of the Evidence Act is not applicable to cases where the statement made by an officer is not admissible as evidence under section 161 or section 162 of Code. [616 G] (ii) A Central Excise Officer exercising powers under the Act is not a police officer within the meaning of section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act. He is therefore entitled to be treated as a police officer for the purposes of section 25. [617 D] (iii) The statements recorded by a Customs Officer under the provisions Of the Act are admissible in evidence against the person accused of any offence under the Act. [618 E] (iv) The statements made by the Customs Officers under the provisionsof the Act are not admissible in evidence. [619 C] (v) The statements of the appellant and other accused persons recorded by the customs officers under the provisions ofthe Act are admissible under section 161 of the Code even though they may have been recorded by a police officer under section 25 of Evidence Act. [603 F] (vi) The statements which are recorded by the officers under the Act are inadmissible in evidence. The statements made before them are not admissible under section 162 of Cr. P.C. [620 H]
5339: The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. During the assessment year 1957 57, it claimed deduction of Rs.26986 being interest paid to Barivallabndas Kalidas Estate on loans taken by her. The Income tax Officer found that out of the loan advanced to her, the assessee had borrowed money from her and had invested in the same. The assessee claimed that she should be allowed deduction under section 57(iii) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim but the Tribunal held that the expenditure could not be admitted under section 57 (iii) of Income tax Act. In further appeal before the Tribunal the assessee contended that the expenditure under the head 'income from other sources ' should have been treated as revenue expenditure and the claim for interest in respect of such loans should have been admitted. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the assessee. The High Court answered the question against the assessee holding that the expenditure was not an admissible deduction under section 12(2) of the Act. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the amount of interest paid to the assessee was not an allowable deduction under section IT Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. 5892: The petitioners in these two writ petitions were candidates for admission to MBBS/BDS Course. They applied for the same. The Director General of Health Services, Government of India, issued a letter dated 25th September, 1988 stating that the decision regarding allocation of seats in the MBBS/BD Courses was taken by the Central Board of Secondary Education and that the said decision should be communicated to the State Governments. In response to the said letter, the State Government informed the Director General of health Services that the decision had been taken by the Board of Governors of the Medical Colleges in Delhi and that the decision would be implemented within three weeks from the date of receipt of the letter. The petitioners in the two writ petitions who are residents of Punjab, and who have since joined the said college, challenged the said decision on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions. Hence these appeals. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The decision of the Central Board is not final and binding on the State Governments as it has no power to make any law or issue directions which may affect the rights of the citizens. [901 G] 1.2. The decision taken by the State Government cannot be questioned before this Court. It is only if the decision is against the petitioners that they can challenge the same. [902 B C] 2.1. In the instant case, the decision of the State Government is not final but only an interim direction. The petitioners have already been admitted to the MBBS/ BDS course. They have not been denied admission to the MBBS course. [903 A B] 2.2. In the present case, the petitioners have not been able to show that they have been discriminated against. [904 D E] 2.3. The decision to allot one seat to the petitioners in order of merit is not open to judicial review. [905 F] 2.4. The decision does not violate any fundamental right of the petitioners. [906 A B] 3.1. There is no merit in the contention that the decision of allotment of one seat to a candidate who has already been allocated seats to the medical colleges in Delhi is arbitrary or unreasonable. 748: The respondent was employed in the factory of the appellant as a 'C' class contractor. He claimed that he had been employed in the said factory since 1948 and that he had not been paid overtime wages due to him from April 1, 1949, to September 30, 1954. The appellant denied this claim and pleaded that the delay made by him in filing the present application should be condoned because jointly with his co workers he had been in correspondence with the railway administration in regard to the payment of overtime wages since 1948 and had also been in correspondence for more than three days prior to or the three days subsequent to the said date. The appellant contended that the delay in filing the application should be explained on the ground that the respondent had not been given a holiday within the three days prior thereto. Held, that the appellant was not entitled to claim overtime wages under section 59 of the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948 (Bom. 79 of 1948) because the respondent had been in contact with the railway authorities in regard to payment of overtime work and had been in touch with them for about two months before the said date and had been regularly paying the same. The appellant was therefore not entitled to any relief.

7115: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1959. The appellant company is a subsidiary of the Kerala State Electricity Board. The appellant had entered into an agreement with the Kerala State Power Corporation Ltd., for purchase of land and other lands. The appellant, who was a member of the Kerala Electricity Board, purchased the land and other land from the Kerala State Government. The appellant filed a petition before the High Court under section 446(1) of the Companies Act, 1956, seeking winding up of the appellant company on the ground that it was not liable to pay any amount to the Kerala State electricity Board. The High courts are right in their view that the appellant has no locus standi to challenge the order passed by the High Court. [540E] 3. The High Cour t has taken the view that the offer made in the case of the appellant is not binding on the Board. The Board has been given the power to accept or reject the offer. The Board may decline to accept the offer if it finds that the offer is not acceptable. The Board can refuse to accept the highest bid. It cannot be said that the Board has acted arbitrarily or unreasonably in refusing to accept the lowest bid. [541A B] 4. 1257: The appellant was convicted under section 307, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a period of two years. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the condition of acute emaciation in which Bimla Devi was found on 5th June, 1956, was not due to any calculated starvation but it was on account of prolonged illness, the nature of which was not known to the accused till Dr. It followed the assurance given by the appellant that he would be able to leave the house and only sometimes a morsel or so used to be thrown to her as alms were given to him; (ii) the fact that the appellant had been living with his wife at the time when she went to her brother 's place and stayed there for about a year showed that he intended to commit suicide and that he did not intend to commit suicide. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The condition of acution in which B is found on 5.6.1956, was not because of any calculated starsment but it was due to prolonged illness. [801 G] (2) The fact that the condition of the acute emanated from the appellant 's own mother 's place was not due for any reason whatsoever, could not be said to have caused an intention to commit suicide within the meaning of section 308, Indian Penal code. [802 A B] (3) The fact of the appellant having been living with the wife at the relevant time was not due either to any deliberate act of omission or commission on his part. [803 C D]
4865: The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court set aside the conviction and acquitted him. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that (i) the High Court 's judgment was vitiated because the High Court had not considered the evidence in its proper perspective; (ii) the High court 's view that the prosecution had failed to establish the motive for the offence is erroneous; and (iii) the High 'Court 's finding that the appellant was guilty of murdering the deceased is based on conjectures and surmises. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court has given cogent reasons for reversing the order of acquittal passed by the trial court. [862B] 2. The High 'Court has clearly dealt with the reasons given by the trial Court in support of the order of conviction and has demonstrated in a good measure as to why those reasons cannot be accepted. [863C D] 3. The High Courts have been consistent in their approach in dealing with the evidence of the witnesses who are interested in the success of the case. It is not necessary to refer to the evidence of each one of them. [864E G] 4. The High courts have also taken into consideration the evidence of Bodu Lal, who was an independent witness, in whose cycle rickshaw the appellant and the co accused Kanahiya Lal were evading to pay the debt which created bitterness between the two brothers on one hand and accused Nos. 3 and 4 on the other. The High Commission had also found that the appellant had been actively involved in the commission of the crime. [865F H] 5. The High Com mission has given cogent reasonings for setting aside the order of the acquittal passed by it. [866A C] 6. The High Commissioner has given cogent and convincing reasons for interfering with the order of acquital. [867D]

Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has rightly come to the conclusion, that the appellants are not entitled to the benefit of Section 35C. 3786: The appellant was appointed as a Subordinate Judge in the State of Manipur on 1st January, 1935. He joined the erstwhile State of Manipur as a junior clerk in 1935. On the enactment of Manipur Courts Act 1955 the Court of Subordinate Judge was abolished with effect from 1st December 1962. The appellant was served with a notice dated 30th June 1966 that he was required to retire from Government service with effect from the date of his attaining 55 years of age. The appellant did not earn good reports from superior officers. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of compulsory retirement. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned order of compulsory retrenc hment was null and void because the Fundamental Rule 56 at the material time contained no reservation of any powers in the appointing authority to retire an officer who had completed years ' qualifying service. HELD: (i) The power under F.R. 56 is a power exercisable by the appropriate authority to retire a Government servant compulsorily. It is open to the appropriate authority either to accept the opinion formed by the Government that it is in public interest to do so or to withhold permission to retire if made out by the Government servant. [560 C] (ii) The power conferred on the appropriate authority under F. R. 56 is not absolute but is subject to the provisions of the Constitution. The power is coupled with duty to act fairly and reasonably. The exercise of the power must be within the four corners of the relevant law. [566 D] (iii) The power to retire a government servant compulsorily is a power exercised by the President under Article 310(1) of the Constitution of India. The President has the power to retire him compulsorily after he attains the age of 55 years. The power to compulsorily retire a government serva nt after he attained the age of 50 years is vested in the President. The power of compulsory retirement is a power which is exercisable by the President in accordance with the rules framed by him under Art.311 of the Constitution and the Rules framed by him. The power under the rule is discretionary and the same cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. [565 E G]
891: The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. He died on November 11, 1947. His widow and two daughters were his legal heirs. The assessee claimed that the income from property should be assessed in the hands of the three widows as " association of persons ". The Income tax Officer issued notices to the legal heirs of the deceased and after considering the evidence adduced by the parties, he came to the conclusion that the entire estate of the deceased was inherited by the three widows. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire income from the property was liable to be assessed in their hands in the hands 'of the three widows and accordingly he passed an order for partitioning the properties. The Tribunal held that the income derived from the property could not be assessed separately in the hands or in any event the income from the properties would have been liable to be taxed in the hands. The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The Tribunal was right in holding that the entire interest of the deceased in the property was inherited and possessed by the three claimants. [901B] 2.1. In the instant case, the Tribunal has found that the entire share of the deceased had been inherited by him and the other three claimants. The Tribunal has also found that the income of the deceased from the property had been assessed separately in its hands. [902C D] 2.2. The Tribunal is right in coming to the conclusion it has reached. [903E] 3.1. It is not necessary to enter in the present case that the three widows should have been assessed separately and not as an " association of person" and that the income therefrom must be assessed separately. [904A B] 3.2. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court was right in coming into the conclusion that there was no " association of individuals". [905D]

The respondent company received a sum of Rs 42,073.00 from the Government as cess in respect of the said colliery. The respondent claimed exemption from the assessment of cess in respect thereof under section 10(2) of the Bengal Cess (Amendment) Act, 1959. The Collector rejected the claim of exemption treating the said sum of Rs. 42,074.00 as one of the items constituting the annual net profit derived from the mine in the process of extracting coal and by using the company 's instruments equipments and staff. The respondent appealed to the Collector who held that the cess levied was not contrary to the provisions of the Act and the rules freedom there under, as the income was derived by the employment of machinery and staff of the coalmine. The Collector also took the view that the cess imposed was not contrary thereto. The Commissioner of Taxes confirmed the order of the Collector. The respondent moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the correctness of the decision of the Collector and the High Court allowed the petition. The cess was levied as a revenue receipt. The cess must have some relation to the cost of construction of the land. [358 E] 5. 1135: The appellants, who were collier holding mining leases under the Government of Madhya Pradesh for the extraction of coal from collieries situated in the Chhindwara District, filed their respective writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the notices issued by the respondent Sabha. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and quashed the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had erred in holding that the appellants ' claims were barred by res judicata by reason of the earlier decision of this Court in the case of the Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd. The appellants contended that the decision of this court in the case was binding on the High Court and that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions. Held, that the High court had rightly held that the appellants had not been able to make out a case for interference with the impugned notices. The appellants were carrying on business as mining lessees in the State of Madhya Pradesh and they had been collecting coal tax for the purpose of meeting the cost of the colliery. The appellants had been paying the coal tax for its collieries. The appellants could not be said to have been deprived of the benefit of the exemption granted by the Government of India Act, 1935, which was made applicable to the State of M.P., and the appellants could not claim any relief against the State of Bihar. The appellants having failed to establish that they were entitled to continue the levy and recover the tax in question, they cannot now turn round and contend that the demand notice issued by the State of Orissa was illegal.
5329: The appellant assessee was manufacturing tyres and tubes. It had claimed exemption from duty on the said goods under Notification No. 17/78 dated August 1, 1978. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise, Bombay, held that the excise duty paid on the said products was not exigible to duty under Notification No, 17/78. He also held that the notification dated July 14, 1978 was applicable only to the extent of duty payable on the inputs and not to the percentage of the duty paid on inputs. The Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise confirmed the demand for differential duty. The Tribunal in appeal upheld the order of the Assistant Collector. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the notification granting exemption from duty was intended to apply only to the specified goods and not to all other goods which were exempted from duty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The notification dated August 1. 1975 is a statutory one and it applies to all excisable goods which are produced or manufactured in India. [817E] (2) The notification was issued by the Central Government in exercise of its powers conferred by section 3 of the . The notification was in the nature of an executive instruction. The notification was meant to be applied to the specified class of goods. The notification does not say that the exemption would be available only to those specified goods which are specified in the notification. [818F G] (3) The notification is not intended to apply to the specified classes of goods. [819A] (4) The notification merely clarifies the position. It does not alter the position. [820B] (5) The notification cannot be construed as giving effect to the notification dated August 14, 1978. [821C] (6) The notification has to be read along with the notification dated June 16, 1975. The notification is a general one. It is not intended for any particular purpose. It is intended to apply uniformly to all goods which are covered by the notification. The notification must be read as a whole. [822D]
6051: The assessee was a co operative society constituted under the Cooperative Societies Act, 1961. The assessee was engaged in the marketing of cotton and ginned cotton. For rendering services of ginning and pressing cotton, the assessee charged the members a certain amount by way of ginning or pressing charges. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that having regard to the circumstance that the receipts were from members only, that there was a general market for ginning and pressing cotton only and no evidence appeared of any dealing in raw cotton, the ginning activities were to be regarded as an integral part of the marketing activity, and therefore the receipts from those activities were not liable to tax by virtue of section 81(1)(c). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed orders of the Income tax Officer. In second appeal the Income Tax Appel late Tribunal held that having regard t o the circumstances that the receipts are from members only and that there is a general market, the receipts from these activities were not taxable. The Revenue appealed to the High Court contending that having regard tao cation of the proviso to section 81(I)(c), the receipts from ginning and selling were exempt under Section 81(i) (c) of Income Tax Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'agriculture ' has been used in the Explanation to section 2(1)(a) of the Act. It includes the operation of any existing or future business of agriculture or the carrying on of any of the following operations: (i) the cultivation of the land; (ii) the use to which the land is put; (iii) the produce of the land, (iv) the building, machinery, plant, furniture, utensils, implements and other things necessary for the purpose of manufacturing, leather goods or for any other purpose incidental thereto. [560C D] 2. The expression "agricultural produce"
6421: The appellant, a State Government Undertaking, was created by the erstwhile State of Bihar in the year 1948. The re cruitment and conditions of service of the said cadre were governed by the 1939 Rules. In the new set up the cadre of District Engineers was constituted under the 1948 Rules. The re spondents were functioning as Executive Engineers in the Public Works Department. The re gularisation of the services of the respondents was done on the basis of the re commendation of the staffing pattern of the Public Works Depart ment. The respondents challenged the merger order before the Patna High Court which dismissed their writ petitions. The respondents filed appeals against the dismissal of their writ petitions before the Division Bench of the High Court. The Division Bench allowed the appeals and quashed the merger order. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The impugned merger order is not violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. [819B] 1.2 The impugned merger orders are not violative of any statutory rule or regulation. [820C] 1.3 The impugned merger Order is arbitrary and is liable to be quashed. [821D] 1.4 The impugned merger does not violate Article 14 of tile Constitution. [882E] 1.5 The impugned merger has been made in violation of the provisions contained in the 1948 Rules and the 1959 Rules. The impugned merger is contrary to the provisions contained therein. [883F] 1.6 The impugned merger cannot be sustained. [884G H] 1.7 The impugned merger can only be by an executive order. [885A] 1.8 The impugned merger will have no effect whatsoever on the rights of the respondents. [886H] 1.9 The impugned merger would be violative of Article 16(1) of the Constitution inasmuch as it violates Articles 14 and 16(1). [885B] 1:10 The impugned merger could not be justified on the ground that the posts of Assistant Engineers were merged with the cadre of Executive Engineers of the Public Work Department. [881C] 1:11 The impugned merger was not violative of Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the constitution. [880C] 1
6116: The appellant, a mortgagee in possession of the property mortgaged with him by the respondent, filed a suit for redemption on 28.12.1973, contending that he had purchased the property from the original mortgagee and that the sale deed contained an acknowledgment of the right of the mortgagor to redeem the property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the sale was not a fresh starting point for computation of the period of limitation but it was a fresh transaction which was not intended to be a mortgage but only a sale. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The recitals in the document do not serve as an acknowledgement. It merely states that what stands transferred to the purchaser is not only the fight of the mortgagee for recovering the principal amounts and interest according to the mortgage deed (which, as earlier stated, still remained outstanding) but also "the rights and inter est" regarding the redemption of the mortgaged land. [613F G] 2. The recital in the document does not serve as a mere narration of the previous mortgage that had been created on the property. It merely says that what stood transferred to the mortgagee is not only his right of redemption but also the right of re dition of the mortgage money. The recital does not serve any such purpose. The recital is clear enough to show that the right of redemption accrued to the mortgagor on the date of the sale deed i.e. 1.11.19 13. The recital clearly indicates that the right to redeem the mortgaged property was not only the right of redelivery of the mortgaged property but also the rights and inter se rights regarding the redemption thereof. [614A B] 3. The recital made in the document cannot be construed as an acknowledgment within the meaning of section 17(1)(b) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. The recital shows that the right was not only of redemption but of re ssion of the mortgaged lands. [615E F] 4. The recital that the right is not only of rendition of the mortgaged properties but also of rendence of the mortgagor for recovery of the principal amounts due under the mortgage deed is not sufficient to hold that the sale is a fresh transaction. 1597: The appellant Company was a public sector undertaking. It had been in existence for over 20 years and its business was closed down. In the year 1959, the Company applied to the Industrial Court under article 227 of the Constitution for an order directing the payment of gratuity to the employees of the appellant company on certain rates. The Industrial Court held that the Company was in a sound financial position and could easily bear the burden of payment of gratuity at the rate of 1 month 's average wage to be calculated for the period December 1, 1959 to November 30, 1960 to every 515 employee who had to his credit uninterrupted service of not less than five years on termination of his service, except by dismissal on account of misconduct. The Industrial court directed the payment of the gratuity to the Company at the rate 1 month ' 's average wages to be calculated on the basis of the average wage payable to the workmen for the period from December 1, 1958 to November 30 1960. The Company appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The provision for gratuity scheme is not based on any statutory enactment but has been evolved by industrial adjudication as a step towards securing social justice. [519 B] (ii) The provision made in the award for payment of gratuity is not based merely on the capacity of the employer to pay the amount of gratuity but also on the capacity to pay it. The provision for payment of retrenchment compensation is not dependent upon the capacity of an employer to pay or to make payment of gratuity. The provision made for payment of compensation to the workmen at the rate mentioned in the award is not dependent on the capacity or capacity of the industry to pay the gratuity. [520 C D] (iii) The provision in the award regarding payment of gratuity cannot be said to be arbitrary or unreasonable. It is well settled that the power conferred on the State Government under section 3(3)(b) of the Act is administrative in character and does not confer an enforceable right on the workman. The power to fix the amount of compensation is a part of the wide powers given to the State Government by section 3(1). 6094: The appellants, who were dealers in the State of Andhra Pradesh, sold to them the goods mentioned in the First Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. They claimed that they had paid sales tax at the rate of 10 paise per rupee on the sale price of the goods and that they were liable to pay tax at the point of sale. The assessing authority rejected their claim. In appeal the appellate authority upheld the assessment. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions filed by the appellants. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The expression 'sale ' is defined in section 2(g) of the Andhra Pradesh Act as meaning a transfer of property in goods for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration. [310C] 1.2. The definition of 'sale ' in section 2 (g) of Andhra Pradesh Act means a transfer of the property in goods involved in the execution of a works contract whether such transfer, delivery or supply of goods is made in the course of trade or commerce. [311D E] 1.3. The word 'sale ' has been defined in section 3(d) of the Act to mean a transfer of ownership of goods from one person to another in the course or furtherance of business. [312E F] 1.4. The word "sale" in section 2 of the Act includes every kind of transfer of property but does not include a mortgage, hypothecation, charge or pledge. [313A B] 1.5. The word sale ' in section 3 (d) of Andhra Act means a transaction whereby the ownership of goods passes to one or more persons. [314B C] 1.6. 199: The Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to income tax. Section 2(1) of the Act defines "income" as meaning "any income accruing or arising by way of a transfer of capital assets for the purposes of the business or profession". Section 2(2) provides that "incomes which accrue or arise in India shall be deemed to have accrued or arisen in India." Section 13 of the Indian Finance Act, 1950, provided that "income arising from any business connection in India shall not be included in the total income of an assessee unless such business connection is a part of the business of the assessee". The Mysore Legislature passed the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1950. By section 2(3), "income " means "income accruing or arising in India " and "income earned in India ". The Mysore Legislature made a law imposing a tax on the income of the assessee. The Mysore Legislature enacted the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Mysore Act was amended by the Indian Finance (No. 2) Act, 1948, by adding a proviso to section 2(4). The Mysore Act also made provisions for the levy, assessment and collection of income tax and super tax. The Mysore legislature passed the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Ordinance, 1948, which replaced the Indian Income 'tax Act, 1922 and the Mysore Income tax Act. The Mysore Income tax (Second Amendment) Act, 1949, introduced a new section 13A in the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961, providing that "incidence of taxation shall be conclusive proof that the income has been received in India". The Mysore Act again came into force with effect from April 1, 1950. The Mysore General Clauses Act, 1899, was repealed by the Indian IncomeTax Act, 1922 (Act XI of 1922), and the Mysore General Clauses Acts were extended to the State of Mysore by the Indian Independence (Adaptation of Bengal and Punjab Acts) Order, 1948. The Mysore High Court held that the Mysore Act applied to the Mysore Act and that the Mysore Income Tax Act did not apply to the Mysore State. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Mysore Act does not apply to Mysore State. It only applies to the Mysore Income

4302: The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of certain shares in Mitra Prakashan Pvt. Ltd., which had been held by his wife and two sons. In the year 1956, the appellant filed a return of estate duty valuing the estate of his wife as his nominee. The Assistant Controller of Estate Duty did not accept this part of the return and included the shares in Mit ram and the benamidars. The appellant 's appeal before the Appellate Tribunal was dismissed on the ground that the shares in the benami transactions were not benamidar but were merely benamidari properties. The High Court answered questions Nos. 1 and 2 against the appellant holding that the shares were not benami properties. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the shares could not be regarded as having been acquired by the deceased in his own right and that they were not benams. HELD: (i) The shares in the case of a Hindu undivided Hindu family are the property of the joint family and the share scrips in the case cannot be regarded as belonging to the joint family. [675 B] (ii) The shares were not held by the deceased as benamidaries or as benamidar. They were merely benami properties and were not liable to be included in the principal value of the estate passing on his death. [677 D E] (iv) The shares of the deceased in the case were not held as benamdars. The shares were held by his son in law and were held by him as benamdar. 1940: The appellant, a shareholder of the Sangi Bank Ltd., was incorporated in 1945. By the end of April, 1946, the Company was able to find subscribers for 4,860 shares only. In view of section 277(1) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, the company was unable to carry on business unless the subscribed capital was not less than half the authorised capital. In order to comply with the requirements of section 276(1), the directors of the Company decided that they or their nominees would subscribe for a large number of shares. In view Of section 277 (1) of Indian Companies Act 1913, the Company, was unable to pay the amount due to the shareholders. The directors of the company decided that they and their nominees would repay the amount. The directors also agreed that the amount should be paid by the Company on interest at 41/2 per cent per annum and the amount should not be repaid. The directors accordingly issued a notice to the appellant calling upon him to pay the balance amount within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice. The directors further held that the amount of Rs. 1,00,000/ required for the purchase of the shares could not be paid by him as he had not given any guarantee for repayment of the loan. The directors however held that the payment of the amount was not made by the company but by the appellant. The directors therefore directed the appellant to pay the remaining amount of Rs, 1,00.000/ within 15 days failing which the appellant was liable to pay interest at the rate of 41/2% per annum. The directors thereafter issued a notice under section 277 of the Indian companies Act to the appellant asking him to pay a sum of Rs. 2,00, 000/ within 15 day from the date thereof. The appellant filed an application before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution praying for quashing the said notices. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allotment was invalid and that the appellant was not liable to repay the amount as he had failed to

6373: The appellant along with two others were convicted for murdering Kumari Mangala in furtherance of their common intention and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life under the first count and to pay a fine of Rs.2,500 each with default clause and directed both the substantive sentences to run concurrently. The High Court confirmed the conviction of all the convicts but reduced the sentence to seven years rigorous imprisonment. The State appealed against the order of the High Court. The High court did not issue notice to the appellant nor afforded him any opportunity of showing cause against the enhancement while enhancing the sentence. The High Cour t also enjoys the power of revision under Section 397 read with Sec. 401 Cr. The High Co urt does not exercise its revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 r/w Sec. 401 IPC to exercise the power of a Court of Appeal under Section 386(c) of the Code. The High COurt has enjoyed the power of an appellate Court under Section 377 Cr. The question whether the High Court exercises its revisional jurisdiction or not is no longer res integra. In Nadir Khan vs The State (Delhi Administration), [1975] 2 SCC 406 wherein a question was raised that the High Court enjoys the powers of a Court under Section 374 Cr. The Supreme Court held that the High Courts have inherent powers to enhance the sentence even though the sentence may be enhanced by the High Court under Section 376(1) Cr. The Court further observed that the High Cou rts are empowered to direct the public prosecutor to present an appeal to the High Court against the sentence on the ground of its inadequacy. The High Courts have been given the power to act suo motu to enhance the sentences in appropriate cases while exercising its revisional jurisdiction even in the absence of an appeal by the State for enhancement of sentence. 1049: The petitioners, who were the owners of a bull or bullock in respect of which a certificate under section 3(1)(b) had been issued by the Veterinary Officer, who has the necessary technical knowledge, are aggrieved by the order of the State Government imposing restrictions on their right to slaughter. They have also challenged the validity of the Act as being violative of article 19(1)(g). The petitioners contended that the Act was bad for the reason that it imposed unreasonable restrictions on their fundamental rights guaranteed by articles 14 and 19(1) (g) of the Constitution. Held, that the Act is not ultra vires the Constitution. It is well settled that the Act does not infringe any fundamental right guaranteed by article 19(l)(g) of Constitution. The Act imposes restrictions on the right of the petitioners to carry on trade or business and it is not open to the State Government to impose such restrictions on the petitioners ' fundamental right. The Act does not offend against the provisions of article 19 of the Constitution because it imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by article 19. The Act is not discriminatory but is intended to prevent the slaughter of bulls and bullocks. The Act provides for the regulation of slaughter of bull and bullocks and prescribes the conditions subject to which they may be slaughtered. The Act therefore imposes reasonable restrictions upon the right of a person to do business in the matter of slaughtering bulls and calves. The Act thus imposes reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public. The Act, therefore, cannot be said to be invalid merely because it imposes unreasonable restrictions on the fundamental right of the petitioner.

4023: The respondent was a member of the appellant 's Union Board. He had been elected to the Corporation as a Councillor on the basis of his election to the Corporation. 2301: The appellant Society purchased the land in auction sale held under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The land was put to public auction and the highest bidder was declared as the highest bidder. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the acquisition proceedings were mala fide and in fraud of the Act and therefore null and void and that the Government should be directed to acquire the said land. The Trial Court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it on the ground that the Government had not made any enquiry under section 5A before the notification under sec. 6 was issued. In appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that (1) the acquisition proceedings being mala fide and without jurisdiction could not be sustained; (2) the acquisition was mala fide and the Government was entitled to an injunction against the Government taking possession of the land; (3) the acquisition having been made for a Girls ' High School of which the appellant was the prime spirit and the Government had no authority to make the acquisition; (4) the acquisition being mala fide, the Government was not entitled to an order of injunction against the State Government. HELD: (i) The acquisition proceedings were not mala fide. [901 G] (ii) The notification under sec 6 was issued after the amendment of sec. 6 by Act 38 of 1923, which substituted the words "when the ' Local Government is satisfied ' for the words "whereas the Governor is satisfied that the land is required" the notification did not show such satisfaction. The notification under section 6 was issued when the Government had already taken possession of the said land and the appellant had no right to the land. [902 B C] (iii) The notification was bad because the Government had failed to comply with the requirements of the proviso to section 6(1). The notification under s.6 was issued after a lapse of time and the Government could not have invoked the proviso to s.6(1) for the purpose of acquiring the land. The notification was not intended to be a notice to the appellant. [903 A B]
4878: The assessee company was a private limited company. It had gone into liquidation and its assets were taken over by the Official Liquidator under section 4(1) of the . On that date, the official liquidator took charge of the assets and liabilities of the company and a balance sheet as on the same date. In support of the return the assessee contended before the Income tax officer that there could be no liability to super profits tax in respect of a company in liquidation since the formula laid down in the Second Schedule to the Act for calculation of the 'standard deduction ' was inapplicable on account of the fact that a company in winding up is not liable to pay any amount which can be distinctly designated as paid up share capital of the company or as 'reserve ' with respect to which the capital of the Company is to be worked out as provided in Second Schedule to Income tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Tribunal held that after a company has gone into liquidation there cannot be said to be in the hands of the liquidator any amount that can be distinct from the amount actually invested in the assets of the company. The High Court also agreed with the view taken by the Tribunal that after a Company has gone into winding up there cannot be a separate fund of the company for calculating the 'standards deduction '. The High court also agreed with this view. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the Tribunal erred in holding that after a private limited Company is not liable for payment of any amount which could be distinctly described as paid up shares capital of the assessee company or as "reserve" with respect to the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'paid up share capital ' in section 2(d)(i) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, means the sum total of all the liabilities of the assessee including the liability to pay any dividend declared by the assessee. [975 B] 2. The word 'pay ' in section 3(2)(a) of the Act must be construed in its popular sense meaning that the liability to make a payment is not to be read as being one which arises out of an obligation or liability. 3872: The appellant was a tenant of the disputed lands in accordance with the Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, 1932. He was a sub tenant under the Bhopal State. He was holding a civilian post. Therefore, he does not fall within the definition of public servant. [814F G] 5. The appellant being a Public servant he can be removed from service only by the competent authority. [815A] 6. 418: The respondent was charged with an offence under section 7 of the East Punjab Essential Services (Maintenance) Act, 1947. He pleaded guilty to the charge and was convicted by the Magistrate. HELD: (1) The Magistrate had no power to take cognizance after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed for filing a complaint. 1886: The appellant company was a private limited company. The Government of India acquired land belonging to it for the purpose of constructing roads and drains in the area. The Government had requisitioned the land under the Defence of India Rules, 1962. The Government did not pay any compensation for the acquisition of the land but the Government claimed that the land should be restored to it on payment of compensation. The Government contended that the contract was a sham transaction and that the appellant was entitled to the refund of the earnest money deposited by it. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the contract could not be said to have been discharged because of the fact that its performance was rendered unlawful. On appeal the High Court held that the contract being one for the supply of the road and drains, the appellant was not entitled to the return of the earnest amount. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that the appellant had failed to prove that the contract had been terminated by the Government. 2018: The respondents filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that they were the legal heirs of Raj Kaur against the Raja of Faridkot. The Raja was impleaded as defendant No. 1 in the suit and the respondents were added as defendants 2 to 4. The appellants contended that the suit was governed by article 141 of the Limitation Act, 1908, as held by the High Court but either by article 142 or by article 144 and is on that basis barred by time. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit being governed by article 142 of the Limitation act, 1908, the suit was not within time. On appeal the District Judge confirmed the decree. In second appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the first appellate court and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) article 142 of Limitation Act, 1963, applied only when the suit was instituted after the period of limitation prescribed under article 141; (ii) the suit was barred by time because the suit was filed beyond the period of three years from the date of the adoption of the Raja by the Raja of the latter 's estate and that the suit must therefore be deemed to have been instituted on the date when the adoption took place; (iii) the suit having been filed within three years of the death of the Raja, the suit could not be said to be barred by time; (iv) the suit being one for pre emption of the land against the Raja, it was not barred by time since the suit was brought within three years from that date; and (v) the suit had been filed within two years of the adoption and the suit was therefore within time. HELD: (i) Article 142 of the Limitations Act, 1963 applies only where the suit is instituted after the expiry of three years of adoption. [851 G] (a) The suit was not governed by article 143 of the Limitation law. The suit was therefore clearly within time. [852 B] (b) The suit being one which was governed by articles 141 and 142 of the limitation Act, 1908 the suit was within time. The suit having been brought within three year of the adoption, the suit would be within time. It was therefore not barred by limitation

3187: The appellants, who were operating their respective routes in the State of Uttar Pradesh, challenged the validity of the schemes for nationalisation of the routes in question.
