Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The scheme is not a mere proposal but an agreement between the parties. It is only when the State Government has approved the scheme that it can be said that the scheme is a mere proposal. [173E] (a) The scheme does not involve any competition with private operators. The scheme is merely a proposal. It is nothing more than a proposal. The scheme does neither involve any competition nor it involves any competition. [174F] (b) The scheme, therefore, cannot be regarded as a mere proposal because it is not intended to be a mere proposal; it is only a proposal which is intended to be considered by the State. [176A B] (d) The scheme further visualises the termination of the services of the operators including the appellant. The scheme, however, does not involve either the carrying out of any commercial or domestic operations or the carrying out any other operation incidental thereto. [177B C]

3607: The appellant was convicted under section 27(1)(a) of the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949. He was acquitted by the magistrate on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to show cause against his conviction and that he had failed to give any satisfactory explanation for his absence from duty during the period in question. The State appealed to the High Court which dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Explanation indicates that potteries industry includes the manufacture of articles of pottery including the manufacture of the following articles of potteries: (i) plastics; (ii) plasticizers; (iii) rubber; (iv) rubber; and (v) cardamom. It was further contended that the appellant was not given an opportunity of showing cause against his acquittal. HELD : (i) The expression "potteries industry" is used in entry 22 in the Schedule to the Act and the Explanation does not cover the industry of the appellant. [813 E] (ii) The object of the Explanation is to enlarge the meaning of the word 'articles of pottery ' so as to include all possible articles of pottion. [814 F G] (iii) The object is to enlarge those articles of potters which are generally used as a word of extension, but the meaning of a word or phrase is extended when it is said to include articles of potmovie. [815 B C] (iv) The object and scope of the Explanation are to be construed according to their plain grammatical meaning. [816 D]
8: The appellant, a Hindu, was the adopted son of a Hindu undivided family. He executed a will on 13th March, 1905, bequeathing certain properties to his wife and two daughters. The testator died on 25th April, 1905 leaving behind him as his near relations, a widow and two daughters, and a daughter. The testator 's widow gave an authority to her mother to adopt the remaining estate after the death of the testator 's father. The appellant 's claim was resisted by the respondent who contended that there was no intestacy as regards the suit properties after the death, and that under the terms of the will, the testator ' had only one daughter and that the remaining estate vested in the plaintiff as the adopted son and heir of the deceased. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the adoption was valid and that the appellant was entitled to succeed to the estate of the deceased as the adopted child was born after the death. On appeal, the High Court held that the adoption took place after the death and that the property vested in the appellant as the adopted daughter and heir of her husband. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the High Court erred in holding that the appellant had not adopted a son before the death of his father; (ii) the High Courts were wrong in holding that there was a custom which required that a son should be adopted before his death; (iii) the High courts were wrong in thinking that the adoption did not take place after the date of the death of a person who was not a natural guardian but was a minor; (iv) the High court was wrong in holding the adoption to be invalid because the adoption was made after the death when the person who was a major was alive; (v) the High Cour t committed error in holding that a son could not be appointed as a guardian without the consent of the minor and (vi) the High 983 Court was wrong in taking into consideration the fact that the widow was given an authority to adopt a son after the death if she so chose. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that under the will the widow was entitled to get the properties in question in equal shares after the death in preference
2608: The appellant was a citizen of India and was governed by the Goa, Daman and Diu (Administration) Ordinance, 1962. He was in occupation of the said territory since December 20, 1961. On December 19, 1961 he was occupying the said territory for about 450 years. In the meantime, the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 came into force on December 20, 1960. The appellant was arrested and detained under section 3(1)(a) of the Act. The Judicial Commissioner held that the Geneva Convention ceased to apply after the coming into force of the Act and that the Municipal Courts in India could give him no redress against an Act of State. The Judicial commissioner held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Genesis Act did not apply to the appellant as he had been convicted by the Judicial Commissioner and sentenced to imprisonment for more than one year. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Genesissory Conventions were not applicable to the appellant because they were not made applicable to him before the coming into operation of the Act, and the Municipal Courts were competent to issue notices to the parties to show cause why their claims should not be referred to arbitration. [560C D] 2. The Geneva Protocol is not applicable to persons who are in occupied territory. It applies only to persons who have been convicted or charged with offences committed within the limits of the area covered by the Act. [540E F] 3. The Gensisian Act does not apply to persons who were convicted or charged for offences committed outside the limits of India. The Greevia Conventions do not apply to those who were convicted and charged with offences outside India. [541A B] 4. The Great Eastern Ry. of India (Portuguese) Ltd. vs Hooghly Coal Co. Ltd., [1946] A. C. 704, relied on.

The Union raised three demands and served notices on the Deputy Chief Engineer, Major Project, Chambal, Bhopal. The State Government, the first respondent in the appeal refused to refer the matter to the Tribunal by its order dated 15.3.1969. The appellant took the matter before the High Court by filing Miscellaneous Petition No 29/69 for a mandamus to the State Government to refer the dispute to the Tribunal. The High Court allowed the petition and directed the Government to take suitable action under Section 12(5) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court in this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the State Government had by refusing to refer the reference to the Tribunal gave rise to an industrial dispute is no longer res integra. [801 G H] 2. But the Government cannot decline to make a Reference merely because the Government considers that the dispute is not likely to be resolved amicably. [802 A B] 3. The Government can decide the dispute itself or refer it to the Tribunal for adjudication. If the Government decides to refer the case it must do so without delay. [803 D E] 4. The Government is entitled to consider the question whether a reference should be made or not. The Government cannot refuse to make the reference merely on the ground that the dispute does not relate to the dispute which is pending before the Tribunal. [804 F] 5. The Government could have decided the dispute itself but it did not do

2081: The appellant Lakhan was convicted under sections 326/149, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years each. The High Court confirmed the conviction of Lakhan but reduced the sentence imposed upon him by the trial court to a period already undergone. The State Government preferred an appeal against the acquittal of Lakhan before the High Court which allowed the appeal of the appellant on the ground that he had been acquitted by the trial Court on charges under sections 326, 302/149 and 307/149 IPC. The High court held that it was competent to it in the appeal preferred by the appellant to alter the conviction of the appellant under sections 326 and 307/34, I. P. C. and regard being had to the gravity of the offence, the High Court maintained the sentence imposed on Lakhan. The State appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that he had not been acquitted by a single charge under section 302, I.p.C., but on the other hand he was convicted under section 307, I.PC. and sentenced accordingly. 3944: The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of tea. [795C] (3) The expression employed in Rule 2 is not confined merely to the payment of salary or wages to an employee but includes all such other allowances and perquisites as may be admissible to him in accordance with the rules applicable to him. 2337: The appellant was a member of the Bombay Medical Service Class and as such was an employee of the State of Maharashtra. He was posted at the Civil Hospital, Ahmedabad and on February 18, 1950, he was in charge of the Medico Legal Section of that hospital. Rathod as well as the representation of the appellant to the Government made by his letter dated February 1, 1950, requested for the suspension of the appellant and to withhold full remuneration for the period of suspension under Rule 151 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The appellant was suspended from service with effect from February 18, 1951. On March 14, 1952, the appellant made a representation to the Government praying that he should be reinstated in service. The Government applied to the High Court for leave to appeal against the decision if the High Court and on the application being rejected, the Government applied to this Court for special leave to appeal. The High Court held that the appellant had inherent power to suspend the appellant and directed him to be placed under suspension pending further orders from the date of the receipt of the memorandum. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the order of suspension passed against the appellant was not illegal or unjustified. The order of suspension did not amount to punishment within the meaning of article 311(2) of the Constitution. It could only be made after the enquiry into the charges against the appellant had been completed and before the report of the Enquiry Officer had been submitted to the Government.
2405: The respondent brought a suit for pre emption of the land in dispute, which was sold under a sale deed dated February 6, 1942. The case of the respondent was that there was such a custom of pre emption prevailing in the whole of the city of Benaras and therefore he was entitled to pre empt the property sold which was a khandar (i.e. a house in ruins) and also as a shafi i khalit (i. e. a house of the town of Benarasi. The trial court held that there was a custom of predominance in the city of Banaras and that the respondent was entitled to the pre emption. The High Court allowed the appeal and granted a decree for pre emotion. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the custom of preemption had not been proved by the respondent and that the High Court should have decreed the suit. HELD: (1) The respondent could not be said to have any right to sue because he was not a resident of Calcutta. [558 F] (2) The respondent was not a tenant but a lessee. He was entitled to a lease hold land or parjoti land. The respondent was entitled only to a leasehold land. [569 G H] (3) The respondent had no right to sue. The respondent could only sue for pre emission. [560 A B] (4) The respondent did not claim any right to pre emption nor did he claim any right in respect of the land. [570 C D] (5) The respondent 's case was that there were two customs of pre emulsion in the city. One is a rule of law and the other is a rule in equity. The respondent has failed to prove that there was any custom of preemmiss ion in the city or that the respondent had any right to enforce the custom. [571 E F] (6) The respondent cannot be said to be a tenant. [572 F]
3961: The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police in the Uttar Pradesh Police Service. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been found guilty of misconduct by an enquiry officer appointed under the Police Act, 1861. The order of dismissal was challenged before the High Court on the ground (1) that the order of dismissal did not amount to punishment and (2) that it was an order of termination simpliciter passed in accordance with the rules applicable to temporary government servants. Held, that the order terminating the respondent 's services was not made by way of punishment but was an order which affected his future career. The order was not one of punishment because it related to the conduct of the respondent as a Sub Inspector. The order merely stated that the respondent 'was being discharged from service without any departmental enquiry. The order did not amount either to punishment or to a reflection on the competence of the authority passing it. The order could be said to have been made in the exercise of the power conferred by section 7 of the Police Act and the order was not an order of discharge simpliciter.
40: The appellants were charged with offences under sections 147, 148 and 302/149 I.P.C. for causing the death of one B. B. Sinha. The prosecution case was that on the night between 29th November, 1949, a mob of about fifty persons came on to the field armed with ballams, lathis and other weapons and that the first appellant Logendranath Jha, who was leading the mob, demanded a settlement of all outstanding disputes with the complainant and that the complainant refused to do so. The appellants pleaded not guilty to the charge and claimed trial. The Sessions Judge convicted the appellants under section 302/34 I.P., I.P,.C. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the convictions but reduced the sentence to one year 's R.I. The appellants preferred an appeal to this Court by special leave. Held, that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of acquittal passed by the Sessions Judge. The High Courts should be slow in interfering with the order passed by the Session judge. The High courts are not competent to reappraise evidence or to substitute their own view as to the credibility of witnesses. The High court has power to review the evidence and come to its own conclusion. In the present case, the Sessions Judge had taken into consideration the entire evidence and arrived at his finding of guilt against the appellants. The High 'Court could not have interfered with the order made by the Sessions judge.
1848: The appellant was granted a right to cut trees in certain demarcated areas of certain forests of the Zamindari on payment of a sum of Rs. 7,131/8/ . The appellant started cutting the trees and felling them under the powers vested in the State. The forest authorities took action against the appellant for cutting the trees but the appellant did not pay any heed to his request. The forest officers seized the timber from the appellant and removed it. The forest officer thereupon issued a notice to the appellant to remove the timber within 15 days. The appellant replied that he had no right to the timber and that he could only do so if he wanted to cut the timber. The forest officials then proceeded to take action against the forest officer. The forest department then filed a suit for recovery of the timber and the forest revenue. The suit was decreed by the trial court. (b) of section 5 (aa) was applicable to the case. Held, that the words "or any other person" used in cl. (a) of section 4(1) must be construed as including the appellant who was entitled to the trees in question. The word "or" in cl. 2(a) means "any other person". The word "person" is defined in section 2(2) of the Act to include a person who has been granted a right of way or prescription to cut timber. The word 'person ' in cl. 1(a) includes a person who is entitled to the rights of way or to the produce of such land. The word person' in cl. I(a) does not include a person whose right to cut or cut timber is conferred upon him by the Act. The word `person ' in clause (a) includes every person who has a right to the trees or to the forest produce. The word, 'person ' occurring in cl. II(a) must mean a person who possesses a right to fell or cut
2932: The respondent was appointed as a member of the Indian Police Service on 25th January, 1937 and at the material time he was holding the substantive rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police in Bihar. In June 1962 he was posted at Ranchi. He was transferred to Patna and appointed as Special Officer, Political, General and Transport Department on July 23, 1964. On July 23, 1963 he was posted as Special Officer Political, General & Transport Department on the allegation that there was a prima facie case made out against him. The Government of India after carefully considering the available material and having regard to the nature of the charges and circumstances of the case, came to the conclusion that it was necessary and desirable to place the respondent under suspension. The respondent filed his writ petition challenging the order of suspension contending that since departmental enquiry had been initiated against him and the charge sheet had been served upon him, the order placing him under suspension was not proper. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the order of detention was not proper; (ii) the order was passed without application of mind; and (iii) the order being an administrative one, it could be challenged only by way of a suit or a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. HELD: (1) The order of suspension is not a punishment but is merely a continuation of the earlier order of suspension which has already been set aside by the court. [717 D] (2) The order does not suffer from any infirmity. It is not a mere formality. It is a punitive action. It is based on the subjective satisfaction of the authority concerned. [718 E F] (3) The order is not a final order. It is open to the Government to pass an order placing the officer under suspension if it is satisfied that it is necessary to do so in public interest. [719 G H]
903: The assessee was a Baroda State and its income from investments in shares, securities etc., was exempt under section 10(2) of the Income tax Act. The assessee claimed that it had a permanent establishment in India and its income was taxable under the Income tax law. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee was not entitled to any concession under the Merged States (Taxation Concessions) Order, 1949, with regard to the net dividend income of Rs. 47,120. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In appeal the Tribunal held that the assessee had a permanent Establishment in India and the income from investments was taxable under section 10 (2) of Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The assessee is entitled to the benefit of the Concessions Order applied to the assessee. [249E] (ii) The assessee has a permanent establishment and its income is taxable under the provisions of the Income 'tax Act. [240B] (iii) The assessee cannot be said to have a permanent establishment or an establishment in India. [245C] (iv) The assessee was entitled to the benefits of the Concession Order applied to it. [246D]

5544: The appellant was a partnership firm. It had taken on lease certain lands for the purpose of running a tea estate. The Corporation, however, invited tenders for the sale of the property. The tender notification was published in the newspaper. The appellant submitted its bid and offered to purchase the property for Rs.1,20,000. The Corporation also invited tenders for sale of the properties. The Corporation itself had to purchase the properties for about Rs.1.65 lakhs. The Corporation therefore could not take possession of the property for about Rs 1.65 lakhs and it was only after the auction sale was held that the Corporation decided to sell the property to P.M. Gumraj Plantations. The Corporation ultimately invited tenders for this property. The Corporation accepted the highest offer and decided to sell it to P. M. Gumram Plantation. The Corporation cannot lightly assume that the action taken by the Government is unreasonable or without public interest because as we stated above, there are a large number of policy considerations which must necessarily weigh with the Government in taking action and therefore, the Court would not strike down governmental action as invalid on this ground, unless it is clearly satisfied that the action is unreasonable or not in public interest. [1084E F] 2. The Corporation having accepted the highest bid, the Corporation thought it proper to accept the highest bid. The Corporation acted bona fide in accepting the highest bid and the
245: The petitioners who were the Rulers of certain Indian States, entered into an agreement with the Government of India for the formation of a new State in the United Provinces. Under this agreement each Ruler agreed to be bound by the covenant and the provisions of the Constitution relating to the administration of the State. The agreement was signed by the Secretary of State in Council and the Secretary of States. The petitioners contended that the agreement was not binding on them because it was made under the authority of the sovereign authority of the State and was not binding upon them as against the Government of the State; and that the agreement did not bind them. Held, that the agreement could not be enforced against the Government and the petitioners were entitled to succeed. The agreement did not purport to create any new rights or obligations between the parties and did not affect the rights of the parties. The agreement merely embodied the terms of the agreement which were binding on the parties. It did not alter the nature of the rights of any party nor did it change the character of the agreements. The agreement only provided for the continuance of the existing laws and not the rights of individuals.
5358: The petitioners in these petitions for review of the Judgment of this Court dated December 21, 1987 were appointed as Chairman and Vice Chair man respectively. They challenged the appointment of the Chairman and Vice Chairman of the Administrative Tribunal on the ground that they had not been qualified to be a Judge of the High Court. The petitioners contended that the observations made by Bhagwati, CJI in his judgment should be read as obiter and should not be treated as binding precedents. The petitioners also contended that the appointments of the Chairman, Vice Chairman and members of the Administrative Tribunals should be made by the concerned government only after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. Dismissing the Review Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The observations made by the Supreme Court in the case of the Union of India vs N.C. Paliwal & Ors., ; , are not intended to lay down any general proposition of law but are meant to emphasise the need for prompt action to be taken by the Government in appointing the Chairman, a Vice Chairman and a Member of the Administrative Tribu nal. [575F] 2.1. In the case of recruitment to the Central Administrative Tribunal the appropriate course would be to appoint a High Powered Selec tion Committee headed by a sitting Judge of the Supreme Court to be nominated by the Chief Justice. The learned Attorney General has drawn our attention to the observations made in the case in which the Supreme Court observed that the appointment of Chairman, Vice Chair men and members of Administrative Tribunals should not be made by a High Power Committee consisting of a sitting Judge or an Additional Judge of the same court. [566A B]
3956: The appellant was a research scholar and asked to give his consent for the investigation of the case. He filed an application before the Magistrate praying that he may be given custody of the two pillars to enable him to make a detailed study. The Magistrate rejected the said prayer on the ground that the investigation was not complete and the report had been submitted by the police after investigation. The High Court allowed the appeal, holding that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to start a fresh investigation under the Criminal Procedure Code. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the Magistrate should have taken cognizance of the offence and should have directed the investigation to be conducted by the Police in accordance with law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Magistrate has no power to direct the investigation to the Police. [928C] 2. The Magistrate cannot take cognizance of the offences without the permission of the Court. [929E] 3. The Magistrate is not bound to take cognizance of any offence except upon a complaint in writing made by the Public Prosecutor. The Magistrate can only take cognizance if the complainant satisfies the Court that there are sufficient grounds for proceeding with the case. [930F] 4. The appellant then moved the High Court by way of a writ petition challenging the validity of the order of the State Government. 59: The petitioner 's fundamental rights under article 19(1) (f) and article 31(1) of the Constitution were infringed by the Central Bank of India Ltd. a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and having its registered office at Bombay, and its registered office was situated in Bombay. 5172: The appellant was the owner of a flat in a building owned by the respondent. The appellant contended that she had no other reasonably suitable accommodation to occupy the said flat. The learned single judge dismissed the eviction petition holding that the landlady had not reasonably suitable accommodation. The appellant preferred an appeal before the Division Bench which allowed the same. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the land lord had bona fide need of the premises for his residence and that he had no other reasonable suitable accommodation. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The landlady in this case had two other reasonably suitable residential accommo dents. The land lord has been given sufficient time to vacate the premises. [285F G] 2. The landlord had let out the premises to the tenant. The tenant had left the premises for her residence and the land lords were living there. The landlord could have easily vacated the premises if he was the owner thereof. But the land lor is not so. 49: The appellant firm was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of cloth. In October, 1941, the parties entered into a contract to supply to the appellant bales of cloth of certain specifications manufactured by the New Victoria Mills, Kanpur, and the Raza Textile Mills, Ramput, for the supply of the goods to the appellant. The respondent firm undertook to deliver to the appellant the goods contracted for. The appellant supplied the goods to it from time to time and the respondent firm also paid the price of the goods. The appellant 's claim for damages was resisted by the respondent firm contending that the performance of the contract had been frustrated by circumstances beyond their control and hence the appellant 's suit must fail. Held, that the appellant ' s claim must fail. The agreement between the parties provided that the appellant should deliver to the respondent firm the goods contracted to be delivered by the respondent. The agreement did not say that the delivery would take place only if the appellant agreed to do so. The agreement merely stated that the appellant was to deliver the goods at the end of each day of the month. The agreement further provided that the goods were to be delivered within 15 days after the expiry of the said period. The agreement was not an express term of the contract but was a mere camouflage to avoid payment of damages. The agreement expressly provided that the respondent firm was to deliver to it the goods contracted by the appellant. It was not necessary to have the contract specifically performed or to have been performed. The agreement, therefore, could not be construed as conferring upon the respondent firm any right to demand damages for breach of the contract.

1859: The assessee was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It purchased a building and made substantial alterations, additions and improvements therein. 2736: The appellants, who were the sons of one Kothandaraman Naidu, adopted by him on 26th January 1955, as his son and partitioned the property in dispute. The adoption was challenged by the respondents on the ground that the adoption was not valid under Hindu Law. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the adoption had been validly made. On appeal, the High Court held that the adoption having been proved, it was not necessary to obtain consent of the nearest sapindas of the family. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The adoption was valid under Hindu law. [502 B] (ii) The adoption is a condition precedent for the validity of the adoption. It is not necessary that there should be an express or implied consent from the near relatives of the deceased. [503 C] (iii) The adoption has to be proved by the evidence of the person who claims it. If the person claiming the adoption is not available, then the adoption cannot be said to have been validly made unless the person claiming it is available. [504 D] (iv) The adoption must be in accordance with the custom of the community to which the parties belong. [505 E] (v) The adoption can only be challenged on the grounds mentioned in section 16(1)(c) of the Act. [506 F]
1201: The respondent was granted a lease of the village in 1787. The appellants were granted a lease for a period of 20 years from 1787 to 1918. The respondent 's case was that the village had been granted as bilmakta with a fixed sum which was payable in perpetuity for any land granted by the Ruler or the jagirdar to any person. The respondent claimed that the village was granted as bhudkasht and therefore the respondent was entitled to possession of the village as well as to recover mesne profits at the rate of Rs. 931 12 0 0 per year. The trial court held that the village being a bilmark, the grant was not a permanent lease but only a permanent lease. The High Court on appeal reversed this decision and decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the village having been granted as a bhud kasht, the grant could not be regarded as a permanent lease and could not be treated as a permanent grant. HELD: (i) The grant of the village was not a bhusa bazar but a bhukta. It was a bhoomic arrangement between the parties and the grant was made under the terms of the grant. [1917 D] (ii) The grant was not an assignment of the bhudki right of the bhayats to the respondent. The grant was merely a bhuggi contract. The grant did not create any interest in the bhusarai estate. The grant itself was a bhikarari. The grant is not a bhiyanyadraiya. The grant does not confer any title on the bhuktas. The grant has nothing to do with the bhogis. The grant in favour of the respondent was not a grant of permanent nature. [1920 C E] (iii) The grant in question was not a lease but a bhuinhari. The grant being a bhokta, the grant must be regarded as one of permanent character. [1921 G]

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for damages for breach of contract and claimed damages to the extent of Rs. 3,00,000. The appellant contended that the respondent had committed breach of the contract by not supplying the stipulated quantity of timber under the contract and as such claimed damages to that extent. The Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit holding that the respondent was entitled to recover damages for breach committed by it of the contract. On appeal the High Court held that the respondent could not be allowed to claim damages for breach in respect of excess quantity of timber alleged to have been delivered and that the respondent would be entitled to recover the amount claimed from the appellant. 3044: The Andhra Pradesh Backward Classes Commission was appointed by the State Government under section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Backward Class Commission Act, 1983. The Commission submitted its report on June 20, 1970. The Commission recommended that the reservation of 30% of seats in professional colleges for Backward Classes be made in favour of the backward classes and that the percentage or proportion of such reservation should not exceed 50%. The Commission also recommended that the percentage of reservation to persons belonging to the Backward Classes should not exceed 40% of the total number of seats in the professional colleges. The Commission also suggested that the percentage should not exceed 25% of the available seats in the State. The Commission further recommended that the seats reserved for the Backward Classes may be filled up by the candidates belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes. The Commission accordingly fixed the percentage of reservations at 25% of seats. The Commission however, did not recommend any reservation for the Backward Class. The State Government thereupon issued a notification dated September 23, 1970, declaring the said reservation as invalid. The appellants who were members of the Scheduled Castes, Backward Classes and Backward Classes respectively filed writ petitions challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the reservation was valid. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the reservation was not in excess of the prescribed limit; (ii) the reservation is not in excess or beyond the prescribed limits; (iii) the reservation has been made in excess of 50% of the prescribed percentage; (iv) the reservation in educational institutions maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds is not violative of Article 14 of the Constitution; (v) the reservation of seats in educational institutions is not violative either Article 15(1) or Article 16(2); (vi) the reservation cannot be made in excess or contrary to the prescribed percentage of reservation; (vii) the reservation can only be made in respect of the seats in the educational institutions maintained or aided by the State; (viii) the reservation could be made in the case of seats in any educational institution maintained or aided wholly or substantially financially by the State and (ix) the reservation would not violate Article 16(4). 3896: The assessee was a contractor. He supplied certain goods to the Government for being used in the execution of works under the contract. The Government had agreed to pay him a sum of Rs. 70,000 as compensation for loss of profit and the balance of Rs. 80,000 was payable by way of cash payment. The assessee claimed that the cost of the stores/materials supplied by the Government should be added to the figure of cash payments received by the assessee on the ground that the stores/ materials supplied by the military authorities were 'muni ties ' and not 'rules '. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the cost or value of the stores supplied by the government could not be added to its total cash payments received from the Department under the contract for the purpose of estimating the income or profits derived by the contractor from such contracts. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the view of the taxing authorities. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the cost incurred by the assessee for the stores/articles supplied by the State to the assessee was not to be included in the total cash payments made by the assessee to the contractor but was to be added to his total cash payments which would have been available to the contractor if he had actually purchased the stores/ material. The cost of the materials supplied by a contractor is not to be added either to the total cash receipts received by the contractor or to the amount of cash payments made to the contractor by the Government. The cost must be determined with reference to the terms of contract between the parties. [206A] 5. The cost has to be added back to the total price paid by the contractor. [207B C] 6. 5965: The respondent assessee was a company which had been carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of cotton yarn. In its assessment for the year 1959 60, the Income tax Officer disallowed the claim in respect of the loss incurred by it in the sale of shares held by it. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the said order. The Tribunal took the view that the sale had been affected only to enable the assessee to claim the loss and could not be allowed as genuine. The Tribunal also relied upon the circumstances that the shares had been sold to a company which was an allied concern of the assessee, that is, be longing to the Thapar group. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the Revenue that the sale was effected with the object of earning profits and that the profit was earned by the assessee in the ordinary course of business. The Tribunal further pointed out that there was nothing to show that the purchase of these shares had anything to do with the control of the companies concerned. The Tribunal referred to the facts that the shares were purchased on 22nd February, 1958 and were sold on 31st March, 1959. The Tribunal found that the sale price was shown at Rs.2.50 per share whereas the market quotation on 31st December, 1958 was Rs.8.06 per share. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that the sale of the shares had taken place in the normal course of business and that the sale did not have any nexus with the control or management of the companies. The Tribunal accordingly dismissed the appeal preferred by the Revenue. The High Court in reference to the Tribunal held that the sale took place in the ordinary way of business and the sale was not affected merely to enable the asses see to claim the losses. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue: (i) that the Tribunal had failed to take into consideration the fact that the shares in question were purchased in the normal mode of business; (ii) that the sale in the instant case was effected with a view to earn profits and that it was not a trading loss and it was not the case of the Department that in arriving at its decision the Tribunal had taken into consideration any irrelevant material or failed to take note of any relevant material or failed in taking into consideration any relevant material; (iii)
4035: The appellant was detained under section 3 of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. He challenged his detention on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in a case registered against him under the Bombay Prohibition Act and that there were no materials to show that he had indulged in any anti social activities. The High Court rejected the contention and held that the detaining authority must always consider the possibility of launching a criminal prosecution if it relies on certain facts for which prosecution may be launched or may have been launched. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of detention was bad because the grounds of detention served on the appellant contained an irrelevant material and that the detaining authorities did not apply their mind to the vital question whether the appellant could be prosecuted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The object of preventive detention is not to punish a man for having done something but to intercept him when such intention cannot be attributed to the detaining authority. [576C] 1.2. The purpose of preventive detention being different from punitive detention, the same offence can be said to have been committed by the detenu while acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. [577E] 2.1. If the detaining authority has failed to consider the possibility or likelihood of launching criminal prosecution, then the order of preventive detention would be vitiated. [578F] 2.2. It is not necessary that the detaining Authority should consider the possibility for launching a prosecution. The fact that the detaining authori ties are aware of the existence of the fact that the person who is alleged to have indulged in the activity of smuggling goods is likely to be convicted, will not make the order of detenti ng invalid. [579G H; 580A]
4920: The appellant was a tenant of the land in question. He had been cultivating the land for more than 30 years and had been paying rent to the State Government. In the year 1956, he applied for permission to terminate his tenancy on the ground that he required the land for personal cultivation. The Collector granted him permission but the appellant did not vacate the land. The appellant filed an appeal before the Commissioner who dismissed it. Thereafter, he filed a revision petition before the Financial Commissioner which was also dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by the High Court holding that the provisions of section 7A were applicable to the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The provisions of section 8(2)(a) are mandatory and they must be strictly complied with. [901 B] (2) The Act does not provide for any special procedure for termination of tenancy. It is only when the tenancy is terminated under section 8(3), that the tenancy may be terminated. [902 C D] (3) The Act provides for two grounds for termination of the tenancy namely, (i) that the land comprising the tenancy has been reserved by the landowner for his personal cultivation; and (ii) that the landowner owns standard acres of less land and the land falls within his permissible limit. [903 A B] (4) The Act clearly indicates that the tenancy can be terminated on any grounds mentioned in secs. 7, 7A and 8. [904 E F] (5) The Act makes no provision for the termination of the lease except in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Act does nothing more than make provision for the determination of the amount payable as compensation for the termination or the reduction of the area of the tenancy. [905 G H]
6588: The respondents were tried for the murder of one Partap Singh and causing injuries to others. The trial court convicted them under section 302, I.P.C., and sentenced them to imprisonment for life and ordered to pay a sum of Rs.500 each under section 148, I. P. C. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence of fine to Rs.500. The State appealed against the acquittal of the respondents. The High court acquitted the respondents on the ground that there was no prior enmity between the parties. The High 'Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish the motive for the crime. The High. Court also found that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable. The High, Court further held that the evidence regarding the quarrel which took place in the field of the two parties was not corroborated by any independent witness. The High: Court also found the evidence of PW 1 to be unreliable. The High Com missioner also found that there was some tendency on the part of the prosecution witness to exaggerate matters. The High Commissioner also found that it was not possible to believe that the deceased had been murdered by the accused persons. The High Commission also found that no motive could be attributed to the accused persons for committing the murder. The High Commi ssioner also came to the conclusion that the evidence about the quarrel which had taken place in the fields of the two sides was unacceptable. The State appeal was dismissed by this Court. [666A B] 2.1 The High Court was wrong in acquitting the respondents of the major charge under section 302 read with section 149, I.p.C. and the High Court committed an error in convicting the respondents of offences under sections 304 Part I, I.PC. [667B] 2.2 The High Court erred in reversing the judgment of the Sessions Judge. [668E] 3.1 The view taken by the High Court is contrary to the evidence on record. It is difficult to accept the reasoning given by the High
4620: The petitioner, a member of the Indian Revenue Service, was an intelligent and talented girl who had been friends for over thirty years. She was an intelligence officer in the Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital. She was a member of a family consisting of her husband and two minor children. She was also a member of an intelligant and talented lady. She was married to one Gurinder Kaur. She was living with her parents in a rented house at Delhi. She was employed as a teacher in a school run by the Delhi Administration. She was promoted to the post of Assistant Commissioner of Police. She was posted in the office of the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Delhi. She had been visiting the office of Deputy Commissioner of Delhi every day. She was told that she would be sent back to Delhi only if she wanted to make a statement. She was asked to go back to Delhi on the next day. She refused to do so. She was then taken to the hospital where she died. She was charged under section 304A IPC. The trial court convicted the petitioner under section 304B IPC and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for three years. On appeal the High Court acquitted the petitioner holding that there was no evidence to show that the petitioner had ever demanded dowry from the deceased. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the presumption under section 113A Cr. P.C. is not available to the prosecution; (ii) the petitioner was not guilty of any offence under section 304 B IPC; (iii) the petitioner had been falsely implicated in the case because he was a member in the family of his wife and was a close relative of the deceased. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1. The presumption under section 114 A of the Evidence Act is a weak kind of evidence. It is a rule of prudence which has to be kept in mind before it can be used against the accused. [116E] 1.2. The presumption is rebuttable. The burden of proof lies upon the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [117F G] 1.3. The presumption cannot be raised against the petitioner merely because he was not found guilty of the charge. [118G] 1.
3175: The respondent was appointed as Professor and Head of the Department of the University of Jammu and Kashmir on probation for a period of two years. He was allowed to function as Professor and his probation was extended for a year by the Vice Chancellor under section 13(4) of the Ordinance which had already been replaced on November 10, 1969 by the Jammu and Kashmir Universities Act, 1969. The respondent 's services were terminated by the ViceChancellor under section 13 (4) of Ordinance (which had already been substituted on November 10. 1969). The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order terminating his service. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent 's appointment was not made by the University Council but by the Council constituted under Ordinance (a) of the said Ordinance. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. The respondent was entitled to continue in service till he attained the age of superannuation. [175F] 1.2. The respondent could not be treated as an employee of the University Council or its Board of Management. [176A] 1.3. The respondent has no right to claim continuance in service beyond the age of retirement. [177B] 1.4. The respondent is entitled to continue up to the age of 60 years. [178C] 1.5. The respondent cannot claim any right to continue in employment beyond the age prescribed by law. [179E] 1.6. The respondent having been appointed by the Vice Chancellors of the University, it would be unreasonable to hold that he was not qualified to be appointed as a professor. [170D] 1.7. The respondent being a permanent employee of the State Government, he could not have been transferred to the post of Professor and Head. [171G] 1.8. The respondent had no right to continue to work as Professor and head of the Department. [172H] 1.9. The respondent did not have any right to claim continuation in service beyond 58 years. [180B] 1:10. The respondent does not have any vested right to continue as Professor and HOD of the Department until he attains the age of 58
6448: The petitioner purchased property bearing No. 112 113, Gautam Nagar, Delhi at an auction conducted by the Income Tax Department. The purchasers thereafter attempted to get the property registered by the T.R.O. on 13.4.1988. On 14.4.88 a certificate of sale was issued by the T R O. to the petitioner. On 14th April 1988 a certificate of purchase was issued by T R O to the petitioner and the sale confirmed on 13.04.1988. The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the sale certificate and the confirmation of the sale. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the petitioner had not been able to show any valid reason for non compliance with the requirements of section 84 (4) of the Act. Hence the present appeal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A copy of the certificate of sale sent to the petitioner by the TRIDA is liable to be forwarded to the Sub Registrar within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the whole or any part of the immovable property comprised in the certificate is situate. [183F] 2.2 The Collector was requested to inform the Sub Registrar about the registration of the document. The original of the sale Certificate should have been endorsed to the Sub Registry but it was actually sent to the Sub Regi strate. The original was liable for stamp duty and a further duty of Rs. 4.50 was also chargeable on the copy of the sale cert ificate to be forwarded. [185G H] 3.1 The Collector was directed to inform the TRID u/s 89(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961, to make necessary entries in the registers regarding the sale of the above immovable property on the basis of the copy of sale certificate sent to him by the T rnissioner. [186A B]
1915: The respondents were the sons of Lingayya who died in 1938. Lingayyya was a Sudra by caste and the first respondent was a Brahmin by caste. After the death of Lingaya, the appellants filed an application for maintenance under section 125 Cr. P.C. before the Subordinate Judge, but the Subordinate Judge dismissed it on the ground that the respondents ' claim for maintenance was barred by limitation. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the relevant provisions of the Hindu law as it stood prior to the commencement of the Act applied only to the estates of Hindus dying after the commencement of that Act and that the right of the respondents to maintenance during their lifetime under the Hindu law was not affected by the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The respondents are not entitled to claim any maintenance from the estate of Linga. [801 B] (2) The first respondent is not a Dasi and the second, third and fourth respondents are not Dasiputras of Lingayat. The first respondent being a Brahmin, the connection between Lingayyan and the first respondents was not connected with the estate of the deceased Lingayyam. [802 C D] (3) The first appellant was not a Dastidar or a Shebait. He was merely a Shebaiti. He was not a Shebaitship. [803 A B] (4) The first respondents were not entitled to maintenance under the Hindu Law. [804 E F]
6061: The petitioners were serving as Subedar Major in the Assam Rifles. They were allotted land, grant of title deeds in respect of the allotted land, facilities for movement by air to and from Mohanbari, freedom to develop the allotted areas, grant of advance by way of loans, provision of marketing facili ties for disposal of surplus produce, guaranteed supply of essential commodities and provision of the basic require ments of life for the purpose of encouraging the all round economic development of the area. The petitioners contended that the scheme was not a one time settlement but it was a one time measure and that the scheme should be made applicable only to those who had been allotted land, grants of title deeds and other benefits which were available to them under the scheme. The petitioners also relied on correspondence exchanged between them and the authorities of the State Government and of the Central Govern ment and submitted that the scheme could not be implemented without the approval of the Central Government. The petitioners further stated that the scheme would be implemented after the approval of Central Government. In the counter affidavit filed by the respondents, it is stated that the Scheme was approved by the Central Government and the same was published in the Gazette of India. It is stated that after the approval, the scheme was notified in the Gazette and thereafter the scheme was published in various newspapers. It is further stated that after considering the report of the Director General Assam Rifles and the decisions taken by the Central Governmen t, the Central Government passed an order approving the scheme. It is also stated that the Central Government has no objection if the scheme is implemented. The petitioners have also relied on letters written by the Director General, Assam Rifles to the effect that the scheme will be implemented after approval of the Government. The respondents have also produced before this Court the letter dated 20th February, 1987 addressed by the Director, Assam Rifl es to the Deputy Secretary (NE), Ministry of Home Affairs, New Delhi. The petitioners contend that the scheme is not a onetime settlement but it is a one time scheme and that the Central Gov ernment has no objection to the implementation of the scheme. On behalf of the petitioners, it was contended that the Scheme should be made effective from the date of its publication in the Gazette. Dismissing the writ petition,
795: The appellant, a Hindu, was the owner of certain properties in Tirunelveli District. He made an application to the District Court under section 3 of the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, for declaring that the appellant was entitled to be declared as the sole trustee of the deity and to ask for accounts of the income from the properties. The District Judge held that the appellant had not been able to prove his title to the properties and dismissed the application. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the suit properties were not the personal or private properties of the appellant and that there was no need to join the deity because of an averment by the defendants that the temple was a public one and the properties were public religious endowments. Held, that the appellant 's case was that the deity was a family or private one and the property was not the personal property of the appellant. The appellant could not be said to have been estopped from making such a claim. The appellant was not bound by the declaration made by the District Judge. The appellant did not make any statement in the plaint that the temple belonged to him. The appellant had not produced any evidence to show that he was a member of the family of the appellant or that the temple belongs to him.
2383: The appellants were registered dealers in respect of the goods sold by them to various parties. They had sent their goods to their depots outside the Province of Uttar Pradesh, for example, to Calcutta in the State of West Bengal. The sales tax authorities assessed the outside sales of all the appellants to sales tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, as they were liable to pay sales tax on the turnover of sales effected within the Province of West Bengal at the rate of 3 pies per rupee subject to a rebate of 5% under section 5 of the Act and certain other adjustments. The appellants filed appeals before the Revising Authority under section 9 of the Act. The revising authority held that the out of State sales would be taxable (1) if the goods were manufactured or produced in the Province of U.P., and (2) if the sale was made to a dealer who had not been registered in the State. The appellants took the matter in revision to the High Court which upheld the order of the Revising authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sales tax authorities were entitled to make a reference under section 9(1)(b) of the Act, and that the provisions of section 11 of the Act did not apply to the case. HELD : (i) The sales tax law was a taxing statute and the provisions of the Act applied to the facts of the case. [514 D] (ii) The sales Tax Officer was right in holding that the out levied sales tax was leviable on the turnover relating to the goods sold within the Province. [515 E F] (iii) The sales of the appellants were exempt from sales tax under section 2(h) of the U. P. Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1948. The appellants could not therefore be said to have purchased the goods from outside the Province. The sales of goods were not exigible to sales tax. [516 A B] (iv) The sales were not ex ciseive but were exigible to tax. [504 C] (v) The sales in question were not ex gribe d to the appellants. [503 G H] (vi) The sales are exigible to Sales Tax. [50
183: The appellant was arrested in pursuance of an extradition warrant issued by the Regional Com missioner of the United State of Rajasthan who is the principal officer representing the Crown in the territory of the United States. He was then sent to jail for a period of one month and was released on bail. On his return he was served with a notice under section 7 of the Extradition Act, 1962, requiring him to show cause why he should not be committed to prison for failure to pay the sum of Rs. 3 lakhs within the prescribed time. The appellant submitted his reply denying that he had ever been prosecuted or convicted for any offence under the Extradition act. The trial court acquitted him but the High Court confirmed the order of acquittal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the treaty entered into between the British Government and the Tonk State on the 28th January, 1869, which was continued in force by the "Stand still Agreement" entered into on the 8th August, 1947, was no longer subsisting and its execution became impossible as from the 15th August, 1948, being a date when the British Government ceased to exist; (ii) since the treaty was no longer alive it could not be said that the appellant was liable to imprisonment for failure to comply with the provisions of the Extra Detention Act, 1962. HELD: (i) The treaty was neither repealed nor extended by the Indian Independence Act, 1947, and was not intended to continue in force after the 15th day of August, 1947. [577 G] (ii) It was open to the appellant to prove that he had never been prosecuted or punished for any offence committed prior to 15th August 1947. The fact that the treaty did not extend would not make the appellant liable to imprisonment until the 15th of August, 1948. [578 A B] (iii) The treata tion was no longer in existence and its execution remained unaffected by the provisions of section 7 of Extradition Act. The appellant was therefore entitled to the benefit of section 18 of the Extra Commision Act, 1962 and the High Court was right in holding that the appellant 's case was covered by section 7 of that Act. [579 D E]
2299: The respondents were the owners of certain lands in village Bakhiri. They applied for permission to sell the trees on their land and the Divisional Forest Officer by order dated August 30, 1957 granted them proprietary rights in the land. The Compensation Officer held that the respondents had no interest in the trees standing on their land as the trees were not 'land ' as defined in section 2(5) of the Punjab Alienation of Land Act, 1953, and that the compensation was payable only to the owner of the land. On appeal the Divisional Forest officer held that the trees were "land" within the meaning of section 2(3) of the Act and that the Compensation Officer was not competent to grant the proprietary rights in respect of the trees. He also held that the appellant had no interest or right in the trees. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court which allowed it holding that the trees standing in the land were "land". The appellant contended that the trees could not have been transferred without the consent of Moti Ram, and that they were not 'lands ' within the meaning Of section 2(6) of the Land Acquisition Act. Held, that the trees would be 'land ' within the definition of section 2 (6) of that Act and that they could not have transferred without the permission of Motiram. The word 'land ' is used in the same sense in section 2 (7) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and in the case of a land which is not occupied as the site of any building in a town or village, it must mean land which is occupied as the sites of any building or other structures on such land. The word "land" has been used in the context of the Act in the sense of land which is being acquired or which is being built upon. The word land means land which is used or capable of being used for agricultural purposes or for pasture. The word is used in a wide sense so as to include not merely vacant land but also land which is capable of being converted into a building site. The word has been used to denote the land which is actually being used or is capable ofbeing converted into a residential site. The words "land" and "land" are used interchangeably
253: The respondents in each case claimed exemption from assessment in respect of the sales effected by them on the ground that such sales took place "in the course of the export" within the meaning of article 1115 286(1) (b) of the Constitution. The Sales Tax Authorities rejected their claim as, in their view, the sales were completed before the goods were shipped and could not be considered to have taken place in the course of export. The State appealed to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution against the orders passed by the Sales Tax Authorities. The High Court held that the sales were complete when the goods were actually delivered as a direct result of the sale or purchase and that they did not take place in the export business of the respondents. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the sales fell outside the scope of the expression 'sale ' occurring in article 1116(1)(b) of Constitution and were therefore exempt from assessment. Held, that the sales which were completed before they were exported out of India were not sales in the course. of export but were sales in the export trade. The word 'sale ' is used in the sense of an agreement between two or more persons to do a particular act or to make a contract whereby two or more person agree to do a certain thing at different times. It does not necessarily mean a different thing altogether. A sale may be complete even if there is no intention to do so. But the word 'sale' has been used in the context of article 286(1)(a) of the constitution and in the context it must mean something done after the goods have been delivered as a result of some treat ment or agreement and before they are actually shipped. The word "sale" in article 286(2) means a series of transactions which take place simultaneously with the actual delivery of the goods. The word is used in a wide sense to include every kind of transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of a works contract. The word in its widest sense includes all kinds of movable property other than actionable claims and all materials moveable and immovable which may become due to the Government or the contractor; but it does not include contracts for the performance of any service or the rendering of any service.
2436: The appellant was a surety for the principal debtor. He executed a bond in favour of the respondent. The surety became liable to pay the entire amount due from him. The surety had no right to restrain execution against him until he had exhausted his remedies against the principal debtor and the surety discharged the liability of the principal debtor in spite of demands. The surety died on June 15, 1951. The appellant filed an appeal challenging the legality and propriety of this direction. The appellate court dismissed the appeal. In second appeal the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 140 of the Indian Contract Act. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: (1) The surety is not bound to discharge the debt or to make payment of the principal. It is only when the creditor has exhausted his remedy against the principal that he can enforce his security against the principal. [1235 G] (2) The surety was not bound to make any payment of the debt nor could it be said that he was bound to discharge his liability. The surety was bound to make payment within the time specified by the surety. The surety did not have any such right. [1236 B D] (3) The surety had a right to recover the amount from the principal. The surety could not avoid his liability unless he made a demand for payment of the amount. [1237 C D] (4) The surety 's obligation to pay the amount was not discharged by the creditor because he had not exhausted his remedy. [1238 E F]
2678: The appellant was prosecuted for offences under section 27(1)(a) of the , and section 38(1) of the Act. The Magistrate acquitted him but convicted him under section 27 (1)(b). The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to try the case as he was not a 'motor transport undertaking ' within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. HELD : (i) The word "includes" in section 2(h) of the Cr. P.C., means "shall include any other thing which is calculated or done". The word "means" does not mean merely "is used in relation to something else", but includes everything by whatever designation occurs in that context. [917 D] (ii) The word 'includes' has been given a specific meaning in the Act. It is difficult to limit this specific meaning on any reasonable basis. [918 E F] (iii) The word used in section 2 (g) of Cr. P., is "may be regarded as equivalent to "shall be construed accordingly." [919 G]
4311: The petitioners were selected for promotion to the grade of Section Officers Grade in the Central Secretariat Service. They were included in the field of selection for the purpose of holding a departmental competitive examination limited to candidates belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes for filling up vacancies reserved for them. The petitioners along with others were included in a single list by the Department of Personnel & Administrative Reforms in the Cabinet Secretariat in accordance with the field of Selection determined by the Selection Committee. After an interview by the Selection committee, ninety one unreserved vacancies were filled from the first 90 vacancies, reserved for members of the Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes, remaining unfilled because no candidate belonging to those categories was found suitable for including in the field. The petitioners were not considered for promotion on the ground that they had not been sponsored by the Employment Exchange. The petitioners filed writ petitions challenging the validity of the Central Secretariat Services (Amendment) Rules, 1979 and the Regulations made consequent thereto by the Union of India for the purpose. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Central Secretariat services (Amendment) Act, 1979 did not apply to the Central Secretariat service and that the Central Government could not have relaxed the provisions of the said Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Central Secretariat Service (Amendment)Rules, 1979 do not apply to Central Secretariat Service as they are not covered by the Central Secretariat Rules. [1189 G] 1.2 The Central Secretariat Services Rules do not provide for any reservation for Scheduled Castes and Schedule Tribes. The Central Secretariat Rules do not make any provision for reservation of vacancies for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes. The only provision which is made in the Central Secreta ry Service Rules is Rule 12(b)(i), which provides that the number of posts reserved for Scheduled Castes shall be computed by dividing the total number of posts to be filled by direct recruitment and the number of appointments to be made under sub rule (3). This Rule does not contain any specific provision for reservation for Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe candidates. It merely provides that the total number to be filled up by direct recruitment would be 50% of the total number. [1190 A B] 1.3 The Central Secretariat services Rules do not expressly exclude the
3195: The appellants, small manufacturers of matches, have been subjected to excise duty at the same rate as has been applied to larger producers, mainly on the ground that they are entitled to a higher rate of excise duty than what was being charged by them. They were also subjected to similar treatment in other industries. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification issued under section 3(1) of the . The High Court held that the appellants were not entitled to any relief and dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the appellants had no reason to believe that the impugned notification was based on an irrelevant consideration; (ii) the appellants were discriminated against because they were not similarly situated with the appellants; (iii) the appellants could not be said to be discriminated against merely because they were engaged in the manufacture of matches which were sold in the market; and (iv) the appellants should not be denied the benefit of the exemption granted to them. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants cannot be said to have been discriminated against simply because they were carrying on their business in the manufacture and sale of matches. [408 F] 2. The appellants were not engaged in the manufacturing of matches but were engaged in some other process. The appellants did not fall within the category of manufacturers. [410 A B] 3. The appellants had been subjected to different rates of excise duty for the manufacture of which no process was ordinarily carried on with the aid of power. The appellants could not therefore be said to fall within the class of manufacturers who were entitled to a lesser rate of excise duties than what was actually charged by them from the manufacturers. [442 E G] 4.1 The appellants were entitled to the concession of the rate of excise leviable on the matches manufactured by them. [411 D] 4.2 The appellants were liable to pay excise duty on the match boxes manufactured by them and not on the mats manufactured by them, as the appellants were doing the same work as the matches produced by them. The appellants would be entitled to the benefit of exemption from payment of excise duty on matches manufactured in the manufacture. [412 C D] 413 3.1
725: The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for a declaration that she was the owner of the lands left by her deceased husband and that she had passed to Sahib Singh 's mother, Kishen Kaur, as the heir of her father. The appellant contended that the respondent was not entitled to the properties under the general custom of the Punjab in preference to the respondent. Held, that the respondent could not succeed on the basis of a special custom entitling her to the properties if she established such a custom. The respondent was not bound to establish any special custom entitl ing her to the property unless she established it by necessary evidence. The respondent failed to discharge the onus and therefore the appellant was entitled to succeed. The respondent did not discharge the burden but only discharged the burden. The respondent having failed to discharge its burden, the appellant was not entitled. The respondent had failed to prove any special custom of the tribe or family entitling her the sister to succeed on the respondent 's claim. The respondent could not be said to have discharged the burden and the onus was on her to show that she was not entitled, to the properties.
5671: The respondent No. 3 was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months under section 111 read with Section 135 of the Customs Act, 1968. He was acquitted on the ground that he had not been prosecuted for an offence under the Gold (Control) Act. The Chief Judicial Magistrate accepted the plea of the respondent No.3 and ordered that the prosecution be dropped. The High Court confirmed the order of acquittal. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the acquittal for the offences under the Customs Act would be barred on the basis of the undermentioned facts: i) That the respondents were tried by a competent Court for the offence of being in possession of gold under the Customs act; ii) That they were sought to be prosecuted under the Gold Control Act; and iii) that the prosecution could not be launched against them because the ingredients required to be established in respect of the offence under the Customs Acts were altogether different from those required to be proved in respect of an offence under any other law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The conviction of the respondents for the offences punishable under the CustomsAct is based on the evidence adduced before the trial court. [982B] 2.1 The presumption under section 114(a) of the Gold (Prevention) Act, 1968 is available only when the accused proves that he has committed the offence under that Act. [983C D] 2.2 The burden of proof lies upon the prosecution to establish that the accused has committed the theft or smuggling of goods. [984E] 3.1 The prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused have committed the offence charged. [985D] 4.1 The question whether the prosecution should be allowed to proceed further with the case depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. [986F] 4.2 The prosecution must establish its case beyond all shadows of doubt. It cannot be said that the prosecution has failed to discharge this onus. [987G] 5.1 The fact that the accused persons are prosecuted for the offence under section 111 of the Customs act is no bar to the prosecution of the same person in connection with the charge of having committed the offence.
