2637: The respondent filed a complaint under section 20 of the , against the appellant, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, alleging that he was a "public servant" within the meaning of section 2(vii) of the , and that he had been convicted by the Court of Magistrate for an offence punishable under section 537 of the Act. The Magistrate acquitted him on the ground that the complainant was not competent to file the complaint under section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the complaint petition was not made and signed by the person competent under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 to exercise powers of the Corporation in the matter of institution of legal proceedings. HELD: (i) Section 537 of that Act provides that the Commissioners may institute, defend or withdraw from legal proceedings under the Act; under section 12 the Commissioners can delegate their functions to the Chairman and the Chairman may in his turn delegate the same to the Vice Chairman or any municipal officer. [539 B] (ii) The jurisdiction of the Commissioner is not limited to the cases mentioned in section 537 but extends also to cases which are referred to in section 6 of the Act and which are not covered by section 537. The words "any other case" in section 536 of the Act do not mean only cases where the Commissioner has no power to prosecute the accused. [540 C D] (iii) The expression "any other criminal proceeding" in section 417 includes all proceedings before a criminal court including the trial of offences under the Act. [541 A]
3983: The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. They had purchased the land from the respondent No. 1 under a registered sale deed dated 10th April, 1909. The respondent No. 2 was the purchaser of the land from respondent No. 3. The appellants filed an application for restoration of possession of the land to them on the ground that the land was not in their possession since the date of purchase and they were entitled to get back the amount deposited by them with interest thereon. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the decree passed in Civil Suit No. 403 of 1908 did not recognise any "pre existing" right of Bai Vajia in the property in dispute. The appeal preferred against the said order was dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the decree in Civil Suit 403 of 1909 did not recognize any "preexisting right of Bai Wajibul Ibrahim". It was further contended that the decree was void as the respondent No 1 had no title to the property in question. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "possessed by" is not intended to apply to a case of mere possession without title, and that the legislature intended that the expression "possession by" is to be understood as meaning only physical possession of the property in which event the title of the person in actual possession would pass to the transferee. [511E F] (2) The expression 'possession by ' does not mean actual possession but means actual possession. The expression 'title ' means possession in law. [512A] (3) The expression in section 14(1) of the Act cannot be limited to possession in law and must receive its due interpretation. [513B]
707: The appellant, a member of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly, was elected to the Tamil Nadu State Legislative Assembly. He filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground that he had been disqualified under section 7(1)(c) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, for being chosen as a member of a Legislative Assembly. The Election Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the question whether the nomination paper had been improperly rejected by the returning officer and that the rejection of the nomination paper was improper, did not arise out of the decision of the Election Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the decision of a tribunal which is open to appeal under section 116A of the Act, is open to judicial review; (ii) the decision must depend on whether the candidate is duly qualified or not; and (iii) the decision should depend on whether there were grounds for disqualification which were not taken before the returning officer. HELD: (i) The decision of the Tribunal in the present case was open to appeal against the order of the returning officer dismissing the petition. [626 E] (a) The decision in Hari Vishnu Kamath 's case was not conclusive on the point because the decision was open to challenge in an election petition under section 100(1)(b). [627 F G] (b) The decision was open only to judicial review. It could be challenged even in an appeal under section 115A of the Representation Act, if the decision was one which was open to judicial scrutiny. [628 A B] (c) The decision cannot be said to have laid down any general proposition of law that where a question raised in an election proceeding is not decided by the returning Officer but is referred to the High Court under section 100 of the Act for its opinion, the decision would be final. [629 C D] (d) The decision does not operate as res judicata between the parties in an election matter. [630 H]
1706: The appellants, who were the claimants in a reference made to the Court under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, claimed compensation for their lands at the rate of Rs. 10,000 per acre. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded compensation at the rate fixed by him. The appellants contended that the reference was not maintainable as they had not been given an opportunity to object to the rates at which compensation was allowed and that the reference should be dismissed on the ground that it was barred by limitation. The High Court rejected this contention holding that the reference could not be said to have been made within the period of limitation prescribed by section 18 of Act 1 of 1894. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the objection raised by the appellants did not raise any question of law. [766 B] (ii)The High Court was wrong in rejecting the plea of the appellants that in the absence of a reference on the question of quantum of compensation by the Land Acquisition Officer, the Court had no jurisdiction to consider that matter at all. [767 C D] (iii)The High court was wrong in holding that in the presence of a reference under section 18, the Court could not entertain a claim for enhancement of compensation unless there was a reference under s.18. [768 E F] (iv)The High Courts were wrong in holding otherwise. [769 A] (v)The High courts were wrong in thinking that the reference under section18 was not made within the time prescribed by the Act. [770 H]
4714: The appellant Corporation was a State Road Transport Corporation. The respondent workmen were employed by the appellant Corporation as Conductors in its bus belonging to the appellant Corporation. They were discharged on account of unsatisfactory service. The respondent workman raised an industrial dispute which was referred for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held that termination of services of the respondent workman was bad, and directed his reinstatement with full back wages. The High Court upheld the decision of the Labour Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the termination of the respondent workmen was bad because the order of discharge had not been passed by the employer and the employee had no authority to do so. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of the services of the workman is not retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. [801 B] 2. The definition of retrenchment given in section 2(o) of the Act does not include termination of service by way of punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action. [802 C D] 3. The definition has to be read in the context of the definition of retrenchment contained in section 2 (oo) of which it is not necessary to refer here. [803 A B] 4. The definition is wide enough to cover all kinds of termination of employment of the workman by way of penalty or dismissal. It cannot be restricted only to those cases where the termination of service may be by way of dismissal or other punishment. [804 E F] 5. The definition in section 2 of the Act is wide enough so as to cover all types of termination of service except dismissal or other termination. [805 G H] 6. The definition includes termination of service of a workman by way, penalty or dismissal, but does not include any other kind of termination of services. [806 A B] 7. The definition does not include dismissal or other punishments. [807 A B]
4687: The respondent was detained under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962. He challenged his detention on the grounds that he had been a member of the crew and that he had no knowledge of the contraband goods being carried in the vessel. The High Court quashed the order of detention on the ground that the respondent had not been given an opportunity to make a representation against the order of the detention. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the order of release passed against him was illegal because the maximum period of detention mentioned in Section 10 of the Act had expired and as such the appeal should be allowed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The order of detention is clearly erroneous. [801B] 2.1. It cannot be said that the order has been made on the basis of materials which were available before the detaining authority or the court. The order must be based on some material which was not disclosed to the detenu at the time of making the order of bail. [802C D] 2.2. The order does not disclose any reason for the detention. The order merely states that the petitioner "is released from custody". [803E] 3.1. In the instant case, the order of preventive detention was passed on 7th May, 1979 and the same was served on the respondent on 8th May, 1980. The order was passed on the very next day i.e. 9th May, 1981. The order shows that the respondent was arrested on the first day of the arrest and was produced before the Magistrate on the second day. The order also mentions that the petitioner was released on bail. The order further records that the petitioner 's presence was secured by the police during investigation. The order refers to the fact that the petitioner had been absconded till the date of his actual detention. The question whether the order was passed with a view to prevent the petitioner from continuing his smuggling activities would have to be decided only after the trial is over. [804F G] 3.2. In the present case, the detention order was passed without giving the petitioner an opportunity to explain the circumstances which led to his arrest. The order is therefore bad. [805A B] 3
6019: The appellants, who were the lessees of the coal mines in question, instituted a suit for declaration of their homestead right thereto and for confirmation of possession. The suit has been filed beyond three years from such date. [915C D] 6. The suit does not disclose any cause of action. [916B C] 7. The suit premises are adjacent to a coal mine and are being run by the appellants. The suit properties form part of the mines. The suit cannot be
3467: The appellant was the sole transporter of the cement manufactured by the respondent company. The appellant was carrying on business as a dealer in cement and was also carrying on business of transport work. The appellant had been engaged in transporting the cement from Sindri to different stockists at various places in Bihar and West Bengal. The appellant used to engage thirty six trucks for use in his (sic) transport work, but the price paid by him was much less than the price charged by the appellant. The appellant 's contract with the respondent company commenced some time in March 1963. Since the appellant did not have its own fleet of trucks, it used to engage twenty six trucks out of which three were owned by the respondent. The appellant, therefore, carried on the business of transporting the cement bags from Sindari factory to different stockist at different places in Bihar. The appellant claimed that he was the sole operator of the truck and that he was liable to pay tax under the Act. The Assessing Officer rejected the claim holding that the appellant was the owner of the truck. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Assessing Officer. The Tribunal held that the appellant being the sole transpanger of the truck, was not liable to be assessed to tax under the provisions of the Act. In further appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had no control over the truck and the truck was only a carrier of the goods loaded in the truck. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of owner as given in section 2(d) of the Act is very wide and includes the owner of a public service motor vehicle in respect of which a permit has been granted by a Regional or State Transport Authority under the provisions relating to road transport. [901 G] 2. The definition does not include the owner of any vehicle. It merely means the person who carries the goods for the purpose of carrying them. The owner of a vehicle is the person who is responsible for the use of the vehicle for the purpose for which the vehicle is used. The owner may be a person who is merely looking after the vehicle. But the owner of such a vehicle cannot be said to be the owner of that vehicle. [
3375: The respondent was a carpenter for doing some ornamental work in a cinema hall of the appellant. He served a notice on the appellant asking him to show cause why penalty should not be imposed on him under section 4A(3) of the Orissa Workmen 's Compensation Act, 1923. The appellant replied that he was a casual contractor and that the accident had taken place solely because of his own negligence. The Commissioner held that the injury had resulted in amputation of the left arm of the respondent above the elbow. He therefore made an application to the Commissioner for Workmen 's compensation, respondent No. 2, stating that he was an employee of the appellant and was entitled to compensation under section 4 A of the Act. The Commissioner rejected the application holding that the injury did not fall within the meaning of the expression "accident arising out of and in the course of employment" as defined in section 2(1)(a). The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Commissioner. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Commissioner committed serious error of law in imposing a penalty on the appellant under section 4(3) as the compensation had not fallen due until it was settled by the Commissioner under section 19; (ii) the Commissioner acted without jurisdiction in imposing a penal interest on the appellant; (iii) the Commissioner was not justified in imposing a personal liability on the appellant for payment of compensation under section 3, since the accident had arisen out of and/or in the course, of the employment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Commissioner committed serious errors of law in awarding compensation under section4A(3), in respect of the accident which occurred in the course and in the present case. [876 G] 2. The Commissioner has committed serious error in imposing a punishment on the appellant. [877 C D] 3. The Commissioner was not right in imposing a fine on the appellant, because the injury had been caused to the workman by the accident which admittedly arose out of and during the course of the employment, and the workman was entitled to the compensation under section 19. [878 E F]
5898: The respondent was posted as Executive Engineer in the Industrial Supply Section of the Directorate of Industries, Punjab. He retired from the post of Executive Engineer with effect from October 31, 1982. The appellant filed a complaint against him under section 5(1) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 alleging that he had purchased sign boards in 1979 and had also purchased goods worth Rs. 1,00,000/ for which he had been drawing Rs. 2,00, 000/ per month. The complaint was investigated by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged on August 27, 1980 against the respondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of section 5 of the Prevention o f Corruption Act, 1988. The prosecution against the respondent was quashed relying on the decision in the case of Des Raj Singhal vs State of Punjab. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the said Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules has been misinterpreted by the High Court in holding that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of sign boards in the year 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2. 2.2. The High court held that the view taken by the High court was correct and in view of Rule 2,2 the First Information Report against the respondent could not be quashed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the view expressed by the High 'Court is erroneous in law inasmuch as the rule placed an embargo on initiating judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years of the cause of action or the event referred to in the said rule and the High Court committed an error of law in taking the said view. It was further submitted that the view of the High Court being correct, the High Court should have quashed the prosecution against the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Courts are competent to quash criminal proceedings if the facts disclose commission of an offence by a public servant while acting or purporting to act in discharge of his official duty. [917B] 1.2. In the instant case, the High court has rightly
5256: The assessee was a manufacturer of woolen goods. For the assessment year 1959 60, under the Income tax Act, the relev ant accounting for which was made by the assessee 's firm to pay Rs.50,000 as its distributor. The assessee claimed that it was bound under an agreement with the firm to pay the sum of Rs.50.000 paid to the firm. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was bound under the agreement and not under the agreement. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the agreement in question was an integral part of the bargain between the assessee and the firm and therefore the expenditure incurred by the assessee was deductible from the total income of the assessee. HELD: (i) The agreement in question is an integral part and parcel of the bargains for the acquisition of the technical knowledge of the assessee to have the said trade marks. [760G] (ii) The agreement was entered into by the assessee with the firm and the assessee had no right to insist upon the payment of the amount of Rs. 50,000 paid to it by way of commission. The agreement was only for the purpose of carrying out the object of the assessee company and not for the purpose or business of the assessee Company. [761A B] (iii) The agreement did not create any obligation on the part of the assessee nor did it impose any obligation on it. It merely provided that the assessee would be entitled to use the trade mark for the manufacture of goods manufactured by it. The agreement also contemplated that the assessee should make known to the approved officers of the assessee the technique, practices and application of specialised tanning processes. The agreement clearly stipulated that the assessee could use the trade marks for the manufacture and sale of goods manufactured and sold by it. [762B C]
3259: The appellants were licensees under section 10 of the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961. They were assessed to market fee on the basis that they had purchased the agricultural produce from the appellants and were selling it in their own shops within the notified market area without submitting accounts and by paying the market fees. The appellants challenged the assessment as arbitrary and violative of principles of natural justice. The High Court quashed the order of assessment as arbitrary but granted a certificate of fitness for appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellants are liable to pay fee under the Act. [3A] 1.2 The appellants have not been able to show any rule or bye law which permits them to charge more than one market fee. The appellants have also failed to show that they were not liable to pay any market fee. [3B] 1.3 The appellants are not liable to payment of fee under the Punjab Agricultural Market (General) Rules, 1962. [3C] 1.4 The appellants are entitled to be charged with the market fee at the rate fixed by the Board from time to time. [3D] 1.5 The appellants are also entitled to be paid the market fee on sale of the specified agricultural produce. [3E] 1.6 The appellants are bound to pay the market fee. They cannot escape the liability of payment of market fee. It is open to the appellants to recover the same from the respondents. [3F] 1.7 The appellants are, therefore, liable to pay the fee. [4G] 1.8 The appellants are jointly and severally liable to pay market fee. In case the appellants fail to do so, the respondents will be free to recover the amount from the appellants. [4H; 5A] 1:9 The appellants are neither liable nor liable to pay anything beyond what has been done by the respondents. The appellants are only liable to pay a sum of Rs. 5014/ as market fee on their purchase of the agricultural produce. The appellants can recover the said amount from the respondents only if they prove that they have purchased the agricultural produces from the appellants or from the market committee set up by them. [5B C] 1.10 The appellants are equally liable to pay
6636: The detenu made a representation to the appropriate Government on 1.12.1988, which was rejected by the State Government on 18.2.1989. The detenu made another representation on 19.3.1989, which was also rejected on 20.4.1989. On 21.5.1989, the State Government passed two separate orders of detention under Section 3(1)(iv) of the Act, directing the detention of the detenu. The detenu filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of these orders. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the detenu had not been given an opportunity of making a representation against his detention and that there was no violation of Article 22(5). In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the detenu had been deprived of his right to make a representation to him under Article 22(6); (ii) the order of confirmation of the detention was bad as it was based on irrelevant grounds; (iii) the representation of the detenu should be considered by the detaining authority as early as possible before any order is made confirming the detention; and (iv) the confirmation of the order without the consideration of the representation would be invalid and the subsequent consideration of the same would not cure the invalidity of the order of detention. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The detenu has been deprived of the right to make an effective representation against his continued detention. [926E] 2. The detenu had been detained under the Act for a period of more than one year. The Advisory Board had considered the case of the detenu and also the representation of him and thereafter approved the detention order without the considera tion of the representation. The Advisory Boards report was received on January 4, 1980. The Advisory board did not give its opinion within 15 days from the date of detention. The Advisory boards were also not communicated to the detenu. It was only after the receipt of the report of the Advisory Board that the detenu made a fresh representation. [927F H] 3. The detenu was not given an opportunity to make a fresh representation if he wanted to do so. The representation of the petitioner was not considered before the confirmation of detention order. [928A B]
3624: The appellant was a manufacturer of manganese dioxide. He had imported ten metric tons of manganes dioxide from outside the country. The Assistant Collector, Central Excise, passed an order for refund of duty on the ground that the goods should be assessed under Tariff Item 26 and ordered refund accordingly. 992: The appellant was a shopkeeper and was carrying on his business in the shop. He had been working as a salesman for the past several years, but he was not employed by him. In the year 1954, he was dismissed from service under section 16 of the Punjab Trade Employees Act, 1940. On appeal, the Additional District Magistrate held that the appellant was guilty of contravention of the terms and conditions of his employment and directed his dismissal. The appellant 's writ petition before the High Court was dismissed on the ground that the Act would not apply to his shop because the appellant had engaged no strangers as employees but that the entire work in the shop was being done by himself and by the members of his family. The appellant contended that the Act could not be said to have been passed with the object of preventing the appellant from continuing his business in his shop and that it was not necessary to provide for the application of the Act to his shop. Held, that the Act was not intended to apply to the shop or establishment where there were no " employees" but only those who were employed in the shop or establishments which were being run by the appellant. The Act was enacted to prevent the commission of certain offences committed by the appellant and to make provision for the prevention of such offences. It is not necessary that the Act should be applied to the shop itself. The Act does not contemplate any other kind of legislation which may be made by the State Government. The Act is not meant to control the ordinary activities of the shopkeepers and the general public. The Act has been enacted to regulate the business of the shop and to ensure that the customers are not exploited by the shop keepers. The Act cannot be said to be designed to control the general public or to prevent the business of a particular class of persons.

1543: The assessees were assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1945 46. 6138: The appellant, a medical college affiliated to the Bombay University, was admitted to the M.D. By the Bombay Municipal Corporation for admission to the post graduate courses in the Medical Colleges of the State of Maharashtra. He was given admission on the basis of his merit in the entrance test held by the Bombay Public Service Commission. The appellant was not given any seat in the M.B.B.S. Course. The appellant challenged the validity of rule 4(A) in whole and rule 5 (wrongly stated as rule 6 in the High Court judgment), in so far as it applies to the Government Medical College in the city of Bombay, as discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution and, accordingly, invalidating the impugned rule 4( A). It is well settled that the rule must be strictly construed. [924 B] 3.1 The Rule is not discriminatory nor is it violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [925 D] 3.2 The rule is made for the purpose of ensuring the availability of adequate number of candidates belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in all colleges and universities within the State of Gujarat. 1251: The appellants were in unauthorised possession of the house of Fakira, a non proprietor, and that they had been in unauthorised occupation of the same. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the order of the Deputy Custodian on the grounds that the Deputy Custodian gave no notice or opportunity to them to meet the case and that the Custodian had no jurisdiction in the matter in view of the provisions of the wajibul arz according to which the house of a non proprietor could be let out only by a person who was an evacuee. The High Court held that the Deputy Collector had no jurisdiction to decide whether the appellants were entitled to the benefit of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (i) the Deputy Custodian had no power to give notice or opportunity of being heard before he passed the order; (ii) the order was bad because the Deputy Custodian did not give any notice to the appellants before passing the order; and (iii) the order of 204 the Deputy Custodian was without jurisdiction. HELD: (i) The Deputy Custodian had jurisdiction to pass the order under section 18(1)(a). The Deputy Custodian has no jurisdiction to pass such an order as the Deputy Custodian is empowered to pass under section 18A. [156 G] (ii) The Deputy Collector had jurisdiction to decide the question whether the appellants had become an evacuee within the meaning of the Act or not. The Deputy Custodian was competent to decide the dispute between the parties. He had jurisdiction to determine the question whether or not the appellants were an evacuee within section 18(2) of the Act and the Deputy Custodian could not go behind the order of his own. [155 B C] (iii) The Deputy Commissioner had no jurisdiction under section 18 to decide the validity of the order. The Deputy Commissioner could not have decided the question whether a particular property was evacuee property or not. [155 D E] (iv) The Deputy Director had jurisdiction to hear the objections raised by the appellants against the order of Deputy Custodian. The Deputy Director could not have gone into the merits of the objection raised by the appellant. [155 E F] (v) The Deputy Directors had jurisdiction to entertain the objections raised against the order. [155 H]
6183: The appellants filed a suit for recovery of their dues from the owners of the vessel. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs ' claim was barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the plaintiffs have failed to prove that they were not in possession of a part of the cargo or that they were liable to pay the dues of the port. [5B] 1.2 The plaintiffs have not proved that they were actually in possession of goods. They have also failed to prove the fact that they were paying the port charges. [6C] 1.3 The plaintiffs have failed in proving that they were the owners of goods. The plaintiffs have also failed in proving the fact that the goods were delivered to them at Calcutta Port. The plaintiffs had also failed to establish their title to the goods. The burden of proof lies upon the plaintiffs to prove that the goods belonged to them. [6H; 7A] 3.1 The question whether the plaintiffs were in possession or not is a matter which has to be decided on the basis of the evidence led before it. [7B] 4.

2148: The Assam Primary Education Act, 1947 was to be deemed to have come into force on October 5, 1962. 6927: The appellant assessee was a company carrying on business in the manufacture of aluminium and steel. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended: (i) The documents were filed by an individual after April 1, 1961, but before April 1. 1964, and therefore, they could not be used as evidence against him; (ii) The documents being filed by an association of persons, the same could not be relied upon as evidence against the assessee; (iii) The documents having been filed by the association before April 1 1964, the same cannot be used as proof against the assessee. 1100: The appellant was the Mahant of a Hindu undivided family. He was appointed as a receiver and was in charge of the Court Receiver. In the year of account, he was given charge of the estate to the appellant on January 15, 1950. On January 15, 1951, the appellant submitted a return of income of the estate for the Fasli year 1355 corresponding to September 16, 1948, to September 15, 1949. The Income Tax Officer assessed the appellant to agricultural income tax for the year ending September 16, 1949, and the appellant 's appeal against the order of assessment preferred to the Commissioner of Agricultural Income tax and the Board of Agricultural Income Tax, Bihar, were unsuccessful. The appellant filed an application under section 66(2) of the Bihar Agricultural Income tax Act, 1922, before the High Court of Patna for a direction that the income from the estate be deemed to be agricultural income in the hands of the appellant. The High Court held that the income received by the appellant from the Receiver was not exempt from payment of tax and by virtue of section 3, agricultural income tax was charged upon the income for the assessment year in question. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) Section 13 of the Bihar Act is not a charging section. It only provides a machinery for recovery of tax and does not provide for any other mode of recovery. [408 B] (ii) The income from the property of the appellant was not exempt because it was derived from the Receiver. The receiver was not bound to treat the income as agricultural income in his hands. The receiver could recover tax only if the property was in the possession of the receiver. [410 C D] (iii) The income received by a receiver was not exempt under section 3 of the Act. The receiver had no right to collect the income from him. The receiver can collect the income only when he receives the income from his own source. [411 E G] (iv) The income of the appellant from his property was not exempt. The income from his property must be regarded as agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of the Act and the appellant was liable to pay agricultural income tax. [412 A B]

844: The appellant was convicted under sections 488/406 and 407 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923, as extended to the Municipality of Howrah. 2519: The petitioners were the Chief Minister of the State of West Bengal and the Chief Minister was apparently advised by the Chief Minister to adopt a simple and straightforward act. In the course of their work they had published an article in which they had made statements that they "had no intention whatsoever of causing any harm or disruptive action against the Government". The petitioners ' speech was not intended to be prejudicial to the public interest but it was intended to be so used as to bring about a change in the political scenario of the State. The petitioners contended that the speech was likely to have the effect of defeating the Constitution and the law; that the object of the speech was to promote the policy underlying the Order and the consequences thereof, particularly with regard to the position of supply of milk and the question of continued employment of the persons working in the sweetmeat shops in the area, that the propaganda had misrepresented a piece of illegal legislation before the Court had an opportunity to decide the matter, and that the statement was aimed at preventing widespread agitation in connection with the Order, that the speech did not like that, and that it was likely to cause unemployment for many that the object, purpose and nature of the Order was to promote widespests and the danger of widespersing the evil. 3807: The assessee was a shareholder of a Private Company in which the public were not substantially interested. It is a power to be exercised either immediately or within a reasonable time and therefore the exercise of the power by the Chief Justice must be held to have been intended to be exercised for the purpose of making the order. HELD: (1) The tax was not properly levied as a tax on profession, calling or employment. [635 B] (2) The tax is not a tax directly on the trade of the appellant. It is a tax on the sale of goods. 914: The Karnataka Public Service Commission invited applications from candidates for appointment to the posts of Assistant Engineers by direct recruitment. 904: The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of carding and other items. It had a factory at Bombay. The Government of India, by an order dated April 25, 1955, increased the production of carding from Rs. 1/2 to Rs. 2/3 per day. The appellant company claimed that it should be paid a minimum wage which would include production bonus and incentive bonus. The Government amended the order by substituting for the words " basic wages" the words " production bonus " and " incentive bonus ". The appellant contended that the Government Order did not require or justify the company in including the additional emoluments being paid by way of production bonus and the incentive bonus. Held, that the Government order did not require the company to include the additional emoluments in the calculation of the rates of basic wages for the purpose of the order. The word " basic wages " is not defined in the Act but it has been used in the sense of basic wages as well as dearness allowance. The definition of " basic wages", therefore, includes both basic wages and dearness allowance. In the present case, the Government order does not require the appellant to include the basic wages for this order. The definition in cl. 8 of the order only requires that the basic wages must be paid by the company. The definition does not require that the basic wage must be paid directly by the company itself. The definition merely provides that the basic pay must be paid direct by the company through its employees. The definition also does not require any such payment to be made directly by the Company. The definition is intended to cover all payments made by the company directly by way of wages, bonus, etc., and does not require payment of any amount by way of bonus. The definition cannot be read so as to mean that the payment of bonus by the company is not a kind of wage. The definition, therefore, does not require either the payment of any bonus by the Company directly by way wages, bonus or incentive bonus.
2946: The appellant was appointed as Head Mistress of a school in the State of Madras. She applied for recognition and aid to the school under the Madras Elementary Education Act, 1920. The rules were framed under the Act and they did not confer any right on the appellant to claim recognition or aid from the Government. 1758: The appellants were displaced persons who had been rehabilitated by the allotment of evacuee agricultural land in Hyderabad State to them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order was not one which directed the cancellation of the leases but only an administrative order. It was merely an administrative order which was made under section 20 of the Act. The order did not purport to have any effect on the rights of the parties. [440 F G] (iii) The order did nothing more than merely directing the cancellation of leases. 6422: The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of respondent No. 1 from the suit premises on the ground of default in payment of rent for a period of more than six months. The trial court decreed the suit and the appeal preferred by the appellant against the decree was dismissed by the High Court. In the second appeal, the High Court held that the undertaking given by respondent No.1 to vacate the premises was not unconditional and that the appellant had set up its Chairman, respondent No. 2, to file the undertaking as directed by the order dated 5th March, 1987. The High Court also held that the appellant was entitled to recover possession of the suit premises from respondent No. I. The High court further held that the decree for recovery of possession passed against respondent No. 3 was not binding on the appellant. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts ' jurisdiction under Article 227 is limited to see whether the lower courts have acted within their jurisdiction or not. [560C] 2. The High courts ' jurisdiction under article 226 is limited to seeing that an inferior court or tribunal functions within the limits of its authority. It does not extend to correct errors of fact however gross it may be. A court or a Tribunal while exercising supervisory jurisdiction cannot act contrary t o law or of facts nor can it reappraise evidence to come to a conclusion contrary to what has been recorded by the subordinate courts. The undertaking given by the respondent No. l was conditional only with regard to the arrears of rent for six months. [567F G] 4.1 The undertaking given to the High Court by respondent No, 1 was conditional only regarding the arrears of the rent for six month. The undertaking clearly implied that on the date of the undertaking, respondent No., 1 was in possession of the property and in order to defeat the decree for eviction passed against him, respondent No, 2 was in possession. The undertaking specifically expressed that
2624: The appellants were employed by the Company in its depots. They had been working as depots for a number of years and had been doing their work at different places. In 1962, the Company gave notice to the Union of the appellant workmen that out of 21 depots mentioned therein would be closed down with effect from 30th September, 1963. Thereafter, an industrial dispute was raised by the workmen which related to the closure of the depots. The Tribunal held that the closure was not justified and directed the Company to pay compensation to the workmen. The Company challenged the decision of the Tribunal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the closure of a depot amounted to closure of business and the Government was entitled to refer the dispute for adjudication under section 10(1)(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The closure of a depot does not amount to closure of the business of the Company. [801 G] (ii) The closure is not a mere change of opinion or a change in the character of the business but it is a change in real nature. [802 B C] (iii) The closure must be genuine and real. It cannot be said that the closure is genuine and real and the Government has no power to refer the matter for adjudication. [803 A B] (iv) The closure does not amount either to closure of a business or to retrenchment of the workmen. [804 E] (v) The closure may be bona fide and real. [805 F] (vi) The closure can only be on account of the circumstances beyond the control of the employer. [806 D] (vii) The closure should be bona fide. [807 H] (viii) The closure need not necessarily mean the termination of the services of all the workmen concerned. [808 A B]
124: The appellant company was incorporated in 1937 with an authorised capital of Rs. 10,00,000 divided into one lac shares of Rs.10 each and the Company had a managing agent for the Mills. The Company resigned from the managing agency on the 16th September, 1939. The Company continued to act as the managing agent of the Mills till the 30th June, 1939, on which date it resigned the managing agency. Subsequently, the Company resigned and the new managing agents were appointed by the Company. The Company did not pay either of the calls. (in liquidation) under section 38 of the Indian Companies Act. The trial Court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the appellant was entitled to relief under section 38(1)(b) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant company could be said to have been declared a sick industrial undertaking within the meaning of section 2(m) of the , and the appellant could not be said to be a sick industrial company within the meaning Of section 2(n) of the . [356 A] (ii) The appellant was not a shareholder in respect of 5,000 shares of Rs,. 10 each. The appellant was merely a managing agent of a company and was not a 'shareholder ' in respect of the shares held in the company. [355 B C] (iii) The appellant could not claim any relief under section 40(2) of the Indian Partnership Act. [354 D] (iv) The appellant cannot be said to hold the shares in the company without the consent or knowledge of the other shareholders. [353 E] (v) The appellant is not a shareholder of the company. 3112: The respondent was a citizen of India and had entered India on April 1, 1955. He applied for and obtained an Indian visa which was valid upto January 26, 1955. On January 27, 1955 he again applied for and received a permit from the Government of Assam in respect of his foreigner entering India. In the revision application filed by him in the High Court, the High Court held that as in the case of Fida Hussain 's case (1) the respondent was a natural born British subject, that being so he was at the date of his entry in India in April 1955 a citizen of Pakistan under article 5 of the Constitution and that he was not required to obtain a permit under cl. 7 of the Foreigners Order, 1948. The High Court also took into account the fact that the respondent had left India for Pakistan after he had served out the sentence. Held, that the High Court was wrong in holding that the respondent was not a foreigner when he entered India on January 27, 1950. The respondent having migrated to Pakistan during the period between March 1, and January 26, 1950, he could not be deemed to be a foreigner within the meaning of article 5 of Constitution.
490: The respondent company was carrying on life insurance business. In the year 1939, the respondent issued annual fire insurance policies and received a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 as premiums thereof, the whole of it would be shown as income in the statement for the year 1939. The company did not include the amount of premiums received by it during the chargeable accounting period ending December 31, 1940, but included the amount of the premiums received from the respondent. The Income tax Officer treated the premiums as capital under r. 1, Sch. 11, and assessed them to excess profits tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. On reference, the High Court held that the premiums were capital receipts and were not revenue receipt. Held, that the premium received by the respondent was not capital receipt and could not be deducted from its profits. The premiums received were capital receipts, and were liable to be taxed as such. The premium received by an assessee was not capital expenditure. The premium paid by him was not capital in nature. The premium was paid out of the profits earned by the assessee. The premium collected by the assessee was not revenue receipt, and was not capital.

[568E F] 1.4. The evidence shows that the appellant received Rs. 7,000 from P.W. I Niranjana Dass and as a result of that he had taken the money from P. W. I Nirnanjan Dass. The evidence establishes that the money was handed over to P.Ws 1 Niranjankar and others who were present at the time of trap. The evidence therefore establishes that the accused had accepted the money with himself. [571D E] 1.8. The evidence indicates that the appellant took the stand that
3668: The appellant was the sole proprietor of a Hindu Undi sity. He was the sole surviving member of the family of his father and brother. The appellant filed an application under section 25A of the Income Tax Act, 1922 claiming partition w.e.f. in the year 195556 against the Hindu Undi vided family of Bapalal Purshottamlal Modi, an application under Section 25A of Income Tax Act. The appellant preferred an appeal before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal which dismissed the same on the ground of limitation. The High court was right in dismissing the writ petition. [115B] 2. The High Courts have consistently held that the provisions of the Income 'tax Act are intended to be used only for the purpose of carrying out the objects of the Act and cannot be used for the purposes of avoiding any possible conflict between the provisions of a statute and the provisions of another statute. [116C D] 3. The High courts have consistently held in several cases that the provisions contained in the Income Tax Acts are intended to operate only for the purposes mentioned therein and not for the purposes specified in the other Acts. [116D E] 4. The High has rightly relied upon the decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. Porwal Estate Ltd., [1962] Suppl
2272: The respondent club was granted a licence to hold racemeetings at both the courses and for which it paid a sum of Rs. 22 lacs as licence fees. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that considering the unique nature of the use of the premises by the Club, the proper method for determination of the annual rent was the profits basis method but upheld the Club 's objections as regards the disallowance of the several items of expenditure. [1323 B] (2) The High Courts decision in the case of the respondent Club was based on the peculiar facts of that case. The High Courts judgment was based on a misapprehension of the true scope and effect of the provisions of section 154(1). The High Courts view was that the proper method of determining the annual rent would be the profits basis. [1324 C D] (3) The High courts decision was based on misappreciation of the relevant provisions of the Act. The High courts judgment was based upon misappreciation or misinterpretation of the relevant statutory provisions. [1325 E F] (4) The High court was wrong in holding that the proper way of arriving at the net rateability of the premises was the profit basis method. 364: The petitioners, who were the owners of the disputed properties, filed a suit against the State Government and the State Government for declaration that the properties had vested in it by virtue of the provisions of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The State Government issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Act declaring that the estate of the petitioners was vested in the State. On the date of vesting the disputed properties stood on the land in the notified estate. The petitioners claimed that the lands were not liable to be taken over by the State Government under the provisions of section 4(a) of the Bihar Act. The State contested the claim contending that the lands did not vest in the State under the provisions contained in the Bihar Land Reform Act, 1950, as they were not used as office or cutchery for the collection of rent of the notified estate of the petitioner No. 1. The State contended that the lands belonged to the petitioners and were not liable for acquisition under the provisions Of the Bihar Land Acquisition Act, 1950 (Bihar Act I of 1951). The petitioners also claimed that the disputed properties were not liable under the Bihar Land Tenures Abolition Act, 1950 as they were neither the property of the petitioners nor of the State Government. The State resisted the claim contending inter alia that the lands had been leased out to the petitioners for a period of 20 years from the date of the lease and that the petitioners had no right to continue in possession of the lands. The State also contended that the disputed lands were not used for the purpose of the petitioners ' estate. The State further contended that the petitioners were not entitled to any compensation for the structures put up by them on the lands. Held: (i) The State could not acquire the lands without paying compensation to the petitioners. The State could only recover the compensation paid to the petitioners if the lands were actually acquired. [901 B] (ii)The State could not take advantage of its own wrongs in acquiring the lands. [902 C D] (iii)The State was not entitled to take away the lands from the petitioners. It was open to the State to take away from the petitioners the lands which were already in their possession. The State was entitled to recover the compensation from the petitioners if they were actually deprived of the
2670: The assessee was a registered shareholder in the assessment year 1945 46. He had paid the dividend income tax on the shares held by him during the accounting period ending September 30, 1955. The Income Tax Officer treated the said dividend as income of the assessee and assessed it under section 12 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer but the Tribunal referred to the High Court the question whether the amount could be regarded as dividend or not. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The assessee was not entitled to claim any deduction from the dividend income received by him for the years 1945 to 1954. [801 B] (ii) The assessee had not claimed any interest on the amount of Rs. 43,925/ which was received by him as his share in the said shares. The assessee had only a right to receive the said amount as dividend. The assessee was therefore not entitled to any relief under section 10 of the Act. [802 C D] (iii) The assessee did not make any provision for payment of dividend on the shares of the company. The assessee merely made an offer to pay the dividend income which he had earned in the previous years. The assessee did so because he was not a registered shareholder. [803 E F] (iv) The assessee 's contention that the amount should be treated as dividend was not correct. The assessee never claimed any dividend nor did he make any provision in respect of the same. [804 A] (v) The assessee could not be said to have acquired the shares on which the arrear dividends were declared. [805 G]

As the instance of the Commissioner of Agricultural Income Tax, Kerala, a reference was made to the High Court of Kerala under sub section (2) of Section 60 of the Kerala Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1950. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the decision of the High Court was erroneous as it proceeded on the basis that the remission in the present case could not amount to agricultural income. [173G H] 1.3. The expression 'agricultural income ' has been used to describe the income derived from agriculture. [174B] 1.4. The expression has been used with reference to the income derived by the assessee from agriculture. The expression is used in the sense of income derived from sources other than agriculture. [180C] 1.5. The expression means income derived from property held under trust wholly for religious purposes. [189E] 1.6. The expression does not include agricultural income. The expression includes agricultural income. Therefore, the remission in this case could not be treated as amounting to agricultural income within the

The High Court also found that the respondents had not made any claim for property which had been notified as evacuee property under section 8 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have taken the view that Section 8 has outlived its utility and hence the concerned officers of the State need not entertain any applications made in future under section 8 regarding the house, the property being evacuee property and belong to one Shah. [475C] 2. The High court was right in holding that Section 8 did not apply to the facts of the present case. [476D] 3. The High courts are justified in taking the view that the provisions of Section 8 do not apply to cases where the property is evacuee property. [477E] 4. The High Cour t erred in holding that the provisions contained in Section 8 would be applicable only if the property is an evacuee property. The High Co urt committed error in holding that since Section 8 does not apply to a case where the property was an evacuee property, the provisions of section 8 would not be applicable. [478F G] 5. The High COurt has rightly held that Section 6 has relevancy and operative force and notifications could still be made under that Section, Section 8 also will have to be retained and made use of by genuinely interested persons. [479A B] 6. The High Commis sion has rightly held in favour of the respondents. [470B] 7. The High Commission has given cogent reasons for rejecting the claim of the respondents on merits. [471C D]
1432: The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 149 and section 201 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. They were sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had erred in holding that the eye witnesses had seen the occurrence and their evidence must be accepted, that the trial court had not given reasons for disagreeing with the opinion of the third judge and that the judgment should be treated as a judgment in rem and that the High court had failed to consider the effect of the acquittal of the appellants. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was no reason for disbelieving the eye witnesses who had seen the incident and their evidence is corroborated by the medical evidence. [901 G] (ii) The High court was wrong in holding that it was not possible for the appellants to have sent for the cart, to put the dead body on it and take it out of the village and that within the time between the commission of the murder and the time of the making of Report at the police post. [902 B C] (iii) The High Courts had been wrong in holding the appellants guilty of the offence of murder without any basis or justification. [903 D E] (iv) The High courts had not considered the evidence of the eye witnesses in regard to the manner in which they had seen the murder and their evidence was not reliable. [904 A B] (v) The High has not considered the effect of their acquittal in regard to an accused who was acquitted by the trial court. [905 F]
3853: The appellant was convicted and sentenced by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 I.P.C. The High Court acquitted him of the charge but convicted him of the offence under section 304 Part II I.P., I.P,.C. The State appealed to this Court. It was contended that the convictions were bad because the deceased had not been able to give a true account of the occurrence, and that the evidence of the eye witness was not reliable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The prosecution case is that the deceased Nainsukh was shot dead by the appellant. The post mortem report shows that there was no injury on the person of the deceased. The doctor who conducted the autopsy found two injuries caused by fire arm on the head of the deceased, one was a lacerated wound on the right parietal bone and another was a contusion on the left side of the chest. The doctor also found a fissured fracture of the right parieto occipital bone. The doctor found a fisticuffed wound on the head and the straws were also recovered from the scene. The doctor further found a fist blow on the head. The doctor however did not find any injury on the head or on the back of the deceased and he opined that the death was due to shock and haemorrhage as a result of the injuries received by the deceased. [911B C] (2) The prosecution has failed to prove that the deceased died of the fatal injuries sustained by him. The prosecution has miserably failed to establish that the deceased was killed by the appellant in furtherance of his common intention. [912E F]

The petitioners claimed that the provisions contained in the Principal Act were violative of their fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution. The petitioners further contended that the impugned Act violated their fundamental right under Articles 25(1)(a), 26(b) and (c) of the Constitution and that the impugned legislation infringed their fundamental rights under Articles 25 (2) and 26(d). The petitioners also contended that the Act violated their right to freedom of religion guaranteed under Articles 26(b), 26(c) and (d) of the constitution. The petitioners prayed for a declaration that the Act contravened their fundamental rights. The respondents contested the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the petitioners were entitled to the protection of Article 26(b); that the Act offended their fundamental rights as they were not saved by Article 26(a) and (b) of the Act; that the Act infringed their fundamental right to freedom under Article 26(c); and that the Act is void because it violates their fundamental rights conferred by Articles 25(2) and (3) of theConstitution. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Act does not infringe the fundamental rights of the petitioners. It is only the Act which makes provision for the appointment of office holders and servants in the religious institutions. [819G H] 2. The Act is not violative of the fundamental rights under articles 25 and 26. [820A] 3. The Act has been enacted with a view to provide
5205: The petitioners were employed in the State of Andhra Pradesh as Assistant Engineers. They were transferred to the State of Telangana by an order dated 19th May 1975. The petitioners challenged the validity of clause (5) of Article 371 D before the Administrative Tribunal, which was disposed of on 28th March 1969. The petitioners contended that the impugned clause (5), which conferred jurisdiction on the Administrative Tribunal to deal with service matters specified in the order, was ultra vires and invalid. The petitioners also contended that the order of the Administrative Tribunal was not a valid order because it had been passed without any notice or hearing to them. The petitioners further contended that the Administrative Tribunal had no power to pass an order modifying or nullifying the decision of the State Government under Clause (3) of Article 372 of the Constitution. The petitioners therefore prayed for quashing the order of transfer and for a direction to the State Government to transfer the petitioners from the State of A.P. to the State. The petitioners relied upon the provisions of Article 371D of the Constitution and contended that the said provision was ultra vires the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The power of judicial review conferred on the Administrative Tribunals is by reason of the Proviso to Clause (5) Of Article 371D subject to the veto of the State government and it is not at all effective or efficacious because the State Government can defeat its exercise by just passing an order modifying, or nullifying its decision. [886C] 1.2 The power of Judicial Review conferred on the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution of India. It cannot be exercised to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the High Court under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution, as has been held by this Court in the case of Union of India vs Pushpa Rani & Ors., ; , and in the case State of U.P. vs Gobardhan Lal, ; , . [887G H; 888A B] 2.1 The petitioners have not made out any ground for interference with the order of transfers. [887E] 2.2 The petitioners have failed to make out any case for interference with their transfer orders.
5302: The respondent plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration that the sale deed dated 28 4 1939, executed by the widowed mother of the respondent plaintiff was invalid and was not binding upon him and for recovery of possession thereof. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the sale was valid and that the decree had become final. The High Court in second appeal reversed the judgment of the lower appellate court and held that the alienation was not something which a man of ordinary prudence would have effected, had the properties been owned by him and thus held it not binding on the plaintiff. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the question of improvements having been made by the widowing mother of the defendant plaintiff, the High Court should have granted certificate under section 20(2) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the alienation being not necessary for the purpose of the suit, the sale could be set aside. [901F] 2.1 The finding of the High Court that the alienation is not necessary for a valid and legal sale is not correct. [902B C] 2.2 The High Court has rightly held that the sale in favour of the appellant was void as it was not binding on him. [903C D] 3.1 The question whether the sale was void or voidable does not arise for consideration in this case. [904E F] 3.2 The finding of fact recorded by the High Court is based on evidence and cannot be said to be perverse. [905A]
5814: The petitioners in the Writ Petition, who belong to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, were appointed as P.T.Cs. on the basis of a competitive examination held by the Union Public Service Commission. They were promoted to the posts of Assistant Engineers (Civil) and Executive Engineers (Electrical). In the year 1973, the Government issued an order that the Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes employees ' Welfare Assocation (Regd.) Delhi and the Federation of All India Scheduled Castes & Scheduled Tribes Employees P & T Department, New Delhi and Petitioner 's Association were given the benefit of reservation for the Scheduled Castes / Scheduled Tribes in the posts filled by promotion/promotions on the basis Of seniority subject to fitness. The said order was modified by another order dated 23.12.1983. The petitioners challenged the said order before the High Court contending that the said order was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution inasmuch as it had been passed without any authority or power vested in the Government and that the said orders were illegal and void. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the order dated 23rd December 1983. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The policy contained in the letter dated 23.11.1983 is only to provide reservations to the Scheduled Caste and the Scheduled Tribe candidates belonging to the Scheduled castes and the Scheduled tribes working in the other departments of the Union Government. [628B] 1.2 The policy contained therein is only to give effect to the policy of reservation in the posts which are filled by promotion on the basis thereof. It does not confer any right on the employees belonging to the scheduled castes and the scheduled tribes to claim promotion to the higher cadre. [629E F] 2.1 The Government has taken a conscious decision to make promotions in accordance with the directions contained in the order dated 11.7.1968. The said decision cannot be said to have been taken without any authority. [630F G] 2.2 The Government Order dated 23.8.1983 was issued after the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Indra Sawhney vs Union of India, [1984] Suppl. SCC 228
4741: The petitioners, who were members of a State lottery agency, had been carrying on the business of selling lottery tickets in the State of Maharashtra. They had also been running their own lottery schemes for the benefit of the State. In the State of Bombay, they had been doing lotteries organised by the Government of India or the Government of a State. The Government of India had made a condition that the lottery tickets should not be sold in another State without the express consent of the State Government. The Government had also made a similar condition that the lotteries organized by the Government should not be transferred to any other State without the implied consent of the Government of Maharashtra. The petitioners contended that the expression "Betting and gambling" includes and has always been understood to have included the conduct of lotteries. The word 'cartel ' in section 3(3)(a) of the Bombay General Clauses Act, 1904, means a series of acts or omissions constituting a single transaction; and the word 'carnal ' in section 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958, means a single transaction of sale of goods in one State. 6018: The respondent joined service as a technical assistant with the Gujarat State Electricity Board (hereinafter referred to as the Board) on 1st April, 1974. While he was posted at Surat as Deputy Engineer he was transferred to Ukai subdivision under the order of the Superintending Engineer dated 29th March, 1974. He made representation for cancellation of his transfer order on the ground that his mother aged years was ailing and it would cause great inconvenience to him if he was required to join at Ukai Subdivision under the orders of the Superintending Engi neer. The respondent filed a suit in the court of Civil Judge, Baroda challenging the validity of the order of his discharge from service by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Gujarat. The Single Judge dismissed the suit holding that the order of discharge was issued without affording any opportunity to the re spondent to show cause against the same. The Division Bench upheld the order of dismissal but directed the appellants to treat the respondent in service without any break in service and pay salary to him which he might be entitled under the rules. The respondent preferred an appeal to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order passed by the learned Single Judge was illegal and void because the respondent had not been given any opportunity to show cause before discharging him from services under Regulation No. 113. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of discharge is not a punishment but only one of dismissal simpliciter. [365F] 1.2 The order of termination of service does not amount to a stigma or penal consequence. The order has to be passed after giving notice to the employee and after considering his explanation. The order is passed after taking into consideration the report submitted by the enquiry officer and the reply submitted by the employee. In the instant case, the enquiry officer did not give any opportunity to respondent to explain his position nor did he offer any explanation. Therefore, the order of termination cannot be said to have been passed in violation of principles of natural justice. [366B C] 2.1 The respondent was appointed as a Technical Assistant in the Board and he was transferred from Surat to Ukhai Subdivision under order of the Chief Engineer.

Therefore, the proviso to rule 2(a) (ii) of Rajasthan Service Rules is inapplicable to him. [613F G] 2.2 The petitioner was entitled, in view of the proviso, to the benefit under the proviso to the said Rule. [614A] 2.3 The petitioner was also entitled to the benefits of the proviso. 3344: The appellant, a new entrant, was granted stage carriage permits for a "short route" in the State of Tamil Nadu. He filed an application before the Regional Transport Authority which evaluated the relevant merits and awarded the permit to him. The Appellate Tribunal rejected his appeal on the ground that he had not been able to show any reason for rejection of his application. The Appellate Authority held that the appellant 's experience as lorry operator could be equated with the appellant ' 's experience in bus operation. The Appellate Court also found that the appellant had secured higher marks than the respondent No. 6. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the Appellate Tribunal erred in holding that because the permit is for passenger transport service, lorry service experience cannot be equated with that of the appellant '. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The Appellate Bench has rightly observed that though the appellant ' s experience as lineman could be equated to the appellant ', the error committed by the Appellate Tribunal in rejecting his application was not so grave as to warrant interference under Article 136 of the Constitution. [560C] 1.2. The Appellate court has taken into consideration the fact that the appellant was a new entrants, who were not entitled to preference. The Appellate Judge has clearly overlooked the fact that there was no reason why the appellant should have been treated differently from other persons. [566D] 2.1. It is true that the Appellate Court has not considered the question whether the appellant ' was a new energetic person or a new entrepreneur. But the Appellate Court did not consider the question whether because the permit was for passenger transport, lorry services experience, even if it falls under Rule 155 A (3) (D), can be equated with a new entrade. [565E F] 2.2. There are two circumstances which require to be stressed when dealing with applications in respect of short routes. One is that the applicant must have business or technical experience in the road transport service as defined in clause (a) of Section 68 A of the Act. The other thing being equal, the Appellate Tribunal ought to have applied its mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. [
2809: The appellant was a dealer in timber. He sold it to the respondent who was a dealer of timber. The respondent claimed that he had purchased the timber from the appellant and sold it to another. The Sales Tax Officer held that the timber was "goods" within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959 and that the respondent was liable to pay sales tax on it. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Sales Tax Officer. The High Court dismissed the petition for review. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the expression "goods" as defined in section 2(7) of the Act means goods as defined in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 and therefore the respondent was not liable to pay any sales tax on the timber sold by him. HELD: (i) The definition of "goods" in the Act is retrospective in operation and the expression "taxable event" has been used in the definition of "sale price" in section 2 of the Act. [801 G] (ii) The expression "goods", in the context of the Bombay Act, is wide enough to include all materials, commodities and articles. [802 B C] (iii) The expression 'goods' in the Act includes all materials, substances and articles. It does not include stock and shares, growing crops, grass and things attached to or forming part of the land which are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale. [803 A B] (iv) The expression goods' in the definition in section 2 (7) of Bombay Sales Tax, 1959, means goods as specified in the Schedule to the Act. The expression "taxes" in the definition is wide enough and covers all materials, substance and articles. The expression 'taxable event ' in the Act cannot be construed to mean only a contingency when the goods are sold at the time of the contract of purchase. [804 E F]
2835: The appellant company was incorporated in the year of account 1952. In its assessment for the year 1952 53, the Income tax Officer computed the income of the company from its business at Rs. 3,39,899 and declined to take into account the loss suffered by it in the share transactions. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer on the ground that the business activities of the company were not the "same business". The Tribunal held that the business in shares and the business in other commodities were not the same business as the business in the other commodities. The High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court had no jurisdiction to call for a statement of the case under section 66(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, because the Tribunal had applied its mind to the facts before it and had come to the conclusion that there was complete unity of control and that the two lines of business constituted the same business. [384 G H] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the Tribunal had erred in law in coming to the conclusion which it did. [385 A B] (iii) The High Courts decision in Shree Ramesh Cotton Mills Ltd. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay, ; , followed.
4235: The appellant tenant by a lease deed dated 1.12.1961 agreed to pay and discharge all taxes, outgoings imposed on the two plots of land. The respondent agreed to deliver possession of the two plots to the appellant free of all buildings, erections and structures and raised and put in good order and condition to the satisfaction of the appellant.
