The appellant paid the arrears of rent and the taxes due in respect of the two properties. The respondent also defaulted in payment of taxes due in the suit. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was always ready and willing to pay all taxes and outgoings as well as the buildings and structures standing thereon. The appellate Court held that it had no jurisdiction to try the suit regarding possession of the structures put up by the respondent. In appeal the High Court held that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court is limited only to adjudicate upon leased premises under the Bombay Rent Act and therefore it had no Jurisdiction to try the suits regarding possession of structures put up on the two lands. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The jurisdiction of the civil court is limited only in adjudicating on leased premises under Bombay Rent Act. It has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit regarding the possession of the structure put up by a tenant. [901 B] (2) The Court 's jurisdiction is limited only when the lease is for a fixed term. The Court 'has no jurisdiction to decide the lease. [902 C D] (3) The Court has jurisdiction to determine whether the lease is a permanent one or a permanent one. The Court has no jurisdiction even if the lease is one for a fixed period. [903 E F] (4) The Court can give relief to the lessee who has failed to pay the arrears of rents and the taxes. [904 A B] (5) The Court cannot grant relief to the tenant who has failed in paying the arrears of the rent. [905 G H] (6) The Court is not
4259: The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions Court. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that there was no corroboration of the testimony of the prosecutrix and that the evidence of the prosecutrix was not corroborated by any other independent witness. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law is well settled that in a case where the court finds that the conviction is unsustainable on account of non compliance with section 376(2) Cr. P.C., it must record its reasons for doing so. [405F] 2. The question whether the evidence of a victim of rape is reliable or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is not possible to lay down an inflexible rule that merely because the victim of rape belongs to a particular caste or community, she cannot be subjected to medical examination. [404A B] 3. The courts below have found that the victim was raped and murdered. The evidence of the victim does not suffer from any infirmity. [403E F] 4. The evidence adduced by the prosecution has been rightly accepted by the High Court. [406B C] 5. The evidence given by the victim does appear to us to be quite convincing and trustworthy. There are no grounds to interfere with the order of acquittal passed by the High Courts. [407D E] 6. The appeal fails and is dismissed.
6345: The appellants who were duly elected Directors of the respondent No. 1, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the requisition notice dated 5.9.89 issued by the respondent No 3 for convening a special meeting of the Committee of the Karkhana to elect Chairman and Vice Chairman of the respondent Society. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the members of the second Category who have got a limited right to vote at a meeting are entitled to sit and vote at the special meeting when the Committee considers the vote of no confidence under Section 73 ID of the Act is required to be served with notices of requisition enabling them to participate in the said meeting and as the two nominees of the Financial Institutions and the expert co opted by the Committee under Bye law 29 of the Society the High Court directed the Registrar of Cooperative Societies to give fresh notice to the elected members as well as to the persons nominated by the Financial Institutions, the expert co optee and the expert Co opted member. The appellants challenged the order of the High Court before this Court contending that the requisition notice was not served on the appellants and that they had no locus standi to challenge the same. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of service of notice upon the members of a general body or a committee of the society is mandatory. [492C] 1.2 The requirement of the notice of requisition is directory and not mandatory. [503E] 1.3 The requirement of notice of requisition cannot be waived by the members of an existing committee. [504A B] 2.1 The provisions of Section 73 IOI of the Act read with Rule 57A and bye laws of the Society require that the requisition must be sent to the Managing Director or the Joint Director of Sugar and Sugar Factories, as the case may be, along with the requisition. The requisition should contain the names of the members of such committee and the date on which it will take place. The requisition must be accompanied by a copy of the resolution passed at the meeting of the committee. [501B C] 2.2 The requirements of Section 73I(1) of the Act are mandatory and non compliance thereof would render the requisition invalid. [502D E] 2.3
5717: The petitioners were appointed as Stenographers Grade I in the Department of Revenue and Central Excise. They were given the pay scale of Rs.650(710) 1040 with effect from 1st January, 1973. Their counterparts were attached to the Joint Secretaries and equivalent officers of the Department of Finance. The petitioners were also given the pay scales of Rs.425 (710) 1003 (i) Petitioners ' counterparts in the Department. The petitioners who were working as Stenographers in the department were given the same pay scale of the post of Stenographer Grade I. The petitioners filed a writ petition before this Court contending that their counterparts are not comparable with the petitioners and that they should be placed in the pay scale applicable to them. The said petition was allowed by a Division Bench of this Court on the ground that the petitioners were entitled to the same pay scales which were granted to the petitioners in the case of the counterparts of the petitioners. The petitioners have filed this petition after the report of the Fourth Pay Commission. It is contended that the petitioners should be placed at par with the counterpart of the petitioners in respect of the pay scale which was granted to the counterpart in the Department and that the petitioners cannot claim parity with the counter part of the petitioners who were similarly situated. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The petitioners are entitled to the pay scale prescribed for the posts of Stenographers Grade II in the Department which are equivalent to the cadre of Stenographer Grade III. [533F] 1.2. The petitioners cannot claim any parity with the petitioners in regard to the pay scales which are being enjoyed by the counterpart. [534A] 1.3. The petitioners do not belong to the category of Stenographers but belong to the cadre which is the feeder cadre for promotion to the post of Section Officer. [535B] 1.4. The petitioners had been drawing the same salary and allowances as the counterpart and the counterpart respectively. Therefore, the petitioners cannot be treated differently than the counterpart or the counterpart who are drawing the same pay and allowances. [536C D] 1.5. The petitioners would be entitled to the benefit of the pay scales
5524: The Public Service Commission issued a notification on July 17, 1973 determining inter se seniority of all the candidates appointed on the basis of 1970 examination in accordance with their position in the list prepared by the Commission under Rule 19 of the Rules. The petitioners and other unsuccessful candidates filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the notification was not ultra vires the Act and the rules framed thereunder. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The notification dated August 19, 1973 is not ultra vires. [168E] 2.1. In view of the amendment of Rule 19 of Rules, the Commission had no power to alter the ranking given to the candidates who were selected for appointment to the service. [169F G] 2.2. The Commission has no power to change the ranking assigned to any candidate. The Commission could have altered the ranking of the candidates if it thought fit. [167A B] 3.1. It cannot be said that the Commission had acted arbitrarily or without application of mind. The Commission had acted in a manner which would violate Article 14 of the Constitution. [165C D] 3.2. In the instant case, the Commission did not act arbitrarily or unreasonably in fixing the ranking for the purpose of selection. The Commission was bound to follow the procedure prescribed by law. [166G H] 3.3. The Commission did not adopt the method of moderation. The method adopted was arbitrary and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. [167B C] 4.1. There can be no doubt that the Commission has the power to fix the ranking as well as the merit of the candidates. But the Commission has no such power. The Commission does not have the power to alter or modify the ranking. [164D E] 4.2. It is true that the Commission may have evolved a method of moderating the rankings but that method should be fair and reasonable. [164H; 164A] 4.3. In the present case, the method adopted by the Commission is arbitrary and unreasonable.
1089: The appellants were under an agreement for the year 1945 46, the company appointed managing agents for 20 years of the company. The appellants claimed that they should be assessed to income tax on the basis of their profits and gains of business in the accounting period ending March 31, 1945. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim but he held that the appellants had not been able to prove that the company was a "business concern" within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Excess Profits Tax Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. On reference the High Court held that the income from the business could not be assessed to excess profits tax because the company was not carrying on any business or profession. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Income tax Officer was wrong in holding that the company had not been carrying on any profession; (ii) the income from business could only be assessed to tax if the business carried on by the company was carried on by its own servants and (iii) the income must be deemed to have accrued to the company when it was first made out of the funds of the company and not when it was actually received by the company. HELD: (i) The income from the company cannot be assessed to any income tax unless it is received by the Company. [447 B] (ii) The income must be regarded as having arisen in the course of the business of the company which has been carried on by it. It is not necessary that the company should have been carrying on a business or profession and it must be shown that the income arose in the course whereof the business was carried on. [448 C D] (iii) The income can be said to arise in the course 'of the business of an assessee only where the business is carried on by him himself. [449 E] (iv) The income cannot be assessed as a business income merely because the company has been carrying on the business of its own. [450 A] (v) The income of the company must be deemed either to have accrued or arisen in the ordinary course of business. [446 F]
2093: The appellant was a workman employed by the respondent company. He raised an industrial dispute which was referred to the Labour Court for adjudication. The Labour Court held that the retrenchment of the workmen amounted to an unfair labour practice and directed reinstatement with full wages from the date of termination of service, but granted only three months ' wages in lieu of one month 's notice. The management appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the retrenchment was illegal because the workmen had not been given any opportunity to explain their position before terminating their services and that the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to sit in appeal over the decision of the management if it found that the retrenchment amounted to an "unfair labour practice" and that the award of the Labour Court was contrary to law. HELD: (i) The appellant was justified in retrenching its employees and that the number of employees required to carry on the work after the imposition of a ban against the business of the appellant could not exceed the number retained by the appellant. [78 B] (ii) The appellant has failed to prove that there was any mala fide or victimisation on the part of the management. The appellant has not produced any evidence to show that the workmen were not given any opportunity of explaining their position before the management passed the resolution. [79 C D] (iii) The appellant had not proved that the workmen had been discriminated against by the management. [80 E F] (iv) The appellant did not produce any evidence to establish that the workmen concerned were not given an opportunity to explain the position before the resolution was passed. [81 G H] (v) The appellant could not be said to have acted mala fide or in excess of his authority. [82 A B] (vi) The appellant cannot be said to be guilty of any mala fides or victimacy. [83 B]

The respondent did not comply with the terms of the agreement and instead filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of sales tax on the ground that the transaction was not within the purview of sub section (3) of Section 51 of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transaction is not exigible either to sales tax or to purchase tax. It is not possible to hold that the transaction falls outside the scope of sub section(1). [805D] 4.1 The transactions are not exigible under sub section (1), the respondent would be liable to pay sales tax/sale tax in respect thereof. [805G H] 4.2 The respondent has not complied with the requirements
5543: The appellant joined the service of the Narang Bank of India Ltd. as a Clerk cum Typist and was confirmed in his service on October 1, 1974. He was confirmed in the service of respondent No. 1 on October 1. 1974. On July 25, 1976 he entered into an agreement with the United Bank of India, respondent No. 2, for taking over the management of the Naranagar Branch of the United Bank. The terms of the agreement were that the appellant would not be entitled to any salary or other allowances except those admissible under the rules of the bank. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant has been impleaded as party in the appeal. [1096C] 1.2 The appellant was not a necessary party to the proceeding before the Tribunal. His case was that he was not aware of the proceedings and therefore he should have been impleaded as one of the respondents. The appellant did not file any written statement. The appellant was given sufficient opportunity to defend the case. The appellant had failed to avail of the opportunities granted to him. [1097E F] 1.3 The appellant was a necessary party because he was not a party to any proceedings before the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal. [1098F] 1.4 The appellant was entitled to cross examine him on the sole reason that
2744: The appellant was appointed as a Professor of Surgery in the Rajasthan Medical College, Jaipur on March 2, 1964. At the time of his appointment he was officiating as Principal of the said College. He was officiating as Director of Medical and Health Services, Rajasthan at Jaipur. On July 28, 1965, he was officiating in the said College as a Professor. In August 1967, he was promoted as a Professor and was confirmed as such. On September 1, 1968, he was appointed as Principal of a medical college by the Rajasthan University. On October 7, 1968, the appellant was appointed to officiate as Principal of an institution affiliated to the Rajasthan University, which was subsequently converted into a University. On November 9, 1969, he was reverted to his substantive post of Professor. On December 11, 1969, the appellant made a representation that he had acquired the qualifications prescribed by Ordinance No. 65 and that he should be considered for promotion to the post of Principal. The representation was rejected by the Rajasthan Public Service Commission on January 20, 1970. Thereafter, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the proviso to sub rule (4) of Rule 30 contained in Part 'VIII of the Collegiate Branch Rules. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the proviso to Sub rule (4), which provided that the State Government may make only a temporary ' or officiating ' appointment, did not apply to the case of the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The proviso to sub r.(4) of r.30 of the Rajasthan Medical Service (Collegiate branch) Rules, 1962 is not applicable to the case because it does not provide for any retrospective effect. [562B] 1.2 The proviso to Sub r.(4), which provides that the State Govern ment may make only one temporary appointment, does not apply to a temporary appointment. [563C D] 1.3 The proviso to Rule 30(4) of the Rajasthan University Service (College Cadre) Rules, 1963, which provides that no person shall be appointed to the post unless he possesses the qualification prescribed by the University Statute, cannot be held to have been contravened by the proviso.
3779: The appellant, a company, was carrying on the business of collecting and selling grains. In the assessment year 1959 60, the Income Tax Officer determined the taxable income of the appellant for the relevant accounting period, and assessed it at Rs. 1,50,000. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the said order. The Appellate Tribunal held that the total gross income of the assessee was Rs. 1.5 lakhs and that the tax payable by the appellant was Rs. 2,00,000. On reference, the High Court held that the net income of the assesseec ted was Rs. 3,00, 000. The appellant appealed to this Court with certificate granted by the High Court. It was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High Court had erred in interpreting section 3 in such a way as to make section 2(b) read with section 5 of the Act inapplicable to the case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The question whether the Act applies only to cases where the provision is capable of one of two interpretations, has been considered by this Court in a number of decisions. [841 B] (2) The word 'income ' in section 2(a) of the Act means "the income derived or accruing from any trade, commerce or manufacture or any adventure in the nature of trade, commerce, or manufacture" and not merely the income from the call money received by the assessee. [842 C D] (3) The word "income" in section 2 (a) of Act means "gross income". [843 A B] (4) The word has been used in the context of the Act in which it occurs and in its popular sense it may mean "gross profits". [844 E] (5) The word is used in a wider sense to cover all kinds of income including income from property, including agricultural land. [845 G]
4798: The plaintiffs ' father served a notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 on the defendant, who was the Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Defence. The defendants contested the claim inter alia on the ground that the notice exhibit A 8 served by the plaintiffs ' father was insufficient and was not a valid notice under section80 of the Code. The trial court held that no further notice under section 78(1) of the Code was necessary as the notice exhibit was sufficient. On appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court holding that no further notices under section 80 were necessary. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (i) the notice exhibitA 8 served by them did not satisfy the requirements of section 80; (ii) the notice was defective inasmuch as it did not specify the name, description and place of residence of the plaintiff and (iii) the suit was bad for want of notice under section 79 of the Code because the notice was not properly addressed and the suit was not maintainable. HELD: (i) The notice exhibit A8 was sufficiently complied with. [240 B] (ii) The notice was not invalid merely because it was given by two out of three plaintiffs but it was given in the presence of two witnesses. It could be reasonably inferred from the evidence that the notice was duly delivered or left at the office of the defendant. [241 C D] (iii) The notice must substantially fulfil its object and it is sufficient if it substantially fulfils its object. [242 E F] (iv) The notice does not strictly comply with the requirement of section 80. The notice must also conform to the requirements of s.80. [243 G H] (v) The notice is not invalid merely due to non compliance with the provisions of section 80, and the suit is not maintainable. [244 A B] (vi) The notice cannot be said to have been properly addressed and delivered to the addressee. The notice was sent by registered post. 532: The respondent was dismissed from service by an order dated December 20, 1948. He filed a revision application before the Inspector General of Police which was rejected on June 7, 1949. 1631: The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, filed a suit against the first respondent for a declaration that he was entitled to redeem the property and for an injunction restraining the first respondent from alienating the same. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal by the first respondent, the High Court reversed the decision of the two courts below holding that the plaintiff had not obtained a valid title to the equity of redemption by the sale deed in his favour. The High Court held that the plaintiff 's right to redeem the suit property was not extinguished by the gift deed executed by the deceased father in favour of the appellant. The High court further held that the appellant could not be said to have obtained a valid mortgage on the basis of the gift deed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in reversing the decision of both the courts below. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the plaintiff has obtained a valid lease or a mortgage on the strength of a valid document is essentially a question of fact which can only be decided after the parties adduce evidence. [539E] 2. The question as to whether the plaintiff had obtained a valid document or not is a mixed question of law and fact depending upon the facts of each case. It cannot be determined merely by the finding of the courts below but must depend upon the evidence adduced before it. [540F G] 3. The question about the validity of the transaction under consideration depends upon the terms of the document. If the document is found to be invalid, the question of its being void does not arise. [541A B] 4. The question regarding the validity of a document arises only when the document is shown to be invalid. [542C D] 5. The question of the validity of any document cannot be decided without examining the document itself. [543D E] 6. The question is whether the document is valid or not. [544B C] 7. The question with regard to the validity of an instrument is a mixed one. The question has to be decided on the basis that the document is validly executed. [545G H]

4749: The petitioner was a Judge of the Madhya Pradesh High Court. He retired from service on 31st December, 1982. On his retirement he was paid an excess amount of Rs. 2,220 by his communication dated July 17, 1982. The petitioner informed the Accountant General that he was drawing the amount as indicated in the communication without prejudice to his right to claim Rs. 24,000 to which sum under the law he was entitled. The Accountant General intimated the petitioner that he was entitled to payment of cash equivalent of leave salary in respect of the period of earned leave at his credit on the date of retirement as provided in Rule 20B of the All India Services (Leave) Rules, 1955. The AccountantGeneral of Madhya Pradesh on March 25, 1983, intimated the petitioner and requested him to make payment of the balance amount of Rs 2,219. The petitioner also wrote a letter to the Accountant General requesting him to pay the balance amount. The Accountant-General informed the petitioner that the amount would be paid within two weeks. The petitioner received a copy of the letter of the Central Government dated March 25,1983, addressed to the Registrar of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh. The petitioner thereupon moved this Court for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to pay the amount of Rs 1,00,000 to him with interest thereon. The petition was opposed by the respondents contending that the petitioner had not been paid any amount towards the leave encashment and that the amount was payable only after the expiry of the leave account. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 5(3) of the Act have no application to the case of the petitioner. [560C] 2. The expression 'earned leave ' does not occur in the Act. It is a term of art. It has a definite connotation. It may mean actual leave without pay or casual leave. It cannot include extraordinary leave. [540E] 3. In view of the provisions of section 4 of the Act, the petitioner is entitled to the benefit of the leave rules. [541A] 4. The petitioner was entitled to the payment of cash equivalents on the basis of Rule 20B. The petitioner did not receive any amount towards leave encashment.

In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the concept "dishonestly" was applicable to the facts of the present case and that the High Court erred in holding that the concept was not applicable to the present case. 273: The respondent, a national of Pakistan, was allowed cash credit limit of rupees three lakhs by the appellant bank on the 23rd June, 1947, shortly before the partition of India. On the 23rd July, 1947, the bank filed a complaint against him under sections 380 and 454 Indian Penal Code read with section 412 of the Code before the District Magistrate of Gurgaon. The case was investigated by the police and after investigation it was found that the respondent had acquired the status of a citizen within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Indian Penal Code. The trial magistrate dismissed the complaint holding that the respondent was not a citizen of Pakistan but was a native of Pakistan. The respondent appealed to the Sessions Judge who upheld the order of the trial magistrate. The High Court in revision held that the respondent 's plea that he was a citizen of India at the time when the alleged occurrence took place was false and that the respondent could not be said to have acquired the status as a citizen of another country. Held, that the respondent cannot be said to be a citizen of a foreign country merely because he was a natives of Pakistan. He was a nage roner of Pakistan and was therefore a citizen of the country. The respondent was not entitled to the protection of article 19 (1) (d) Of the Constitution.
387: The appellants were charged with offences under sections 435 and 436 of the Indian Penal Code. They pleaded not guilty to those charges but on the evidence recorded before the jury, the jury held that the charge was defective and they did not invite the High Court to consider the entire evidence and to acquit or convict them upon the charges framed. The appellants contended that the charge against them was defective as it was based on a misappreciation of the evidence given by the assessors who had been examined in the case and that the jury should have taken into consideration the opinion of the assessors which was not legally admissible. Held, that the finding of the jury that the charge is defective cannot be regarded as erroneous because the assessors had not considered the evidence in the light of the opinions of the assessor and the jury. The fact that the assessors did not examine the witnesses in the case does not mean that the jury could not take any view of the evidence. The assessors had no opportunity to see the correctness of their opinion and the jury had no opportunity of seeing the witnesses in order to ascertain whether the facts stated by the assessor were correct. The assessor had no opportunity at all to see the credibility of the witnesses and to see if the statements made by them were true. The assessour must have done so for the purpose of ascertaining what the witnesses had stated. The assesses were not entitled to cross examine the witnesses merely because they were not examined.

1878: The workmen of the Company were dismissed after a domestic enquiry held on February 4, 1967. The dismissal was set aside by the Tribunal and the dismissal was confirmed in appeal by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the dismissal was justified or not because the workmen belonged to the same Union which was dismissed earlier. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide whether the dismissal is justified or not. [877 G] (2) The Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide as to whether the dismissal order was justified or unjustified. It could have decided the question whether there was any misconduct under cl. 10(XVI) of the Company 's Standing Orders for operators. [878 B C] (3) The Tribunal was right in holding that the dismissal order passed against the workmen was justified. [879 E] (4) The Tribunal erred in holding that there was no misconduct under cl.(10)(XVI) and that the dismissal was bad. [880 A] (5) The Tribunal did not consider the merits of the case and came to the conclusion that the dismissal amounted to dismissal. [881 D] (6) The Tribunal should have considered the merits of each case and come to its own conclusion. [882 F] (7) The Tribunal failed to take into consideration the fact that the workmen were employed in the mill and were working in three shifts and as each auto mill required the attendance of two workmen, twelve such workmen were employed to look after the two mills. The Tribunal also failed to take note of the fact that there was a dispute between the workmen and the management regarding the termination of their services. [883 H; 884 A B] (8) The Tribunal committed an error in holding that it had jurisdiction to deal with the matter. [885 C]

7045: The petitioner 's son Suman Behera was taken from his home in police custody at about 3 a.m. on the night between 1st and 2nd December, 1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police of Jaraikela Police Outpost under Police Station Bisra, Distt. 4879: The appellants were teachers in the service of the State of Punjab. 3182: The respondent landlord let out the premises in suit to the appellant on a rent of Rs. 125/ per month. It was further contended that two substantial question of law and law were involved in this case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The High Court has dealt with the case as if this is a matrimonial proceeding in which the status of appellant as wife was under direct challenge. [526C D] 1.2. The High Courts have dealt with the cases as if this was a matrimonial proceeding. [527E] 1.3. The High courts have dealt with a case where the status of a wife was under Direct challenge. 5094: The respondent assessee was a Hindu undivided family. The expression "as the case may be" occurring in section 8 of the Act indicates that it is only when the person who has been succeeded by his father or mother, as the case may he, is entitled to the benefit of the provision that the income from assets inherited by him from his father or father would be deemed to be the income of that father. 6924: The State of Gujarat issued a notification under section 58A of the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949, authorising the Director to grant a licence for working of the distillery for the manufacture of spirit. 2993: The appellant company was incorporated on October 11, 1941. It was incorporated on July 24, 1942. The object clause in the memorandum of association provided that "the business of the company shall be carried on by the managing agents and other persons who may be employed for the purpose of the company". The Income tax Officer held that as the assessee company had not been able to show that it was a company whose business consisted mainly in dealing in or holding investments, the income from its managing agencies should be treated as an "investment company" within the meaning of section 23 A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In appeal to the Tribunal, the Tribunal held that the assessee company was a "company" and not "any person" and that the income from the managing agency business was not liable to tax under section 23 A. The High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that (i) the assessee company is a company whose main business consists mainly in dealing with investment and that the profits and gains from such investments are not taxable under section 23A; (ii) the assessee is not a "person" within the definition of section 2(24) of the Income tax Act; (iii) the assessee has no concern with the business of the assessee company and therefore the income from such business cannot be taxed under section 23. HELD: (1) The expression "income from other sources" in section 23A means the income derived from any business or profession carried on by a company. [639 B] (2) The expression 'income from business ' in section 23 A must be construed in the light of the context in which it occurs. [640 C] (3) The expression in section 23AA means the income from any source of income. [641 D] (4) The expression is used in the sense of "profits and gains of business or profession". [642 E] (5) The expression has reference to the income from business or profession. [643 F] (6) The expression does not include the income from a business of a banking company. [664 G H]
4400: The appellant was a registered dealer under the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, 1969. During the period from May 6, 1964 to March 31, 1970, he purchased raw materials from a Registered dealer who had obtained a certificate in Form No. 19 as provided under section 13(1)(B) of the Act read with Rule 24(4) of the Gujarat Sales tax Rules, 1970. The appellant was assessed to sales tax on the turnover of sales of raw materials during the period from April 1, 1964 to December 31, 1970 and the appellant claimed that the raw materials purchased by him were not liable to purchase tax under section 16 of the Act. The assessing authority rejected the claim but the Tribunal held that the appellant was liable to pay purchase tax under Section 16 of the Gujarat Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the appellant was not liable to pay tax on the raw materials; (ii) the appellant could not be said to have sold the goods at the time when they were purchased and (iii) the sale of the goods was not taxable because the appellant did not have a permit or a licence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellant was not entitled to claim exemption from payment of tax under section 17(2) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. [982F] (2) The appellant could not claim exemption from liability to pay tax under section 18(3) of the Sales Tax Act because the appellant was neither a licensed dealer nor a registered dealer. [983A B] (3) The appellant had no permit or licence to sell the goods. He had only a permit or licence which was valid for the purpose of manufacturing the goods. 4960: The appellant was a sub tenant of a piece of land. He had been granted a licence to construct a building on the land in question. The respondent became a sub tenant under the appellant and the appellant continued to be in possession of the land till the expiry of the period he had terminated the licence. The appellant filed a suit for a mandatory injunction directing him to vacate the premises. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended that the appellant 's rights under the lease by the original owner could not be interfered with the provisions of the Act, because the lease was revoked before the institution of the suit and the appellant had become a sub tenant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A sub tenant is entitled to protection against eviction from the property leased to him by the original landlord if he has acquired title to the property by adverse possession. [912E] 1.2 The right of the appellant to evict the respondent from the suit shed came to an end when the appellant was evicted. The appellant did not vacate the shed after the expiry of his licence. The respondent had purchased the entire property including the suit shed as tenant under the original owner. Therefore, the appellant cannot be denied relief merely because he had become a licensee of the suit shed. [913F G] 2.1 The appellant should not be denied relief simply because he had couched in the form of a suit for mandatory injunction as what would be given to the plaintiff in case he succeeds is possession of the property to which he may be found to be entitled. [914A B] 2.2 The appellant should have been denied relief merely due to the fact that he had been dispossessed by the respondent. [915C D]
1255: The appellant was the owner of a forest in Bihar. He had obtained a lease from the Governor of Bihar for the purpose of cutting and removing bamboos and certain other timber to be found in a specified area of the forest village. The appellant, however, did not pay any rent or compensation for the period of the lease. The State Government issued a notification under section 14 of the Bihar Private Forests Act, 1946 declaring that the forest land was vested in the State Government free from all encumbrances. The appellant thereupon filed a suit for possession of the forest on the ground that the notification under section14 was invalid as it was not served on him. The trial court decreed the suit with costs. On appeal by the State the High Court held that the notification dated February 23, 1949, which was published under section 14 was invalid because the name of the appellant as the landlord had not been mentioned in the notification issued under section 14 and consequently the notification was invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the notification was bad because the name was not mentioned in the said notification and the notification was not served upon the appellant. HELD: (i) The notification under section 15 was invalid because it was not published in the official gazette. It was not necessary that the notification should have been served on the landlord. [703 C] (ii) The notification was not published within the meaning of section 2 of the Bihar Forest Act, 1946. The notification was merely an intimation to the landlord about the intention of the State Government to take possession of the land. The notification does not contain any reference to the notification. The notification is only a communication to the landlord informing him about the intention to take possession. [704 E F] (iii) The notification dated February, 23, 1949 was not a notice to the landlord but was a declaration to the effect that the forest lands were vested in the Government free from any encumbrances. The notification did not specify the date on which the notification was to come into force. The notification merely stated that the notification would come into force from the date of its publication. The notification must therefore be deemed to be a notification under the provisions of section 2(a). [705 G H; 706 A B]
