The Central GOVERNMENT has the power of taking over management of these companies. The Central Gover nment has the right to take over these mills. The Central govt. has the power, if necessary, to take over any of the mills which is deemed to be a sick
5268: The respondent was appointed as a Subedar in the Central Reserve Police Force on 1.1.1976 and was confirmed in the post of Subedar on 20.9.1985. He applied for absorption in the Force. His application was rejected by the authorities on the ground that he had not completed 20 years of service in the Force prior to his appointment. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order rejecting his claim for absorption. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that there was nothing which stood in the way of absorb ing the respondent in the Force, and directed the appellants to consider the respondent 's case for absorption in accordance with law. The Division Bench upheld the direction and dismissed the appeal of the appellants. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In regard to the question whether the respondent is entitled to be absorbed in the Force or not, the scheme of the rule is indicative of the position that in regard to that category of officers benefit of absorption was not admissible and consequently the respondent would not be entitled to absorption. [386B] 2.1 Rule 107(2) made under the Central Reserve police Force Rules, 1955, does not provide for any automatic absorption. It only provides that the service shall be temporary and rules and orders applicable to Central Government servants in temporary service would apply. Therefore, the respondent is entitle to absorption in the cadre with effect from the date the amended rule came into force. [387C D] 2.2 The respondent has been given a permanent status in the Force w.e.f. 1.1, 1976. He was being continued in the promotional post by orders of the President from time to time which is clearly indicative of his position that in respect of that category of officer benefit of absorption would not be admissible and he would be treated as if appointed on contract basis and such re gularisation would be limited to year to year basis. [388E F] 3.1 The respondent was not entitled to claim absorption in the service of the Force. [380F] 3.2 The view taken by the High Court that the respondent was entitled to absorption in terms of Rule 107
6438: The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) and 3(1) (iii) of the COFEPOSA Act, 1974. He challenged his detention on the ground that he had been deprived of his right to make a representation to the Central Government as well as to the detaining authority. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there is no delay in considering the representation and that the same has become stale and there is no other material to establish any nexus or live link between the alleged date of smuggling and the date of detention. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that though the alleged smug gling of gold was said to have been taken place on 17.9.87, the detention order was passed on 21.5.88 i.e. after a lapse of eight months and that too it was a solitary instance and because of the delay, the same has became stale and therefore the detention order must be held to be invalid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power of the Central Government to revoke an order of detention under section 3 of the Act is one of the statutory powers vested in the Central Government which are not subject to any limitation prescribed by Article 22(6). [729E] 2.1 The question whether the power of revocation can be exercised at any time after expiry of the period of detention is left open to be decided by the appropriate authority. [730A] 2.2 The power of revocation under section 3 is discretionary and the same cannot be lightly exercised. [731B] 3.1 The order of detention is made after a lapse period of eight months from the date of the order and the detenu is entitled to make a fresh representation to the Advisory Board within such time as may be specified by the Board. [732C] 4.1 The object of the Act and the purpose behind the enactment of the Act are two different things. The power of preventive detention is a precautionary power exercised in reasonable anticipation and it should be exercised with great care and caution. [733D] 4.2 The detaining authority is required to consider the grounds of detention together with the documents furnished therewith and thereafter pass the order of detention
4364: The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacture and sale of certain articles. It retrenched its employees on the ground that they had been employed in an industry which was closed down by the respondent company. The question for decision was whether the retrenchment was illegal and invalid as it did not comply with the requirements of section 25 FF of the Act. Held, that the termination of service of the workmen amounted to retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(OO) of the Act and was valid. The definition of 'retrenchment ' in section 2(oO) of 'the Act is a well known concept of the law of contract and has acquired significance in the context of industrial jurisprudence. The expression 'retrenchment' in section 2 (OO) means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include (a) voluntary retirement of the workman; or (b) termination of the service for any reason other than the one mentioned in clause (c). The word 'retrenchment" in section 2 OO has been used in a wide sense so as to cover all possible contingencies which may arise in a large number of cases including the ones covered by the definition. In the present case, the termination of the services of the workmen was not retrenchment but retrenchment simpliciter. The definition in section 2 0O(OO), therefore, cannot be construed as excluding the termination of services of the respondents by the appellant company from the purview of the definition of retrenchment.
159: The appellants were convicted under section 182, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The High Court set aside the convictions and sentences on the ground that the offence was one under section 181, Indian Penal code, and not under section 190, Criminal Procedure Code. Held, that the offences were distinct from those of which cognizance could be taken by a magistrate. The offence was committed in the course of the performance of an official duty and it was not necessary that the offence should have been committed in the discharge of a public duty. It was not necessary to establish that the act complained of was done in the performance or execution of a public duties. The offence of criminal trespass was not committed in the performance of a private duty but in the performance and execution of a private function. The offence did not involve any breach of trust or dishonest misappropriation of property. The offence also did not involve the commission of an offence of criminal misconduct as defined in section 21 1, Indian Penal Cod. The offence therefore did not fall within the provisions of section 195, Criminal Procedure, Code, and was not punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months or with fine or with both.
2605: The appellant was a workman employed in the appellant company. He filed an application under section 33C(2) of the , before the Labour Court, Hubli, for recovery of certain amounts due to him from the respondent workmen. The Labour Court dismissed the application on the ground that the jurisdiction of the Labour Court was barred by the fact that the same relief could have been claimed by the workmen by filing applications under section 20(1) of the Act. The High Court held that the jurisdiction was not barred by the law of limitation and dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition as the Labour Court had no power to deal with the claims of the workmen under section 20 of the Act, and that the Labour Court could only proceed under the general law of limitation. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the jurisdiction to deal with claims of the employees under section 20 was barred by virtue of the provisions of section 20(3) of the . It is clear that the Labour Courts were competent to deal with such claims under section 20. [639 B] (ii) The High Courts were wrong in holding that all these amounts could be claimed by the appellant by filing applications Under section 20(I) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. [640 C D]
5889: The appellant was granted permission to start a college of education in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Government granted permission for starting a college of educational nature. The appellant challenged the cancellation of his permission by filing writ petition No. 812 of 1986. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the parties did not comply with the conditions of grant of permission and that the Government had no power to cancel the permission. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government has the power to withdraw or cancel the permission granted under section 23(2) of the Act. The Government is entitled to do so if the conditions are fulfilled. [897C] 1.2 The Government cannot be said to have acted arbitrarily or unreasonably in cancelling the permission. [898E] 1.3 The Government has power to cancel or suspend the permission granted. The Government can also direct the University to take action against the College. [899F] 1.4 The Government may consider whether the College should be closed down or not. If the Government decides to close down the College, the Government shall give notice to the College to show cause why the permission should not be withdrawn. The Government may pass such orders as it deems fit. [900B] 1.5 The Government has no power to interfere with the decision taken by the Government. The Government has only the power to cancel an order granting permission. It does not have any power to cancel a permission granted earlier. [901G H] 1.6 The Government has a duty to see that the conditions imposed by the Government are complied with. The Government must ensure that the conditions are strictly observed. [902A B] 1.7 The Government has to examine the case of the appellant in detail and accord permission. The Government would consider whether the college should be closed or not. [903D] 1.8 The Government has jurisdiction to cancel the grant of permission. The power to cancel is subject to the condition that the Government has done so. [904H; 905A] 1.9 The Government has got a duty to look into the case of an educational institution. The Government cannot interfere with the discretion exercised by the
3809: The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Court for an offence under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. He filed a petition before the High Court for confirmation of his sentence. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the death sentence should be substituted in place of life imprisonment awarded by the trial court and confirmed by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the death sentence has been inflicted more than two years ago is not a circumstance to bring down the death sentence if otherwise the act is taken brutal, depraved or meriting the highest penalty. It will be an idle formality in a situation like that to remit the case to reconsider the question of sentence to the Sessions Court. [713E F] 2. The appellant had two other assailants with him who were awarded life impris on the same day. There was no reason why he should have been given the severer sentence and hence there was no justification for awarding the lesser sentence. [714F G] 3. The appellant was aged about 20 years at the time when the incident occurred. He was a young man of 22 years of age. His father was also a young man. He was living with his mother. He was suffering from various ailments. He was admitted in the hospital. He was treated as an indoor patient. He was discharged from the hospital after a long period of time. The appellant did not know what happened thereafter. He was not able to speak. He was unable to give any explanation for the delay in lodging the FIR. The delay in lodging FIR was due to the fact that the appellant was suffering from mental illness. The appellant could not explain how the delay occurred. [715G H; 716A B] 4. The appellant cannot be said to have been involved in any criminal activity which would justify the imposition of capital punishment. [717D E] 5. The appellant must have been a habitual offender. He was found guilty of murder and was sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High court was right in confirming the death sentence. [618B C] 6. The appellant is entitled to the benefit of doubt
4605: The appellant was appointed as Principal of a college by the State Government. He applied for and was selected by the Selection Committee constituted under section 16F of the Intermediate Education Act, 1921 (Act No. 19 of 1921) for the post of Principal. The Selection Committee held interviews on April 12, 1981 and recommended the appellant 's appointment to the post of principal. The appellant was informed that he had assumed charge of the post of the Principal on May 1, 1981. The appellant filed an affidavit in opposition stating that the appointment of the appellant was not valid as the power to appoint him was withdrawn by the State government. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the radiogram dated April 7, contained an order of the State Government in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointment of teaching staff including Principal and therefore the appointment of appellant alleged to have been made on May 1. was not valid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the selection committee had no authority to make any appointment and the selection committee was not competent to make any appointments. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The selection committee was constituted by the State of U.P. The selection was made by the Selection Board consisting of the Chairman and two members. The Chairman and the members were nominated by the State. The Chairman was the Head of the Institution and the other members were the members of the Selection Committee. The selection of the appellant is vitiated because the constitution of the Selection Board was not approved by the State and the selection of the Principal was not approved. [16 G H] 2. The selection is not vitiated merely because the Head of an institution has not been authorised to do so. It may be that the Head of a institution may have been authorised to act as the Head of another institution but that would not vitiate the selection. [17 A B] 3. The selection Committee was not competent enough to select the appellant as Principal. The selection could not be set aside on the ground that the Head was not authorised to do the same. [17 C D] 4. The selection cannot be set aside only on the ground of mala fides or bias. [17 E F] 5. The selection must be made by the
5006: The appellants were the owners of certain documents seized during search. They had been issued a warrant of authorisation under section 132A of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for return of the same to the appellants. The appellants filed an application before the Income Tax Officer for taking action against them under section 132(1) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Income Tax Officer passed an order directing the appellants to produce the documents and materials seized during the search. The appellants challenged the said order in appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal. The appellants then moved the High Court by way of a writ petition. The High Court held that there was nothing illegal in the issuance of search warrant when there was no material on record which may permit an inference that any document which in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to any investigation or proceeding under Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 was secreted in the house of the appellants. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred on the officer under sec. 132A of Income Tax Act is not a judicial power but a quasi judicial power. [801H; 802B] 2. The word "judicial" has not been defined in the Income Tax Acts. It means giving a finding whether a particular thing is done or not done by a particular person in performance of duty. In the context of the Income 'tax Act, it would mean giving a finding as to the nature of the thing done or to be done. [803C D] 3. The word 'judicial' has not been used in the Income tax Acts. It is a word of common English meaning. It includes all powers incidental to the performance of those duties. [804E F] 4. The word `judicial ' does not mean merely the exercise of judicial discretion. It connotes something more than a judicial power. It signifies a body which is empowered to act judicially. It is therefore clear that the word 'judicial ' is used in the sense of a judicial power with reference to matters within its jurisdiction. [805F G] 5. The word expression 'judicial ' in section 132A must be construed in its popular sense and in its popular meaning. It should not be confined to the
6378: The respondent workman was detailed to work in the first shift for picking up certain employees of the second shift and general shift. On that very day, the management sought approval under section 33(2)(b) of the Act of the action taken and towards meeting the requirement of the provision paid to him before hand a sum of Rs.607.90 as wages for one month, before hand a pare! allowance and the benefit of the free telephone and newspapers which were paid to him at the time of his promotion. The Industrial Tribunal held that the domestic enquiry was not vitiated on account of non compliance with the provisions of section 33(1) (a) of the , and that the finding of the Tribunal that the domestic inquiry was vitiated on account non compliance with section 33(3) (b) of that Act was not correct. The High Court allowed the appeal by the employer and set aside the award of the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. The two items could be properly regarded as part of the respondent 's wages and had to be taken into calculation of the gratuity pay able to him. [976 B] 2. The words "wages" and "daily allowance" are significant to convey that the car allowance and the benefits of the free phone and newspapers were held allowances including the benefit of free telephone and newspaper. [977 C D] 3. The word "wages", in the context of section 33 (2)(b), means all remunerations capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would otherwise have gone into his family budget and were therefore items relevant in fixation of fair wages. [978 E F] 4. The words used in section 33(4) are "wages". The words "total emoluments" are not synonymous with the words "salary". They are intended to connote the amount of salary payable to the employee during the period of service. [979 G H] 5. The expression "wages' is not defined in the Act. It has been defined in section 2(r) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as meaning "any remuneration or other benefit or perquisite capable of being express ed in
5478: The appellant was appointed as a Principal of the College by an order dated January 27, 1986. She was suspended from service on January 29, 1986 and she was reinstated in service on February 28, 1986. On her reinstatement, the appellant was placed under suspension pending enquiry into certain charges against her. The appellant challenged the said order of suspension before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to review its own order because the power of review is not expressly conferred on it by the Statute. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the power of reviewing its own order lies with the Vice Chancellor. [365F] 1.2 The High Court was wrong in holding that the power to review is impliedly conferred on the Vice Chancellor by the Statute and that the power can be exercised only by the Vice Chancellor when there is a provision in the Statute for review. [366A B] 1.3 The High Court erred in holding that it was not competent to the Vice Chancellor to review his earlier order of suspension. [367C D] 1.4 The High Court should have considered the fact that the order of suspension was passed by the ViceChancellor without any authority or sanction of law. [368E] 1.5 The High Court ought to have considered the facts and circumstances of the case before passing the impugned order. [369B C] 1.6 The High Court failed to consider the fact that in the absence of any provision in the statute for review, the power of the Vice Chancellor could not be exercised. [364D E] 1.7 The High Court committed error in holding that there was no power of review available to the ViceChancellor. [363G H] 1.8 The High Court did not consider the fact and circumstances of this case that the order was passed by a subordinate authority who was not competent. [362H] 1.9 The High Court wrongly assumed that the power was conferred on the Managing Committee of the College. [361A B] 2.1 The power of review conferred on the managing committee of the College vests in the Managing Committee. The power of reviewing the decision
2126: The appellant, a religious endowment, was the owner of certain properties in Schedule Kha. He claimed that these properties were public charitable endowments and were not 'public religious endowments ' within the meaning of the Act. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments, Orissa, hereinafter called the Commissioner, held that the properties in suit were public charitable trusts and were not "Public religious endowments" within the meaning Of section 6(13) of the Act and that the properties constituted a 'religious endowment ' to which the Act applied. The Commissioner held that the property was not a 'math ' as defined in the Act and therefore did not fall within the definition of 'public religious endowment ' under section 2(12) of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939. The Commissioner further held that the income from the properties in Schedule 'Kha ' was not available for payment of contribution under section 49 of the Act but it was available only for the purpose of maintenance of the temple and its worship. The Commissioner also held that the temple was a 'minor trust ' and was not a public religious endowment. The Commissioner dismissed the appeal. The Commissioner appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to decide whether the properties in question were public religious endowments or not. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Commissioner was competent to decide whether any property was a 'Math ' or a 'Dharmasala '. The Commissioner could not have decided whether the properties were 'public religious ' or not. [440 B] (2) The Commissioner had no power to decide whether a particular property was a public religious trust or not. The Commissioner had merely to determine whether the properties involved in the case were 'public' or not. It is not open to him to decide whether there was a trust or not and he cannot decide whether the property involved in the trust was a 'public religious trust '. [443 C D] (3) The Commissioner has no jurisdiction to determine whether a particular trust was a public trust or not, because he can only decide whether the trust was 'public religious institution '. [441 E F] (4) The Commissioner could decide whether the temple was 'public ' or not, and if he decides
3656: The appellant was appointed as a teacher in the Municipal Corporation of Delhi. He was dismissed from service by the Deputy Commissioner (Education) on the ground that he had misbehaved with his son, Surinder Kumar in the School premises during recess time on 2nd and 4th September, 1967. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal before the High Court which quashed the same holding that the appointing authority of the appellant being the Commissioner under section 92 of the Act, his dismissal from service being a quasi judicial order is vitiated as the disciplinary authority having regard to its findings on the charges, was not competent to pass the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appointing Authority of the appellant was the Commissioner under Section 92 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 and the order passed by him was without jurisdiction and therefore void ab initio. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The impugned order of the appellant's dismissal from service is vitiated as it did not expressly state either the conclusions of the dismissing authority or the findings recorded by the enquiring officer or that the dismissing authority accepted the findings of the enquiring authority or the finding recorded by the inquiring officer or unless the said conclusion was reached by the disciplinary authority or the appellate authority. [912B] 1.2 The appellant was not given any opportunity to show cause against the proposed punishment. The order of dismissal from service was passed by the Deputy commissioner (Educa tion), who was not the appointing authority. The appellant was merely asked to show cause why he should not be removed from service. The order does not indicate either the conclusions arrived at by the enquiry officer or the findings of such enquiry officer. [913C D] Bimal Kumar Pandit vs Union of India & Ors., ; , followed.
4018: The appellants, who were owners of lands in the State of Gujarat, filed a suit for declaration that the notification under section 4 was illegal and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the respondents from proceeding with the acquisition of their lands. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the notification was illegal and invalid and directed the respondents to acquire the lands in accordance with law. The High Court dismissed the appeal by special leave. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the declaration under section 6 was illegal and void because the notification under sections 4 and 6 was not published within two years from the date of the notification. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A notification under section 6 is a statutory requirement and the Government can issue a notification under section 5A after the expiry of two years from its publication. [5B] 1.2 The proviso to section 6(1) provides that in respect of a notification issued under section 4 before the commencement of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, no declaration under section 4 shall be made after the expiry Of two years from such commencement. The proviso to Section 6(1), however, introduced by the same amendment Act, provided that in respect ot a notification issued after the commencement of this Act, no declaration shall be made beyond a period of two years. [6C D] 1.3 The proviso to sub section (1) of section 6 makes it clear that if the Government is satisfied that the declaration has become necessary or desirable it may make a declaration but the Government cannot do so unless it considers that the proposed declaration is likely to result in undue hardship to the owner. [6E G] 1.4 The proviso to subsection (1) does not affect the power of the Government to issue a notification after the expiry or earlier publication of the notification under sub section (2). It merely enables the Government to direct the Collector to take possession of the land which is the subject matter of the notification and to proceed with the acquisition accordingly. [6F G] 1.(a) The proviso to the section does not affect any power of the government to issue a declaration under section 5. [6G] (b) The proviso does not
547: The appellant was a workman employed with the respondent company. He was dismissed from service by an order dated November 27, 1952, passed by the respondent company under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The respondents raised an industrial dispute which was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the dismissal of the respondents amounted to retrenchment and retrenchment being one of the matters specified in sub section (1)(b) of section 7 of the Act and that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order made by the Industrial Tribunal granting the appellant permission to discharge the respondents. The Labour Appellate Tribunal also found that the termination of the respondents ' services by the appellant was not a breach of section 33 of the Act but it was a case of misconduct as defined in section 2(oo) of the Act. The appellant appealed against the decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the appellant had committed a breach of the provisions of section 33 and set aside the award of the Labour Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The Labour Appellate Tribunals were right in holding that the termination by the appellant of the respondents' services was a breach of Section 33 of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 and that the appellant could not be said to have committed any breach of section 25F of the Act or of the terms of employment contained in the Standing Orders. [560 B] The appellant was entitled to maintain an appeal to the Labour Appellate Tribu nal under section 33 A of the Act, because the appellant had been dismissed from service without notice. The appellant had not challenged the validity of the dismissal order before the Labour Appellate tribunal. The appellant was therefore entitled to maintain the appeal. [540 C D]
6237: The appellant landlord filed a petition under section 14(1)(e) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 for eviction of the respondent tenant from the premises in question. The respondent tenant contested the petition on the ground that he was not a 'specified ' landlord and that the premises were required by him for his own occupation. The Rent Controller held that the respondent was a 'specified landlord ' and that the petition was liable to be dismissed. The Appellate Authority affirmed the order of the Rent Controller. The High Court allowed the appeal of the respondent and set aside the order of eviction passed by the Rent Controller and remanded the case back to the Rent Controller for fresh disposal after giving an opportunity to the parties to lead evidence. The High court also directed the Rent Controller to decide the matter afresh after affording an opportunity to both sides to adduce evidence. In the meantime, the respondent tenant died. The appellant landlord moved an application for bringing on record his legal representatives. The Rent Control Tribunal rejected the application holding that the respondent had failed to prove that he was a 'notified ' landlord. The High Commissioner dismissed the revision petition. The respondent landlord then moved this Court for special leave to appeal against the decision of the High Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts judgment is binding on the High Courts. [96 B] 2. The High courts judgment is open to review under Article 226 of the Constitution. [97 C] 3. The Highs Court has jurisdiction to examine whether the finding of fact recorded by the Rent Control Tribunal is based on no evidence or is perverse. It cannot reappreciate the evidence and substitute its own conclusion for that of the Rent Control Court. [97 D] 4. The High Level Committee has considered the matter and has given its report. The High level committee has found that the respondent landlord was not a "specified ' landlord. He was a retired Army Officer and was a member of the armed forces of the Union. His wife was a member and was residing with him. The High Power Committee has also found that the petitioner was a 'unemployed person '. The High power Committee has also come to the conclusion that the respondent is a 'specified "landlord '. The said finding is based on the evidence led before
347: The appellant was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for life under section 302 I.P.C. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellant but granted a certificate of fitness under article 134(1) (c) of the Constitution. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the High Court had no jurisdiction to alter the decision of the trial court dismissing the revision petition filed by the appellant. The order of dismissal passed by the High Court did not preclude the appellant from filing an application for enhancement of sentence before the High Court. The High court could have exercised its power under article 136 of the Constitution in the circumstances of the case. The High Courts ' powers under article 226 are wide enough to confer on the High Court the power to issue a writ of certiorari or a writ in the nature of habeas corpus. The High courts ' power to review their decisions is not limited to the exercise of revisional powers by the High Courts. The Highs Court has inherent powers which are plenary and are subject to limitations imposed by articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution and also by the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High,Court can interfere with the findings of fact only if it is shown that those findings were based on no evidence or perverse. In exercising its power under articles 226 and 136 of the constitution the High Court cannot act as a court of appeal and reappraise the evidence for itself. The High. Court can examine whether the lower court has acted within its jurisdiction or exceeded its jurisdiction or failed to exercise the jurisdiction or exercised the jurisdiction illegally or improperly. The High 'Court can set aside the conviction and sentence if the lower court had acted within its limits or had acted in excess of its jurisdiction or refused to exercise the right conferred by section 439(6). The High Court may call for the record of the case and pass such orders as it thinks fit in accordance with law.
1969: The assessee company was a firm carrying on business of land development in Calcutta. It sold its entire business concern to the Amalgamated Development Limited, which was promoted by the partners of the firm. The sale price of the business as a whole was Rs. 2,50,000. The Income Tax Officer held that the entire share capital of the vendee company (excepting seven ordinary shares) was taken over by the vendor firm in lieu of the sale price of its business as a going concern and that the profits arising out of the sale were taxable under the Indian Income Tax Act. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the entire amount of Rs. 2.50,000 represented the surplus on the sale of the business and that the Tribunal should have allowed the appeal. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that there was no sale of the entire business concern. The mere fact that in the schedule the price of land is stated does not lead to the conclusion that the entire sale was made with the intention of making profit. [613 F] (ii) The Tribunal has rightly held that the sale was the sale of a business as a googe. The mere circumstance that in the Schedule the price of the land is stated did not lead to any inference that the entire business was carried on by the assessee company. [614 B C] (iii) The Tribunal had correctly come to the conclusion in holding that Rs. 2 lakhs was the value of the goodwill of the business. The Tribunal had also found that the sale of shares was not affected by the transfer of the business but was effected only with the intention to make profit. [605 D E] (iv) The Tribunal could not be said to have committed an error of law in holding that a sum of Rs. 1,83,622 was the value received by the assessee from the vendee. [603 A B] (v) The Tribunal 's finding that the entire consideration was paid by the assessee to the vendee was correct. [604 G H]
4656: The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court, in appeal, confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that: (i) the circumstances that the appellant was previously convicted for murder and committed these murders were extremely heinous and inhuman, constitute a "special reason" for imposing the death penalty; (ii) the fact that the appellant had undergone incarceration for more than two years after the commission of the offence would not justify the imposition of the death penalty as contemplated under Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973; (iii) the fact of the appellant having been earlier convicted for murder, and sentenced to life imprisonment, the appellant could not be said to have been involved in any other crime which would justify the imposition on him of the death sentence; (iv) the fact about the appellant having undergone incarquent sentences during the period of trial and the present one being a case of murder and murder, the sentence imposed should be set aside; (v) the fact regarding the appellant having already undergone incartermisation of incarcerations during the period when he was convicted for murder is a relevant circumstance which has to be taken into consideration while determining whether the sentence should be enhanced or not. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question whether the circumstances of the appellant are special reasons for awarding the death sentence must be judged in the light of the facts and circumstances of each individual case. [357B] 1.2 The fact that the accused was previously convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for a certain period, cannot be considered as a mitigating factor to impose the death sentence. [358C D] 1.3 The fact that there are no mitigating factors pointed out by Kailasam, J., in the present case, can be taken into account while determining the question of sentence. [369E] 1.4 The fact that a very large segment of people, the world over, including sociologists, legislators, jurists, judges and administrators still firmly believe in the worth and necessity of capital punishment for the protection of society, if in the light OF
2373: The respondent was a licensee under the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925. He was assessed to property tax by the appellant for the year 1959 60. In the assessment proceedings he claimed that the value of the properties should be taken as Rs. 90,000/ . The Income Tax Officer fixed the valuation at Rs. 90.000/ . On appeal by the respondent, the Judicial Magistrate fixed the valuation to Rs. 90.,000/ . This order was confirmed in revision by the Sessions Judge. The High Court held that the courts below had committed a material mistake in the exercise of jurisdiction in relying upon the probable cost of constructing a new building of similar type in order to estimate the capital value as contemplated by Godhra Municipality and accordingly reduced the capital value fixed by the Sessions judge to Rs.90,000/. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court 's judgment was erroneous because the High Court did not apply its mind to the question whether the estimated capital value could be adopted as the capital value of the lands (1) [1964] 2 S.C.R. 608 at 616. 486 used with respect to a tax which was levied on the net annual value or rateable value of lands and buildings and not on their capital value. It was further contended that the High court 's judgment had failed to consider the real cost of construction of a new building and therefore the High Court had committed an error in applying the estimated capital values to the lands (2) [1962] Supp. 1 S.C R. 809 at 810. 486 and (3) [1963] Supp. 2 S. C. R. 708 at 712. 485 to the lands and buildings. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The High Court 'was right in holding that the courts were wrong in applying the estimate of capital value to the lands. [487 B D] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding the view that the word "rate" was not defined in the Act. [488 E] (iii) The High court was right in holding, that the courts had committed a fundamental error in applying a estimate of capital cost to the lands
4079: The appellant was the owner of a piece of land in the city of Bombay. He filed a suit for possession against the respondent on the ground that he had been in possession of the said land and that he had acquired title thereto by adverse possession. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the District Judge confirmed the decree. In second appeal, the High Court held that the attachment of the subject of dispute could be effected only if the Magistrate at any time after making the order under Section 145(1) considered the case to be one of emergency and decided that none of the parties was then in possession or that the property was not in such possession. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Magistrate is empowered to attach the subject of a dispute as regards the fact of actual possession of the subject matter of dispute. [145E] 2. The Magistrate has power to attach the property pending his decision under section 145(4). But the Magistrate can attach the subject matter in the execution proceedings. [145F] 3. The Magistrate may either himself proceed under section 145 or may refer the same to the Civil Court for decision. If he does so he will have jurisdiction to decide whether the property is in possession of a receiver appointed by any Civil Court or whether the property has been acquired by the receiver. [145G H] 4. The Magistrate cannot go behind the order passed under section 145 (1) and say that the property is not in possession of receiver. [146A] 5. The Magistrate while exercising powers under section 145 must act judicially and fairly according to natural justice. It is not open to him to take into consideration extraneous matters which are not germane to the issue before him. [144B C] 6. The Magistrate should not interfere with the order of the Magistrate merely because he considers the case to proceed under section 146(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [144C D]
6363: The Karnataka Contract Car ries (Acquisition) Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for the acquisition of contract carriages and certain other categories of public service vehicles in the State. Section 20 of the Act provided that the State Government may acquire any contract carriage or other category of public service vehicle by agreement with the owner of the motor vehicle on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit. Section 20(1)(a) provides that the State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution. The Income tax authorities rejected this claim. The High Court held that the tax was leviable only when the Finance Act, 1950, came into force, and that the exemption was not affected by the amendment of the said provision in 1953, because the Finance Act 1950, which applied the Income tax Act to the whole of India, except the State of Jammu and Kashmir, and substantially amended the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922.
