The petitioners further contend that the provisions of the Act are discriminatory and violative of articles 14, 19(1)(g), 301 and 304 of the Constitution and are therefore unconstitutional. The petitioners point out that the impugned notifications are violative of article 304(a) and (b). The petitioners also point out that in the case of the petitioners, the State has not taken into consideration the fact that the manufacturers of cement are entitled to sell the articles manufactured by them without liability to pay sales tax while the manufacturers in other States and non-manufacturers of the same article selling the same goods in the State are liable to pay sales lax. The petitioners also submit that the impugned provisions of the U. P. Sales Tax Rules, 1948 are violative of articles 301 and 303 of the Constitution because they impose unreasonable restrictions on their right to carry on trade and business guaranteed by article 301 of Constitution. The respondents refute these contentions. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. Article 301 of the constitution confers upon the States a power to make laws imposing reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said clause in the interest of general public. [803B] 2. The petitioners do not fall within the purview of article 301. [804E] 3. The petitioners cannot be said to be 'person ' within the meaning of article 301 if they are engaged in any business or profession. [805F] 4. The petitioners' contention that the impugned Act is violative of articles 19(1) (g) and 301 of the Con stitution is not correct
5104: The appellant landlord filed a suit against the tenant for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he required the premises bona fide for his residence. The respondent landlord contended that the appellant was in need of the premises for his own use and occupation. The trial court as well as the appellate court held that the appellant had proved in this case all the need for expansion of the building for girls ' education which was one of the objects of the appellant society. The High Court, in our opinion, misread the sanctioned plan and in holding that the appellant has proved in this appeal, misinterpreted the sanctioned plan which is Ext. 4, which according to the High Court shows in front side of the building abutting the road, a series of shops are to be constructed. The High court also erred in not interfering with such a question of fact. The High Courts judgment does not suffer from any infirmity. The High courts judgment does not show that the plan indicated that the shops were intended to be reconstructed in the new plan. The Highs Court was of the view that these shops were meant to be let out to tenants. The High 983 Court, therefore, in our view committed error in misconstruing the sanctioned plan. The question whether the plan indicated the proposed construction of the shops or not is a matter which should have been considered by the trial court and the High Court. In the circumstances, we set aside the order of the High Court and restore the order of eviction passed by the trial Court. The appeal is allowed accordingly.
3147: The appellant was charged with offences under section 9 of the , and section 9(1) (a) of the Act. The High Court rejected his application for permission to urge additional grounds. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain a revision petition against an order refusing to grant sanction to prosecute him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was in error in holding that there was no prima facie case against the appellant. [560C] 2. The High Courts were wrong in thinking that the High Courts should not interfere with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the courts below. [566A] 3. The High courts are not entitled to reappraise evidence or substitute their own view as if they are hearing appeals against acquittals. [565B] 4. The High has been rightly held to be competent to consider the question whether the High Court could have entertained a revision petition without examining the correctness of the decision of the lower courts. [564E] 5. The High is right in its conclusion that the High court was not justified in entertaining a revision petition. [563F] 6. The High would be justified in interfering with the concurrent finding of facts recorded by the two courts below. But this does not mean that the High should not be permitted to do so. [567D]
508: The petitioners who were allotted lands in the State of Punjab by the Custodian General of Evacuee Property, Punjab, applied for allotment of their lands under the provisions of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950. The applications were rejected on the ground that the allotment was made on quasi permanent basis and that, therefore, they have acquired certain rights in the lands which constitute 'property '. The Custodian General of evacuee property, however, cancelled the allotments on the ground of non compliance with the instructions issued by the Financial Commissioner, Rehabilitation, or the Custodian, Evacuee Property, East Punjab. The petitioners moved the Custodian General for restoration of the allotment to them but the Custodian General refused to restore the allotment to the petitioners. The petitioners thereupon filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the Custodian General. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allotment could not be restored unless the conditions laid down in the rules were complied with. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the allotment was contrary to the orders of the East Punjab Government or the instructions of the Financial Commissioner; (ii) the allotment is contrary to the instructions of a particular authority; (iii) the allotment has been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation; and (iv) the allotment being contrary to the terms of allotment, the cancellation of the allotment was illegal. HELD: (1) The allotment was made in contravention of the orders of a particular officer. The allotment was in fact made in breach of the orders passed by the Government. [825 G] (2) The allotment is contrary tO the orders of Government and the instructions of Government. The allotment is void ab initio. [826 A B] (3) The allotment cannot be restored unless there are other legal impediments. [827 C] (4) The allotment has been made in violation of the orders and instructions of the Government. The allottee had no right to continue in possession after the allotment was cancelled. [828 D] (5) The allotment does not confer any title upon the allottee. It merely confers a title upon him. [829 E F] (6) The allotment must be made in conformity with the rules and instructions of Government and not in derogation thereof. [830 H]
1186: The appellant, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in hides and skins. In the year 1949, the firm was registered under section 59 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. On January 1, 1941, the firm became dissolved and the firm was dissolved. The appellant filed an application for registration of his firm as a 'Hindu undivided family ' under section 7(1) of the Ordinance. The Assistant Custodian held that the firm had been dissolved on November 2, 1948, and that the firm was not an evacuee. He directed the Assistant Custodian to register the firm as a "Hindu undivided Hindu family" and to issue a certificate to the effect that the firm stood dissolved. The Assistant Collector of the District held that the appellant was not an "Hindu" and that the notice issued by him on the basis of which the Assistant Custodian passed order was invalid. The appellant appealed to the Deputy Custodian General who rejected the appeal. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the notice dated February 1, 1941 was invalid because it did not specify the nature of the assets of the firm and the business in respect of which the notice was issued. It also held that the Assistant Custodian had no power to issue a notice under section 7 (2) of the Act. Held: (i) The notice issued by the Assistant Custodian was valid and could be rectified by the Assistant Collector. The Assistant Controller of Evacuee Property, Madras, had jurisdiction to rectify the order of the Assistant Custodian. The Assistant Commissioner had no jurisdiction to revise the order of Assistant Custodian. (ii)The notice issued by a person who is not an evacuee was not a notice within the meaning of section 7(2). The Assistant Custodian had jurisdiction to correct the order of his own. The Assistant Director of Evacuee Property was competent to do so. The Assistant Directors of Evacuee Property were not entitled to exercise the powers of revision. (iii)The notice was not invalid because it contained a direction to the Assistant Custodian that he should take action against the persons concerned. The Assistant director had no authority to issue such a direction. The Assistant deputy Custodian had no jurisdiction or authority to pass any order in respect of the Assistant Director of the Evacuee Property. (iv)The notice
5786: The respondent assessee, a dealer in wool waste and woollen products, imported from abroad, imported goods of different descriptions. The Assistant Collector of Customs held that the goods were not wool wastes but were "wool waste" and hence they were liable to customs duty under section 130E(b) of the Customs Act, 1962. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assistant Collector. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The goods in question are wool waste, as such, entitled to the benefit of exemption under the notification. [375F] 2.1 The Tribunal has rightly held that the wool materials were wool waste. [376A] 2.2 The Tribunal was right in holding that the goods in question were wool wastes. [374B] 3.1 The expression "wool wastes" is defined in section 2(m) of the Act. It means all kinds of wool wastes which are used for wool or other work incidental to wool. [373C] 3.2 The expression "Wool wastes" has been defined in section 3(a) of the Tariff Act, 1975. The expression "otherwise", therefore, includes wool waste as well. [377D] 3.3 The expression "gold waste" is defined under section 2(n) of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The expression 'wool waste' is defined under Section 2(n). The expression 'gold waste ' is defined under the said Act. [378G H] 4.1 The word "wool" is defined by section 2(p) of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The definition of "wool Waste" is given in section 2 (zc) of the said Act, which defines "wool". [379H; 380A] 5.1 The term "wool", as defined in section2(zc), is defined in clause (j) of section 2(zd) of the . The term "sewerage" is defined as meaning any liquid waste including wool waste which is used for the purpose of wool
5231: The Respondent, Western Company of North America (Western Company) was restrained from pro ceeding further with an action instituted by it in a U.S.A. on the basis of an arbi tral award rendered by an Umpire in London. The Appellant ONGC filed a petition for setting aside the said order before the High Court of Bombay under section 34 of the . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petition was not maintainable as the award had been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation. The Appellant appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the Appellant that the award was not enforceable in India as a domestic award inasmuch as a Judgment in accordance with the Indian law had yet to be procured in an Indian Court, by the Western Company, and that the said Award was not as yet enforced in India as an independent proceeding in a foreign court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The award is not a judgment in accordance with Indian law. [196F] 2.1 The award does not suffer from any infirmity. [196G H] 2.2 The award is neither a decree nor an Order of the Court. [196H] 2.3 The award is a non judicial one. The award has been passed by the Umpire in the proceedings held in London. [196B C] 2.4 The award is an arbitral award which is capable of being enforced in a Court in India. [196D] 2.5 The award is therefore not a nullity. [196E] 3.1 The question whether the award is a foreign award or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The award can be challenged only if it is a foreign Award. [196C D] 3.2 The jurisdiction of the Umpire to decide the validity of the award is limited to examining whether the award falls within the scope of the arbitration agreement contained in the contract between the parties. [196 E F] 3.3 The Umpire cannot go beyond the terms of the contract. [196 G] 4.1 The Umpire has no jurisdiction to entertain the claim made by the Respondent. [196 B C] 5.1 The Respondent has not raised any objection to the maintainability of the claim. [196 C
5500: The appellant, a Christian Medical College and the hospital in which the respondent No. 1 was working as a Lecturer in the University of Madras, was established by an educational institution called the 'Sansthan ' known as 'the 'Sanathan ' 's College ' at Vellore. The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer on probation for one year from the date of his appointment. On completion of the period of probation he was confirmed with effect from 1st April, 1973. The appellant challenged the validity of the provisions of the Act before the Labour Court contending that sections 9 A, 10, 11A and 33 of the Act were applicable to educational institutions established and administered by minorities and that section 9 A was not applicable to minority institutions. The Labour Court held that the provisions of section 9 A were inapplicable to minority institutions and that the reference made under section 10(1)(c) of the Act to the Labour Court was incompetent. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions contained in section 9 A of the Act had no application to minority institutions because the appellant was not a minority institution within the meaning of article 30(1) of the Constitution of India. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions of section 10(2) of the , are not attracted to minority institutions as such adjudication amounted to interference with the right of the minority institution to administer its educational institution. [553C] 1.2 The provisions of the section are not intended to be applied to minority institutions but they are only applicable to minority educational institutions. [554E] 1.3 The provisions of sections 9A, 10,11A and 33 are not applicable to the minority institutions. [544F] 1.4 The provisions of Section 9A of the Act have been made applicable to minority institution also. [556G] 2.1 The Act is not intended to apply to minority institutions or to other institutions where the management has been taken over by the State Government. The Act does not provide for any appeal against the decision of the State Government to the Labour court. [555B] 2.2 The Act does contain provisions for the protection of the rights of minorities guaranteed under Articles 15
4873: The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant under section 13 A 1 of the Bombay Rent Act, 1947. The respondent tenant moved the High Court under article 227 of the Constitution against the decree for eviction on the ground that Section 13 A 1 did not enable a member or a retired member of the armed forces to seek the remedy provided by Section 13 A I of the Bombay Rents Act, 1947, and that the court should pass a decree for eviction in favour of the landlord on the ground of bona fide requirement. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the landlord bona fide required the premises for his own occupation. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the High Court had erred in interfering with the concurrent finding of fact recorded by the subordinate tribunals that the landlord bonafide requires the premises for the purpose of his own occupation, and that since the premises were already in the occupation of the tenant when he became the landlord, the landlord could not be said to have bona fide required them for his own use. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly held that the landlord need not prove bona fide requirement of the premises for himself or any member of his family. [801 B] (2) The High Courts are right in holding that the requirement of the landlord is bona fide. [802 C D] (3) The High courts are also right in holding so. [803 E] (4) The High court was wrong in interfering with concurrent findings of fact recorded on the question whether the landlord bona fi ties required the premises bona fide for his own residence. [804 F G] (5) The High has rightly held the landlord 's requirement to be bona fide. The High court has rightly held so. [881 H]
3529: The appellant was elected to the Orissa Legislative Assembly from the constituency of the respondent. He filed four nomination papers for being elected as a member of the Legislative Assembly. At the time of scrutiny on January 36, 1974, objection was raised at the instance of Balaram Sahu, one of the contesting candidates, before the Returning Officer that the respondent was disqualified under section 9A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 from seeking election. The Returning Officer rejected the objection and held that the respondent had not been disqualified under section 33 of the Act. The appellant challenged the election of the appellant by filing an election petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petition was liable to be dismissed for non compliance with sections 81, 83 and 34 of the Act since the respondent had failed to prove that he had incurred any disqualification under section 9 A of the Act for being chosen as a member. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in dismissing the election petition. [539E] (2) The High Courts were wrong in holding that the election petition was liable for non compliance of sections 81, and 83 of the Act because the respondent had neither pleaded nor proved that he had paid any amount towards the expenses incurred by him in connection with the works undertaken by the Government of Orissa in course of his trade or business for execution of the work undertaken by the government. [540F G] (3) The High court was right in holding that there was no violation of sections 81 and 83 of Act. [541C]
2800: The appellant was granted a lease of 555 sq. yards in village Pahadi, Taluka Borivli for constructing buildings for residential or business purposes. The lease was confirmed on September 28, 1955, by a single Judge of the Bombay High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the decision of the High Court of Bombay between the same parties and relating to the same land in the earlier proceeding for fixation of standard rent was res judicata since it had been finally decided by the High Court between the same party and relating to that land. HELD : (i) The decision of the Bombay Court in Vinayak Gopal Limaye 's case (2), which was affirmed by the Supreme Court in Vinaya Gopal Limayes 's case, is not res judicata because it has been finally decided in the previous proceeding between the same persons. [675 B] (ii) The decision in Vinayaka Gopal Limayade 's case does not operate as res judicata in a subsequent proceeding between the parties if the cause of action is different from the one in the previous proceedings. [676 C D] (iii) The decision rendered in Vinayaks Gopal Limayad vs Hingoo Manohar Missar, A.I.R. 1956 Bom. 747, relied on.
6281: The appellant was manufacturing carpets. He manufactured a carpets which were not of the description of 'textiles ' in Schedule I to the Act and hence the Act applied to every establishment which is a mere entity or an association of persons engaged in any industry specified in Schedule I. The appellant claimed that he had been carrying on business as a dealer under the Act and that he was entitled to be registered as a dealer. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim holding that the appellant was not a dealer within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Authority held that the appellant did not fall within the definition of 'textiles ' and that the appellant could not be said to be a dealer within section 2(d)(i) of the Central Sales Tax Act. The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner. In further appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the word 'texECT ' in the definition of "textile" in section 2(e) of the , must be construed as including 'texURT ' and that even if the word 'sword ' is used in the definition, the same would not mean that the appellant should have been a dealer. HELD: (1) The word 'text ' in the Explanation to section 2(a) of the is not confined to the word 'manufacture ' alone but includes the process of manufacture of goods by the appellant. [401 B] (2) The word "text" in the Explanation means the word 'means ' and does not include 'text. It has no reference to the context in which it occurs. The word 'sweat ' in the explanation means 'to produce or produce something.' [401 C D] (3) The word in the Explanation is not confined only to the word "texury" but also to the word in the sense of the word 'machinery '. The word "sword" in the explanation is not limited to the word as defined in the Act. [410 E F] (4) The word is used in its widest connotation and it takes its colour from the context in the light of which it is used and
922: The assessee was a resident in India and carried on business in the name and style of Sarabhai Chemicals in Baroda. In the assessment year 1947 47, the assessee claimed that it had acquired the business of a company in India and that its profits were received or deemed to have been received in or brought into India. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim and held that the Act did not apply to the business of the assessee. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer but the Tribunal allowed the appeal. In further appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The word "business" has no definite connotation. It is a term of wide import and includes every kind of business which is carried on by an individual. [539 B] (2) The expression "business" as defined in section 2(6) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, means any trade, commerce or manufacture or any adventure in the nature of trade, commerce, or manufacture. [540 C] (3) The word 'business ' in the context must be given a wider meaning than the word 'business'. [541 A] (4) The word business has a wide meaning. It may include any business incidental to the main activity of carrying on that particular business. But the word business does not mean any business of the nature of business of the person who carries on the business. [543 D] (5) The word trade has a wide connotation. The word business is also used in the sense of a business of a person who carries out his business. [551 E] (6) The word profession is not confined to the work of a man who works for another. It covers all activities which are regarded as part of the work of the person concerned. Therefore, the word business is not confined merely to the work done by a person who is engaged in the business of doing some particular type of work. [552 F G]
5970: The appellant No. 1 was the owner of a truck which met with an accident on 3rd December, 1966. He was travelling in the said truck from Udai pur to Udai pur. When he reached near the road, he collided with a truck coming from the opposite direction and hit him with a truck. He left behind him his wife, the appellant No. 2, his daughter, and a child. The appellants filed a petition before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal claiming compensation of Rs. 1 lac as compensation for the death of their son Hari Singh who died in the accident. The Tribunal disposed of the issue as to the claim of the appellants for compensation of Rs, 1 lac as against the Insurance Company which had been impleaded as respondent No. 3. The High Court upheld the award of the Tribunal for Rs. 10,000 in favour of the appellants. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the High Court was not justified in affirm ing the award of compensation as against the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the statutory liability of the Insurance Company was only up to a sum of Rs. 4,000. [787 G] (2) The High court was not justified, in affirm ing its order, in so far as it held that the statutory liabilities of the Insurance Co. were only up to Rs. 4000. [798 A B] (3) The High Courts ' interference with the quantum of compensation is permissible only if there are no grounds for interfering with the same. [789 C D]
4881: The Respondent, who was a tenant in respect of the premises in question, filed an application under section 14A(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 (Act No. 59 of 1958) for eviction of the Appellant from the said Government accommodation on the ground that he had acquired a suitable alternative accommodation by his own occupation. The Rent Controller held that the Respondent was in possession of the said Government premises and that he was entitled to be evicted therefrom. The Rent Control Tribunal dismissed the application holding that the Respondent had not acquired any suitable alternative accommodation. The Appellate Authority affirmed the order of the Rent Controller. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the respondent had acquired a reasonable and bonafide requirement of the premises for his own use and occupation; (ii) the respondent was in occupation of a reasonably suitable accommodation as was the case under clause (e) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 14 of the Act and (iii) the provisions of section 14A (1) were not attracted because the Respondent had failed to vacate the premises in his occupation within the time specified therein. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent was in possession and occupation of the premises since January 1, 1976. He had been paying rent regularly to the appellant. The respondent had also paid rent to the appellant from time to time. The appellant had not acquired a suitable alternate accommodation. [5B] 2. The respondent could not have been evicted from the premises in view of the provisions of Section 14A(2)(a). [6C] 3. The respondent has not acquired any other suitable accommodation. [6D] 4. The respondent is in occupation of the Government accommodation which is a part of the premises let out to him. The respondent cannot be said to have acquired any other accommodation. [7E] 5. The respondent did not acquire any suitable alternative premises. [7F] 6. The respondent 's claim for protection against eviction under section 14 A(1) is not maintainable. [7G] 7. The respondent having failed to vacate his Government accommodation within the time prescribed by law, the respondent is liable to be evicted from the said accommodation. [8
5483: The appellant was the tenant of a shop in Greater Kailash, New Delhi. The respondent landlord filed an eviction petition against the appellant under section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 on the ground that the appellant had sublet the premises to the respondent No. 2 and that the rent in respect of the premises had been deposited by him as per the appellant 's own admission. The appellant contended that the rent was deposited on account of the appellant ' 's husband ' and after the death of his wife, the tenancy was originally entered into between the appellant and the respondent No 1. The High Court held that the tenancy was for the then tenant and not for the appellant '. The High court also held that the appellant ' was entitled to be joined as a party in the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the appellant was not a necessary or proper party to the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The appellant was not entitled to be impleaded as a party to the eviction proceedings. [313F] (ii) The appellant has failed to prove that the rent which was deposited on behalf of his father was for the benefit of the erstwhile tenant. [314A] (iii) The appellant is not entitled to any relief. [315B] (iv) The appellant cannot be said to have been served with notice of termination of tenancy. [316C] (v) The appellant could not be said to be a necessary or a proper party to a proceeding before the High Court. [317D] (vi) The appellant had no locus standi to file the present appeal. [318E] (vii) The appellant having failed to establish that the rent deposited on behalf was for the benefits of the erstwhile tenants, he was not entitled for any relief. The appellant was merely trying to delay the disposal of the case. [319G]
1825: The appellant firm was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Match Works, Madras. The partnership deed provided that the partners were entitled to a share in the profits of the partnership firm. The Income tax Officer refused registration under section 26A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that different firms could not constitute a valid partnership. The Appellate Tribunal held that the partnership deed was not genuine but that the partnership was not genuine. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the reference under section 66(2) of the Act because the partnership deed did not contain any provision for the registration of the firm. HELD: (i) The Tribunal has held that the firm is not a genuine one. The Tribunal has not given reasons for its conclusion. [866 G] (ii) The Tribunal was right in holding that the partnership is not genuine. [867 B] (iii) The Tribunal had rightly held that the partners are entitled to a proportionate share in the profit of the partnership. [868 C] (iv) The Tribunal should have considered whether the partnership deed showed that the partners had contributed to the capital of the partnership or not. [869 D]
2270: The respondent 's application under section 11 of the Act for acquiring proprietary rights in the lands set out therein was rejected by the Forest Department on November 26, 1961. The respondent made an application under section II of the Act to acquire proprietary rights in respect of the said lands. The Compensation Officer held that the respondent was a tenant of the Union and that he was a cultivating tenant of the said land. He also held that the appellant had no right to claim compensation as provided by the Act. The appellant filed an appeal before the District Judge who dismissed it holding that the appellant was not a cultivating tenant but a tenant of a Government. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of the District Judge. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order of dismissal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the Act did not bind the Union or the State Government; (2) the respondent 's applications under section 11 could not lie against the Union or State Government and (3) the respondent being a cultivating tenant was entitled to the compensation payable under the Act. HELD: (i) The Act does not bind the State Government and an application under Section 11 can be filed only against the Union and the State Government. [576 F] (ii) The Act did not lay down any scheme for the acquisition of the rights of the landlord and the State. It merely lays down the procedure for the acquisition and the manner in which the compensation is to be determined. The Act does nothing more than make provision for the payment of compensation to the landlord and his tenants. [577 A B] (iii) The Act clearly provides that the compensation shall be paid to the landlord or his tenants. The compensation has to be paid to him or his tenants and not to the State Government or the Union. [578 C D] (iv) The Act makes no distinction between the State Government, the Union and any other person. The State Government is the owner of the land and the State is the owner thereof. The State cannot be considered to be a person interested within the meaning of section 2(h)(d). [579 E G] (v) The Act deals with the acquisition of proprietary rights
6716: The respondent, a tenant of the appellant 's building, filed a suit for recovery of possession of a building on the ground of arrears of rent, etc. The appellant contended that the respondent was not a tenant of a landlord and that he had no title to the building. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal by the respondent, the first appellate court confirmed the decree of the trial court but the High Court in second appeal reversed the same. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that as a result of the declaration by this Court of the constitutional invalidity of clause (ii) of section 30, which excluded from the purview of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, the appellant 'supervision could not be said to have been made without any enquiry into the question whether the denial or claim was bona fide. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A tenant who has been evicted under the provisions of the Tamilnadu Buildings (Leases and Rent Control ) Act, 1960 is entitled to protection against eviction provided he is in occupation of the building on the date of institution of the suit. [901B C] 1.2 The expression "tenant" in section 2(g) of the Act means a person by whom rent is payable and in the absence of any contract express or implied, such person shall be deemed to include also a person occupying the building as a sub tenant. [902C D] Rattan Arya & Ors. vs State of Tamil Nadu & Anr., ; , referred to.
5332: The respondent was an Inspector General of Police, Haryana. He was the Inspector General of the State of Haryana from June 30, 1980 to July 25, 1980. On his return from leave he was served with a confidential report assessing the performance of the respondent as the Inspector General. In the confidential report for the period ending March 31, 1980, the adverse remarks were duly accepted by the competent authority under the All India Services (Confidential Rolls) Rules, 1970, hereinafter referred to as 'the Rules '. After such acceptance, the adverse remark was communicated to him by the Home Secre tary, Haryana. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the authority of the Home Secretary to write a confidential report, assessing the performances, character and conduct of the respondent, as the InspectorGeneral of Police, and praying for quashing of such report or adverse remarks. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding inter alia that the Home Secretary had no authority to submit any report against the performance of respondent for the aforesaid period during which he was the Inspector general of Police, but directed the Home Secretary, Haryana to reconsider the matter in accordance with law. The Division Bench set aside the judgment of the Single Judge and allowed the writ peti tion holding inter alia, that the Home Secreta ry had no authority whatsoever to submit any reports against the performance o f the respondent for the aforementioned period during which the respondent was the Inspector Gener al of Police, nor could it be said that the Home secretary had any authority to do so. The Division bench also set aside the order of the Single judge directing the Home Secretary not to forward the confidential report to the Government. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1. The Home Secretary is the authority who is vested with the power to write the confidential report. [1036F] 1.2. The Home Secretaries are the authorities empowered to write the report. They have been given the powers of the Chief Secretary to make rules regulating their procedure and the manner of writing the confidential report of the members of the Service. 929: The appellant, a mortgagee in possession of the mortgaged property, filed a suit for recovery of the mortgage money on the basis of a preliminary decree passed by the Court. 5347: The appellant was arrested on the night of January 23, 1986. He filed an application for cancellation of bail granted to him by the High Court. The appellant moved this Court by means of a petition under Article 136 of the Constitution praying that the order of the High Court be set aside and he be released on bail. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Courts should not have been influenced by the fact that the trial had already commenced and the accused persons were in custody for more than three months. [901B] 1.2. In the instant case, the High Court has taken into consideration all relevant aspects including the gravity of the offence committed by the accused persons and the possibility of tampering with evidence or threatening witnesses. [902C D] 2.1. It is well settled that while considering the question of granting bail, the court must keep in mind the nature of accusations and the severity of punishment which conviction will entail unless judgment is delivered. [903E F] 2.2. The object of bail is to secure attendance of the accused at the trial and the proper test to be applied in the solution of the question whether bail should be granted or refused. The Court has also to consider whether there is any likelihood of the accused absconding or fleeing if released on bail [904F G] 3.1. While considering the question as to whether the accused would be readily available for trial, one has to turn to the nature of accusation made against him. Bail is normally granted to a person who is apparently innocent till proved guilty. But it is not so wide or large as to enable a person to overcome normal conditions of life in a given situation. [906D E] 3.3. The considerations which weigh with the Court in granting bail in non bailable cases are the nature and seriousness of the offence; the character of the evidence; circumstances which are peculiar to the accused; reasonable apprehension of witness being tampered with; the larger
4083: The appellant was accused 2 in a complaint filed by the first respondent against the petitioner and S.W. 1 in respect of an offence under section 403, 409, and 477A read with section 34, Indian Penal Code. The Magistrate issued summons to the appellant for production of certain documents. The appellant moved the High Court for quashing the proceedings on the ground that there was no warrant for search and seizure of books, documents etc. seized from him. The High Court held that the provisions relating to search and seizure contained in section 93(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, were not hit by article 20(3) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the power conferred on the Magistrate under section 91 of the Code is not an arbitrary one but is inherently necessary for the proper administration of criminal justice; (ii) the power under section 91 is not intended to be used as a shield or to protect the accused from being questioned in any manner whatsoever; (iii) the power of the Magistrate under Section 91 is not limited to summoning witnesses, examining them on oath, questioning the complainant and his witnesses, compelling the attendance of the accused, requiring the appearance of the accused persons, compelling the production of documents and material objects, etc., and (iv) the power to issue a search warrant under section 91 was not intended to confer on the Magistrate any special powers which are not expressly provided for in the Code. HELD: (i) The power under section 93(2) of the Cr. P.C. is not an absolute one but is subject to the limitations imposed by the other provisions of the Code. [560B] (ii) The power conferred on a Magistrate under section 94(1) is not an unfettered one but is a discretionary one. It must be exercised sparingly and only in those cases where the circumstances of the case so require. [540E F]

The Financial Commissioner accepted the appeal and restored the grant of nautor. The Financial commissioner accepted the appeal on the following two grounds: (i) The appellant felled the trees on the land without waiting for necessary approval of the Divisional Forest Officer and as such he took the law in his own hands; (ii) The appellant did not have any income of more than Rs.2,000 per annum from all sources including lands. The Financial Commis sioner accepted the appeal. The Financial Commission also accepted the appeal, but rejected the same. The Financial Comm issioner accepted the second ground that the appellant felling the trees on his land without waiting any approval of the Forest Department. [110 G H]
1423: The appellant was a guarantor for the repayment of Rs. 25,000/ advanced to him by the respondent Bank. The respondent Bank had agreed to allow an overdraft to the appellant for Rs. 20,000/ and when that was pointed out to the appellant he altered his letter of guarantee to Rs. 20.000/ and this amount was subsequently reduced to Rs.20,000/ . The appellant 's case was that the letter of guarantee was not acted upon and the respondent Bank had no authority to alter the terms of the guarantee. The High Court held that the letter dated May 24, 1947 was not a new contract but only a modification of the earlier agreement. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The letter of guarantee is a document which is made in order to carry out the common intention of the parties. It is not necessary that the letter must be written with the consent of the party who has given it. [536 D] (2) The letter dated May 23, 1947 was a letter of guarantee and the letter of indemnity was not a mere instrument of guarantee. The letter of indemnity merely recites that the appellant had agreed to give a letter of credit for the sum of Rs. 20 lakhs and that the appellant would give a letter to the Bank of the sum of about Rs. 20 lacs. The letter does not contain any reference to the letter of credit or the letter of bond. [537 C E] (3) The letter was not a letter of security but was a letter from the appellant to the Bank giving instructions to the Bank to accept the letter of surety as a letter of assurance. The letter did not mention anything about the letter of Guarantee. [538 A B] (4) The letter did nothing more than a letter of one of the parties to the other. The letter merely stated that the appellant was willing to pay the amount of Rs. 10 lakhs on the basis of the letter of the Bank. The letter also mentioned that the appellant should take up the matter with the Bank and obtain a letter of discharge from the Bank. [539 F G]

4861: The appellant, a Government of India undertaking, entered into an agreement with the respondent for purchase of certain goods. The respondent was to supply certain goods to the appellant. The appellant claimed that the respondent had not supplied the goods to the respondent. The respondent contended that the contract did not provide for arbitration but only provided for arbitration. The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was maintainable under section 33 of the . In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit filed by the respondent was not "in respect of any matter agreed to be referred to arbitration" as required by s.3 of the Foreign Awards Act and that the suit should have been stayed under s.3(a) of the Foreign Award. 607: The respondent, a minor, executed an agreement in 1932 to partition the family properties and to allot one half share to him. In 1933 he executed another agreement in 1932 for the partition of the family properties. On June 21, 1936, the arbitrator made an award which was registered on July 28, 1936. The award was signed by both the parties as well as their respective counsel. The arbitrators gave their consent to the award. The appellant filed objections under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the award. He contended that the award was not binding on him because it was passed after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed by article 49 of the Limitation Act. Held, that the award is not binding on the appellant. It is open to the court to consider whether the award was vitiated by fraud or mistake. The question whether the award is vitiated by fraud must be decided with reference to the facts of each case. The award does not become void merely because it is based upon an erroneous view of law or on a wrong construction of the terms of the contract. The award is not liable to be set aside on the ground that it is based on an erroneous interpretation of the terms or that it is vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record.
3065: The accused was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death on the former count. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the accused. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable and that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The prosecution has proved the motive for the murder of the deceased. The motive is a relevant fact. [813F] 2.1. It is well settled that in order to establish the guilt of an accused person, the prosecution must prove the following facts before it can bring home the guilt of the accused:- (i) That the accused was last seen with the deceased; (ii) That he made no attempt to save the deceased from being murdered; (iii) That he did not know where the dead body of the deceased was lying; (iv) That he had no motive to kill the deceased; and (v) That he committed the murder of his wife. [814E F] 3.2. The prosecution had established the motive for committing the murder of deceased by the accused. The prosecution could have proved the motive by examining the neighbours who were present at the time of the occurrence. But the prosecution failed to do so. [815B C] 4.1. 5060: The petitioners who were direct recruits to the posts of Assistant Engineers in Grade IV in the Indian Economic Service, filed a Writ Petition under Article 32 of the Constitution praying for a writ, direction or order in the nature of mandamus directing the Union of India to confirm or regularise their services in the posts held by them as and from the dates when they became due for confirmation or regularisation in accordance with the Indian Economics Service Rules, 1961. The petitioners contended that the vacancies available to the departmental candidates under Rule 8(ii) of the Indian Economic Services Rules, 1961 had not been filled up on regular basis and that the said vacancies should be filled up only by a selection from among the officers serving in the offices under the Government in Economic/Statistical posts recognised for this purpose by the Controlling Authority. The petitioners also contended that the respondents had no right to insist upon the petitioners ' appointment being made on ad hoc basis for long years and that the petitioners could not be treated as regularly appointed employees of the Department. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 In the absence of any statutory provision or rule providing for recruitment to the post of Assistant Engineer in Grade IV, the petitioners cannot claim to have been regularly appointed against the said post. Their rights are governed by the Recruitment Rules and the Recruitment Rules which govern the service conditions of the petitioners. 233: The appellant was a servant of the Government of Madras. He was charged with an offence under section 161 I.P.C. for having committed the murder of his wife and two children. The trial was held by the Special Magistrate who acquitted him but convicted him on the ground that he had not been given any opportunity to show cause against his conviction. The High Court set aside the order of acquittal, holding that the sanction given by the Government under section 197(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code was invalid because the order of the Magistrate appointing the Special Magistrate did not disclose that all the facts constituting the offences to be charged were placed before the sanctioning authority. Held, that the sanction granted by the Government was valid and it could not be said that the prosecution was instituted without giving the accused an opportunity to show why the prosecution should fail. The fact that the prosecution is instituted without giving notice to the accused does not make the prosecution illegal. It is only when the prosecution is launched after the charge sheet has been filed that the accused can be tried in accordance with law.

The appellant contended that the State legislature having authority to enact a law imposing a tax on the sale of goods, was incompetent to impose a tax on such supply. Held, that the State Legislature having authority to legislate on the subject must necessarily be held to have been competent to enact a statute levying a tax on transactions of sale of goods. The State Legislature having power to enact a taxing statute, it had no power to make a law imposing tax on transactions which are outside the legislative competence of the State Legislature. The State Act is a self contained enactment and the State Legislature has no power to levy a tax on a transaction which is outside the legislative field of the State.

2026: The respondent was a lady workman employed in the appellant concern. On account of her unemployment she had to be taken back into service on the ground that she had not completed 240 days of work during the preceding 12 months. The appellant company terminated her services by an order dated December 31, 1963. The respondent challenged the termination before the Labour Court. The Labour Court held that the termination was illegal and directed reinstatement with full wages. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the rule requiring un married women to resign as soon as she marries is not applicable to married women because there are no such rules exist in other departments of the respondent concern itself and it is only in one department that the rule is in force. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The rule which requires un married woman to resign as early as possible from the employment of the employer is not intended to apply to married women who have to work in the pharmaceutical industry. [495F] (2) The rule does not require any special reasons to justify its departure from the general rule of standing. It merely provides that if a woman has served for more than 240 days in the preceding 12 calendar months, she may be permitted to resign. This rule cannot be said to be in conflict with the general rule laid down in section 2(g) of the Industrial Disputes Act. [496A B] (3) The rule is not intended either to apply to a married woman or to a married women who are not married but who have to be discharged from service on account of their being unemployed. [494C D] (4) The rule applies to married women also. [498E]

There were different aspects of this industrial dispute which required consideration and the Central Government, therefore, formulated each aspect as a separate question and referred those questions for adjudication to the Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta. The Tribunal held that the bonus claimed by the workmen was not available to them because the Bank had not been able to prove that the workmen had actually worked during the accounting year and that they had earned profits on the basis of the bonus claimed. The Tribunal further held that the workmen were entitled to receive bonus at the rate of 20% of the salary or wage earned during the accounting period. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that (i) the bonus claimed was not admissible under section 6(1)(a) of the Act; (ii) the bonus was not payable by reason of any provision in the Act; and (iii) the bonus could be paid only if the workmen had worked during the relevant accounting year. [136 A B] (vi) The bonus is not paid by way of profit bonus. [137 B C]

2374: The appellant was the owner of a factory in which he had been carrying on business. 1385: The appellant in the appeal was a Director of N. The complaint was dismissed under section 203 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on the ground that the offence alleged was committed by him as a director of N. and not as a person who was responsible for the conduct of the business of the company. The High Court held that the appellant was guilty of the offence charged and convicted him under section 120B read with section 109 I.P.C. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the appellant had been guilty of the offences charged. HELD: (i) The appellant was not a person who could be said to have abetted the commission of the offence. 2200: The appellants, who were dealers in iron and steel, purchased cotton from various dealers in Punjab and outside for the manufacture of yarn and cloth. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the amended provision, section 2(ff) was void as it infringed the freedom of trade and commerce guaranteed by article 301 of the Constitution. [740 C D] (3) The amended provisions, section 2 (ff) was valid and could not be challenged on the ground that they violated articles 301 and 304 of the constitution. [741 E F] (4) The amended Act is not violative of article 301 of Constitution. It is a piece of legislation with respect to the same subject matter. [742 A B] (5) The amended Section 2(ff), was valid and does not infringe any of the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19 of the constitution, and the amended section is valid. 1307: The appellant, a money lender, filed a suit for an order reopening the personal decree. The appellant contended that the liability to return the goods seized under section 110(1) on the expiry of the first six months or extended period should be absolute as it is subject to the period being extended for a period not exceeding six months. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The proviso to section 1 0(1) does not contemplate a notice to the person who has made the application for extension of the period of one year. [808 G]
975: The appellant was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1955 55. He filed a return of his income under section 22(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, and claimed that he had not been served with any notice under section 22 (1). The Income Tax Officer issued notices under section 34 read with section 22(1) on the ground that the appellant had failed to make a return within the time prescribed by cl. (a) of sub section (1) of section 22. The appellant 's contention before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was that the proceedings for assessment were commenced within the period of limitation prescribed for serving notice of assessment under section 22. Held: (i) that the words "any person" in section 22(I)(a) must be construed as including a non resident assessee who has no taxable income at all. The word "person" in section 23(1)(b) means a person who is resident in India and who has no income or other income which would have accrued or arisen in India if he had not returned to India. The word 'person ' in section 23 includes a non resident person; and the proviso to section 22(l)(a) applies only to persons who are resident in India but not to persons who do not come within the purview of the proviso. The proviso does not apply to persons who have no income or income which would otherwise have accrued or arose in India. The proviso merely postulates that the person concerned should be a resident in India. [439 B C] (ii)The proviso cannot be interpreted so as to exclude a non resident who has no business connection in India. It is not intended to exclude a person who has no property or income in India from being assessed to income-tax. The proviso is intended to cover persons who have business connection in the country where they may be residing. In the present case, the appellant was not a resident in the taxable territory and therefore could not be treated as resident in India because he did not have any income or income in the taxable territories. The proviso was meant to cover persons resident in India who had no income or incomes in India. Therefore, the appellant could not be said to be a resident within the meaning of the proviso to s.23(1)(
1488: The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The respondents were all jute mill companies which purchased raw jute and manufactured finished goods therefrom. The respondents entered into contracts with the appellant for sale of raw jute and manufacture finished goods therefrom and the appellant was a registered dealer under the Bengal Chamber of Commerce and Industry. The respondents filed applications for revocation of the authority of an arbitrator appointed under the provisions of the Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952, and the notifications issued by the Central Government thereunder, to the effect that the authority of the arbitrator appointed under those Acts had been revoked. The appellant 's case was that the respondents were all foreigners and that the respondents had no knowledge about the existence of any emergency in the matter of the contract. The respondents contended that the appellant had not acted in good faith or in pursuance of any statutory duty imposed on it by law and that the appellant was entitled to revoke the authority of its arbitrator. Held: (i) The appellant was not entitled to revoke its authority under section 5(1)(a) of the . It was not competent to the arbitrators to grant relief to the respondents. (ii)The appellant could not be said to have acted in good bona fide or in pursuance thereof. (iii)The appellant was not bound to act as an arbitrator under the terms of the contract and the arbitration clause did not apply to the facts of the present case. (iv)The appellant had not given notice to the respondents of the existence of the emergency and the circumstances in which they came to enter into the contract. (v)The appellant having failed to give notice to the respondent of the existence or non existence of the Emergency, the appellant was not liable to pay damages.
5826: The appellant company was granted a licence under the Madhya Pradesh Electricity Supply and Consumption Regulation Order, 1975 for supply of electricity in accordance with the terms and conditions mentioned therein. The respondent No. 1 Madhya Pradesh Electricity Board entered into an agreement dated 27.10.1971 with the appellant company for supply of electrical energy in accordance with terms and conditions enumerated in the said agreement. The appellant company had to supply 2,500 K.W. of electricity to the respondent No.1 Madhya Pradesh Electricity board. The respondent no. 1 Madhya Gujarat Electricity Board issued a letter dated 17.5.1975 (marked as Annexure `B ') to the appellant stating that the appellant had been supplying electricity to the Board from 12.11.1979 onwards and that the Board would be charging the tariff at the rate of Rs.2.50 per unit for the period from 12.6.1979 to 31.3.1980. The appellant also stated that the Board had to supply power to the respondent no.1 from 12.4.80 onwards. The respondent company informed the appellant by its letter dated 5.8.1980 that the Board was not able to generate sufficient electricity to meet the full demand of the consumers and with a view to ease the situation two orders were issued by the States of Madhya Pradesh under section 22B of the . The Divisional Engineer, Gwalior informed the appellant that the Board has to supply 2.500 K. W. of electricity from 12.9.79 to 31.12.80 and the Board had no objection if the supply is made at the rate fixed by the State Government. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the Divisional Engineer on the ground that the Board could not have supplied 2,500 k.w. of electricity without the Board 's prior approval and a letter Annexure `T ' dated 5.08.1980 was sent to the appellant informing him that the Board will be levying the tariff @ Rs.2/P. per unit for a period of 3 years. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Board cannot charge the tariff @ 2.50 per Unit for a period exceeding 3 years. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right
6596: The appellant, a tenant of a shop in the city of Jammu & Kashmir, was carrying on business in the name and style of "M/s. Rattan Arya & Sons" at J & K Bank Ltd., J & K, a partnership firm. The appellant was carrying on the business of construction of buildings in the city. The appellant filed an application for eviction of the respondent from the premises under section 14(1)(e) of the Jammu & Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966. The respondent contested the application on the ground that clause (iii) of sub section (3) of Section 1 of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and shops Rent Control Act is discriminatory and arbitrary because it draws an artificial distinction between tenants on the basis of their income. The High Court upheld the validity of clause (iii). The High Court held that clause (ii) of sub sec.(3) of section 1 of the Act read with Explanation, is attracted in respect of the appellant. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The object of the Act is to protect the tenants who are not in occupation of any building or part thereof. [801F] 1.2 The object of clause (i) of sub s.(3) is to prevent the landlord from evicting the tenant if he has let out more than one building or part of a building to another person. The object of this clause is to prevent tenants from letting out more than two parts of a building. The object is to prevent landlords from ejecting tenants from the building occupied by them. [802B C] 1.3 The object of section 1 is to prevent persons from letting out portions of a building which are not let out to tenants. The object can be achieved only by the provision of section 30(ii) of the Act. The object cannot be achieved by the provision in section 30(iii) of the act. [803C D] 1.4 The object of sub section 3 of section 1 being to prevent tenants of the nature mentioned therein from letting out the whole or any part of the building occupied thereby, the legislature has deliberately used the expression 'tenant ' in the said sub section. The word 'tenant '
4229: The respondent was searched by the Customs authorities and a search was conducted in his premises. He was found to have received Rs. 65,500/ as illegal gratification from one of his customers. The Income Tax Officer took proceedings under section 10(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 for assessing him. The Income tax officer held that out of Rs. 65.500/ an amount of Rs. 60,500/ constituted income of the assessee from undisclosed sources. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. In second appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal the assessee represented that if he was regarded as engaged in the business of smuggling gold he was entitled to a deduction under section 10 (1) of Income Tax Act. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the Revenue that the loss incurred in carrying on the illegal business must be deemed to be the income of the person who carried it on. The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the loss of Rs.65,500/ arose out of the confiscation of the currency notes. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "business" has been defined in section 2(6A)(c) of the Indian Income Tax Act and the definition is not confined to the business of the nature of business done or intended to be done by the assessee. [5B] 2. The word "business" in section 2 (6A)(a) includes any trade, commerce or manufacture or any adventure in the nature of trade, commerce, or manufacture. [5C] 3. The expression 'business ' in section 2 has been used in a wider sense so as to include within its ambit all activities which are incidental or ancillary to the main activity carried on by the assessee and which are incidental to the main object. It is not necessary that the business should be carried on in the course of trade or commerce. [5D E] 4. The expression business means the business of doing any act or thing which is the intentional part of the series of acts or omissions constituting the particular transaction which may be described as the principal activity of the assessee. The expression is not restricted
932: The appellant was a resident of the village in which an additional police force was stationed. He was charged with offences under section 147, 148 and 149 I.P.C. for having committed offences punishable under sections 147, 148, 149, 150, 151, 152, 153A, 153B, 153C, 153D, 153E, 153F, 153G, 153H, 153I, 153J, 153K, 153L, 153N, 153O, 153R, 153Q, 153R and 153R of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted him but the High Court confirmed his conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that (i) the exemption granted by the notification was not based on any special reason or ground; (ii) the notification did not provide for the imposition of any condition on the basis of religion, race or caste; (iii) the notification was invalid as it violated article 15(1) of the Constitution; (iv) the notification had been issued in exercise of its power conferred by section 15 of the Act and was therefore ultra vires. HELD: (i) The exemption granted by notification was not founded on any special reasons or ground. [152 B] (ii) The notification was not supported by any special reason. It is clear from the language used in the notification that the exemption was granted only on the ground of religion, caste or community and not on any other ground. [155 C] (iii) The notification does not say that the conditions imposed were such as would make the area of operation of the additional police force difficult or difficult. The words "any portion of the cost of the additional force" are merely descriptive of the area of the additional Police Force. The notification does no more than indicate that the additional force has been posted. [153 D E] (iv) The notification did not impose any condition on any of the grounds set out in article 15(4). [153 F G]
3105: The respondent Company was a fairly reputed company and the appellants were its members. The respondent Company had entered into an agreement with the Union for payment of bonus on the basis of the general bonus paid under the agreement exhibit A.5. The respondent claimed that it should be paid bonus as per the Act in addition to what has been paid as per the agreement exhibit B. The Industrial Tribunal rejected the claim, but allowed the respondent 's claim for bonus under the Act. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the amount paid under the agreements exhibit A. 5 was an ad hoc or ex gratia payment made out of charity and as a supplement to the wages and that it was not an annual payment, nor was it paid in lieu of bonus based on profits. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The general bonus paid by the Company including the one in question is an ad hoc payment made out from the profits of the company. [453 F] (2) The general payment made under the agreement exhibits A.5 is an adhoc payment made out under the agreement exhibiting the same as profit. The payment of bonus under the agreement is an amount paid as production bonus or incentive wages. The payment under the agreement does not depend upon any profit or gain. It is only a part of the general payment which is made under the terms of the agreement. [454 G H] (3) The payment under a particular agreement is an ad interim payment made out in lieu of the general or bonus payable under the agreement. The payment made under such agreement is an item of income which is chargeable to tax under section 4(1)(a). The payment is an ad-hoc payment made under a specific term of the agreement between the parties. The payment itself is an adinterim payment made under an agreement between the employer and the workmen. The payment in question is a part of a general payment made to the workmen.
