931: The respondent firm which was a licensed dealer under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the assessment order on the ground that the order was illegal and not supported by the authority of law. The High Court held that in the case of hides and skins the general provision was inapplicable and a special rule for taxation was laid down by section 5(vi) of the Act and section 6 A was not applicable to the case of a dealer who did not take out a licence for dealing in hides and kins. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had erred in holding that in the cases of hides or skins the rule limiting the operation of the mode of taxation to licensed dealers was ultra vires as it contravened section 5(v) of the Madras General sales Tax Act, 1929. HELD: (i) The rule limiting a particular class of transactions is not necessarily confined to the class of persons who are entitled to be registered under the Act. It may be that the rule does not apply to a class of persons but only to such persons who are not entitled to be so registered. [560 B] (ii) The rule is not intended to restrict the operation of a general provision like the one in the present case. It merely provides for the application of a general rule to all classes of transactions. It is not intended that the rule should be applied to all classes. It is only where the rule is inconsistent with the general provisions of the Act that the rule can operate. [566 C D] V. Syed Mohammed & Co. vs State of Madras, ; , followed.
1225: The appellant entered into three contracts for the construction of a aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and other works at Ranchi. The respondents entered into two contracts for the work of construction of a canal, hangahattes, buildings, stores and other works, and the appellant filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents filed an application to set aside the award on various grounds. The Subordinate Judge dismissed the application but granted a certificate under article 132(1) of the Constitution. The High Court confirmed the decree of the Subordinate Judge but granted a certifi cate under articles 132 and 133(1) Of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the agreement for reference to arbitration did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the Constitutional provision in force at the relevant date, and it was therefore void. HELD: (i) The agreement for reference is not an instrument relating to execution of works within the meaning of section 175 of the Government 's Act, 1935. It must be construed as a contract relating to the execution of works, and if it does not fall within entry 12, in which case it should be executed in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [829 B] (ii) The agreement between the parties for referring the dispute to arbitration contained in the agreement for arbitration cannot be said to be an instrument relating exclusively to the execution or performance of the works. The agreement for refer ment to arbitration does not come within entry 12 of the Act, and the agreement for referring the disputes to arbitration does also not come within the purview of item 2 of the Schedule to the Act. The agreement in question is not an agreement relating to the completion of the works, nor does it relate to the execution and performance of the work. [830 C D] (iii) The agreement in the present case is not an authority for the proposition that the agreement is an instrument relating only to the execution, performance and execution of the works and does not cover the works. [831 E F] (iv
1982: The appellant, a sugar mill, was levying a cess on sugarcane. The State Legislature passed the Madhya Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1961, which provided for the constitution of the Council to regulate the supply and purchase of sugarcane. Section 23 of the Act made a levy of cess payable as prescribed by it. The appellant challenged the validity of the Central Act 526 the (No. 38 of 1961) (hereinafter called 'the Act '), in its application to the State of Madhya Pradesh under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court held that the Act did not represent provisions enacted by Parliament as such but it was merely an attempt to validate the invalid State Statutes. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The Act is not a law within the meaning of article 13(2) of the Constitution. It is a piece of legislation with respect to matters enumerated in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. [532 C] The Central Act does not represent any provision of the State Acts or of the notifications issued thereunder. The Central Act is not concerned with the imposition, assessment and collection of the cess. The State Legislatures are competent to make laws imposing, levying, collecting and recovering the cess. [533 D]
4832: The Appellants were publishers of books for general reading to be kept in school and college libraries. They had been selected by the State Government as a supplementary list of 105 books out of the said 1,718 books which had been submitted for selection. The State Government issued a notification on December 3, 1982 under section 4(1) of the Orissa Education Act, 1981 notifying the selection of the books for the year 1982. The Appellants challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that the State Government had no power to make the selection without the approval of the Central Government. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the State was not entitled to change the selection procedure after the approval of its own by the Central Government and that the State had no right to change the procedure after the receipt of the approval of it. Dismissing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The State has the power to select books for the purpose of selecting the best available persons. It is open to the State Government to prescribe the manner in which the books are to be purchased from the grant made by the Central or the State Government. [330F] 2. The State cannot change the selection process after the approval is given by the Central Govt. The State can do so only if there is any provision in the rules or regulations governing the selection. In the present case, the State Government did not have any such power. [329A B] 3. The State had the right to reject any book recommended by the Assessment Sub Committee and, therefore, the fact that some members of the Assessment Sub committee had also submitted their books for selection, but as further funds became available the Government decided to select more books and accordingly constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of Director of Public Instruction, Orissa. The State was bound to select the best available books and the State had the power to reject any books recommended by the Committee. [328C D] 4. The State could not change the selection criteria after the approval was given by the State Govt. The decision of the State Government in setting up a Committee for the selection to be made for purchase of books from the grant was neither arbitrary nor against public interest inasmuch as the procedure followed by the State was neither arbitrary or against
2885: The petitioners who are traders in foodgrains, challenge the validity of section 7 read with section 2 (v) and section 1 0 read with section 13 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 37 of 1954 and the rules framed thereunder. They also challenge the constitutional validity of section 19(1)(a) and (b) of the Prevention Food Adulterated Act 37 of 1955. The petitioners contended that section 7 read as a whole was ultra vires the Constitution and that the provisions of the Act were not valid. The petitioners further contended that the provisions contained in sections 3 to 9 were invalid inasmuch as they contravened articles 14, 19(1) (g), 21 and 22 of the Constitution. The petitioners also challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution because the Act was discriminatory and violative of article 14. The petitioners urged that the Act was void for want of legislative competence since it infringed articles 14,19(1)(g), 21, 22 and 23 of the Constitution and therefore the Act was bad for non compliance with the provisions of article 14 of Constitution. Held: (i) The Act was a law made by Parliament under entry 33 of List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. It is a law made under entry 11 of List III and not under entry 18 of List II. The Act was enacted by Parliament under Entry 33 of List I of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution which provides that the control of food stuffs including edible oilseeds and oils shall be exercised by the Central Government or the State Government or any officer authorised by them in this behalf. The Act does not violate article 14 of constitution. The Act is a law passed by Parliament under entries 52 and 53 of List I and entries 24 and 25 of List II of the Seventh Sche dule to the Constitution respectively. The Act has been passed by Parliament in exercise of its power conferred by entry 33 of the Concurrent List. The Act being a law made in exercise of the power conferred by entries 52 and 54 of List I, the Act cannot be said to have been passed by the Parliament under entry 66 of List I. The Act, therefore, is not hit by article 14 of State Legislature. (ii)The Act is a piece of colourable legislation because it seeks
4973: The appellant and the respondents were the legal heirs of Asharfi Devi. The respondents filed a suit for declaration that they had validly executed the will exhibit A 6 dated 21 12 1957, and that the appellant was entitled to succeed to the limited right of her deceased husband under the will. The trial court decreed the suit in part holding that the appellant had become the heir of her husband by reason of the adoption and that the second respondent had spent the sum of Rs. 1004.97 towards sewa puja and raj bhog of Gopal Ji and thus she became entitled to the entire estate of Asharffi Devi. In appeal the High Court held that the appellant 's right to succeed to her estate under the will was restricted in the manner provided in section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and that the respondents could not claim any right to the property of Asharfa Devi as the heir of the first respondent. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the second appellant had become her heir of the deceased husband by reason only of the adoption of the first appellant and that the first respondent had spent a sum of Rs, 1004. 97/ towards sewa pooja and rajbhog of the first defendant and that the other properties belonged to the first respondent and that the High court should have dismissed the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was wrong in holding that if a shebait dies leaving behind him a widow and no son she would succeed to the shebaiti rights under the ordinary law but her rights in the shebaits would be restricted in the same manner as they would have been if the successor was the son, which view has been accepted by the Privy Council in Bhabe Foririe vs Ashalata Devi (supra). [378 D] 2. The High court was wrong in its conclusion that the second defendant had acquired the right of the first plaintiff under the will exhibit 7. The High Cou rt committed an error in holding that she was entitled to the estate of Ashera Devi. [379 E F] 3. The High Courts decision is correct and
1518: The appellants purchased the properties in dispute by a sale deed executed on February 27, 1945. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of arrears due from them and obtained an order of attachment of their property. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the sale was without jurisdiction; (ii) the sale could not be held validly for the recovery of Rs. 1,354/9/ , as the amount shown in the proclamation of sale as the arrear due from the appellants had been shown as Rs. 730/13/ ; and (iii) the sale in question was invalid under section 149(2) of the Act. HELD: (1) The sale in question is invalid under section 150(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [560 C] (2) The appellants ' contention that the arrears due from the appellant were due from them cannot be accepted because the amount shown as arrears in the proclamation was not due. The appellants have no right to challenge the validity of the sale on the ground that the arrears were due from the respondents. [540 D] (3) The appellants had not challenged the validity of any sale before the High Court. They had only challenged the validity or otherwise of the sale. [541 A B] (4) The appellants did not raise the plea that the arrears of rent due from them were due from their predecessor in interest. The appellants had merely raised the plea that they were entitled to recover the arrears of Rs. 7,30/13 / which was shown in the sale proclamation as arrears of rent. [542 E F] (5) The appellants could not take advantage of the provisions of section 149(1)(a) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. [543 G H]
447: The appellant, a registered body under the Indian Trade Unions Act, gave its registered office at Delhi. The respondent, the Delhi Improvement Trust, was the owner of the land in dispute and the appellant was the lessee thereof. The respondent applied to the Government of India for permission to sell the land on which the market called the New Fruit and Vegetable Market, Subzimandi, under the supervision of a single authority. The Government refused to grant the permission on the ground that the land belonged to the Trust and that the appellant had no right to sell the same. The appellant thereupon filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The provisions of section 54A of the Improvement Act as applied to the Province of Delhi and the agreement (exhibit D 5) between the respondent and the Trust were applicable to the tenancy created by the Trust in favour of the appellant. [10 A B] (ii) The lease was not a mere one-sided one. It was executed for a period of 20 years with the consent of the lessor. The lease was for a period not exceeding 20 years. The lease did not create any interest in the land. The lease could be terminated only if the lessee was found to have committed breach of the terms of the lease. The lease being for a fixed term, the lessee was entitled to continue in possession till he was evicted by the lessor. [11 C E] (iii) The appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 54 A of the Improvement act as applied to his case. The lease having been granted for a fixed period, the appellant was entitled to remain in possession until he was evicted. [12 G]
5878: The respondent company was manufacturing a steel rod and a hot rolled steel rods. It had classified all rectangular products of thickness less than 3.0 mm and of length more than 75 mm. The respondent claimed that the product in question fell within the definition of "Hoops" as defined in Item 26AA(ia) of the Central Excise Tariff. The Assistant Collector, Central Excise on the basis of certain discussion, held that rectangula sheets were not covered by Tariff Item 26AA. He also considered the definition of 'Hoops' as follows: "Hoop and Strip (heading No. 73.12) rolled products with sheared or unsheared edges of rectangle section of thickness less one tenth of the width, in straight strips, coils or flattened coils." The Tribunal allowed the appeals and held that the flat product of thickness less only 1.5 mm and a width of less than 75 mm was classifiable under sub item (ii) of Tariff Item 26. The Tribunal further held that the product of the respondent was not curled hoops but straight length. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the flat goods of thickness less that 3.0mm and a width less than 75mm were not covered under Tariff Item 26A(ia). Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has rightly held that the flats in question were not ropes nor are they synonyms. [599E] 2.1 The expression "Hoofs" is used in the Tariff Heading 26AA(i) which covers all sorts of ropes. The word "Hoose" is not defined in the Tariff Act. The term "Hoos" is defined in Section 2(f) of the Tariff Act as meaning "all kinds of ropes". [600G H] 2.2 The Tribunal has correctly interpreted the expression "Hooose" in the Brussels Tariff Nomenclature. [606C] 3.1 The word "hoose" in Tariff Item 26 A(ia)
1785: The petitioner was selected by the Madras Public Service Commission as a Lower Division Clerk under the Madras Ministerial Service Rules in 1949. He was allotted to the Revenue Department and posted in South Kanara District. In 1955, he was promoted as Upper Division Clerk with effect from April 2, 1956, but was not selected as he was not considered fit. On May 11, 1957, the Government of India addressed a memorandum (No. Broadly speaking, the Central Government said that some conditions of service should be protected, e.g., substantive pay of permanent employees, certain type of special pay, lave rules unless the Government servant opts for new leave rules, etc. The petitioner was considered for inclusion in the eligibility list from 1955 onwards, but was found unfit. The State contends that the proviso to section 115(7) is ultra vires the Constitution and that the petitioner cannot claim any relief on the ground that he had been discriminated against. Held, that the proviso does not affect the right of the petitioner to claim relief under article 32 of the Constitution. It merely provides that the conditions of service applicable immediately before November 1, 1956, to the case of persons mentioned in sub sections (1) and (2) of section 115 shall not be varied to his disadvantage except with the previous approval of the Central Government. The proviso does not take away or abridge the right conferred by article 311(2). The proviso does no more than provide that the conditions which are imposed by the proviso would be subject to the approval of the President. The proviso is intended to protect the rights of the petitioner who has been denied equality before the law or the equal protection of laws. The proviso therefore does not affect those rights.
351: The petitioners were tenants of certain lands in the State of Rajasthan. They had been paying rent to the State Government for the same land, and they claimed that they were entitled to hold the land as tenants on payment of rent from the first day of July next following the date of the settlement. The Settlement Officer rejected their claim, but he held that the Act was not applicable to them because the rent rates fixed by him were not based on any principle of law or on any statutory provisions. He also found that the petitioners were not impugning the validity of the Act. The petitioners thereupon filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of section 81 of the Act on the ground that it offended article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Act did not infringe the fundamental rights guaranteed under articles 14 and 19(1) (f). In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Act does not purport to affect the rights of the petitioners under article 19(1)(f), nor is it violative of article 31(2). It is only if there is a violation of the fundamental right declared in article 19(I) (f) that Article 19(1 ) (f) can arise. [801 B D] (ii) The Act has no application to the jagirs of the petitioners. The Act applies to jagirdars who are holders of jagir lands. The Act does nothing more than to regulate the cultivation of jagir land. The Act is an integrated one and it cannot be said that the Act is discriminatory. [802 E F] (iii) The Act is not intended to abolish the rights of tenants in the jagirs. The Act provides for the fixation of rents which have to be determined according to the principles laid down in the Act. Section 84 of the Act lays down that all persons holding land in the jagir shall be liable to pay rent at the rates specified in the Schedule. The Act makes no provision for the determination of the rent payable by a tenant in respect of any land held by him. The Act therefore does not infringe any fundamental right of the petitioners guaranteed under article 19 (1) (g) of the Constitution, and the Act is therefore bad as being violative

252: The appellants were charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rent Act, 1947 for receiving from the complainant a sum of Rs. 2,400 as premium or 160 pugree in respect of the grant of a lease. 3092: The respondents were carrying on business in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The prohibition contained in section 5(2) of the Act is not confined to the movement of the tendu leaves but extends to the movement from one place inside the State to other places within the State and to the movement by such persons in the State. 1090: The appellant was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had two units of its own. The first unit consisted of three units, the second unit consisting of three workmen and the third unit consisting of four workmen. The respondents were employed in the factory of the appellant. They applied for leave to their employees on the ground that they were entitled to leave as provided by section 79(1) of the Act. The respondents claimed privilege leave with full salary and dearness allowance on completion of eleven months service in a year with a right to accumulate upto six months, but the Tribunal allowed them. The appellant contended that the respondents ' demand for earned leave with full pay and dearness allowance should be rejected because it was not based on any rational principle of industrial adjudication; and so the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make such an award having regard to the provisions of section 79(I). Held, that the Tribunal had jurisdiction to make an award having due regard to the principles laid down by the Act and the rules made thereunder. The object of the Act is to provide for grant of leave to the employees who are entitled to receive wages at the rate prescribed by the Act. Section 79(1), therefore, has been enacted to achieve this purpose. The words "as they think fit" in section 79(2)(a) must be construed in the light of the objects and reasons set out therein. The object and reasons set forth in section 79 are intended to ensure that the workmen get a fair opportunity of working in the industry concerned. The object is to enable the workmen to secure a fair wage which would include the benefit of leave to their credit. The object being to give them a reasonable return on the capital invested by the employer, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to add to the leave prescribed by section 79.

1611: The respondent was convicted under section 323 and section 324 read with section 511 of the Indian Penal Code. 468: The petitioner was a Sub Inspector of Police in the then State of Bhopal. He was prosecuted for offences under section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Chief Commissioner of Bhopal passed an order under section 7(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952 (No. XXXV of 1952), directing that the petitioner be tried again for the same offence. The petitioner challenged the validity of this order by a petition under article 32 of the Constitution before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that no sanction had been given to prosecute him. The petitioner contended that the sanction had not been given by the Chief Commissioner as required by section 403(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, and that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the case. Held, that the Chief Commissioner had no power to issue the sanction and the prosecution of the petitioner was illegal. The sanction must be deemed to have been given by him as required by law.
2791: The appellants were charged with offences under section 395 and 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. They pleaded not guilty to those charges but on the evidence adduced by the prosecution, their conviction was upheld by the Sessions Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellants had been falsely implicated in the case because they knew that the police party had come to search for the buffalo and that they could be said to have taken the police party to the place where the dead body was found. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellants were entitled to a reasonable opportunity of being heard before their conviction is set aside. [11A] (2) The appellants had no reason to believe that the police had come to the place of occurrence or that they would be concealed or destroyed. [11B] (3) The appellants did not take the police party into confidence at all. They had no reason either to suspect the police party or to suspect the other persons who might have been present at the time when the incident took place. [11C D]
1559: The appellants were dealers in sugar. They sold sugar to the Government of India under a contract for sale of sugar. The Government of India Act, 1935 was passed by the Central Legislature and the Provincial Legislature enacted the Sugar and Sugar Products Control Order, 1950, which provided that no person shall sell or agree to sell any commodity at a price exceeding the maximum price fixed by the Central Government. The appellants contended that the power conferred by Entry 48 List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution was not subject to the provisions of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, and that the Provincial Legislature had no power to impose tax on transactions which were not sales within the meaning of the Bihar Sales Tax Act. Held, that the Provincial Legislatures had no power under the Essential Supplies Act to levy tax on transactions in which there was transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of contracts but which by mutual consent were transferred absolutely from one person to another, in consideration of price paid or promised, and the transactions in which such transfers were made absolutely from one party to the other, in consideration whereof the price was payable. The word "sale" in entry 48 of List II of Sch. VII of the Constitution means, inter alia, a transfer of property; it does not include a mortgage, hypothecation, charge or pledge. The word 'sale ' is used in the sense of transfer of property as understood in common parlance and also in the sense that a transaction of sale may be deemed to be a sale even though the property passes in the course of trade or commerce. The word sale has been defined in section 2(g) of the Bihar General Sales Tax Act, 1947, as meaning a transfer of ownership of goods by one person to a person or a system of payment by a person of money without consideration. The definition of sale in section 2 (g) of Bihar Sales Tax is wide enough to cover every kind of transfer of goods as distinguished from a mortgage, a charge or pledge; and the word "sale " in entry 48 in List II of Schedule VII of the Government of Indian Laws Act, 1935, includes a transfer of the right to use any goods for any purpose. 3193: The appellant was the returned candidate for the Safidon Assembly Constituency No. 30. He filed an election petition challenging the election of the first respondent on several grounds, including corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the appellant had failed to comply with the mandatory requirement of section 81(3) and that the spare copies were actually filed beyond the period of limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the requisite number of spare copies were not filed along with the petition; (ii) the spare copies could be filed only after the prescribed period of limitation; and (iii) the spare copy was not filed within the prescribed time. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The requirement of section 80(3) is that the requisite number must be filed along with a petition under section 81(1). [278C] (a) Section 81(3)(c) provides that every election petition shall be accompanied by as many copies thereof as there are respondents mentioned in the petition. [279E] (b) The requirement that the requisite numbers of spare copies should be filed within the period of four days from the date of the receipt of the petition is mandatory and non compliance with the said requirement would render the petition liable to dismissal. [270F G] (2) The requirement regarding the filing of the election petition within the period prescribed by section 81(4) is directory and not mandatory. [275A B] (a)(i) The requirement about the filing of an election petition within fortyfive days from the last date fixed for filing of the nomination paper is mandatory and cannot be waived. [276B C] (ii) The requirement relating to the filing of a petition within forty five days from the closing date for withdrawal of candidature is mandatory and not mandatory and cannot take away the right of the returned candidate to file an election petition before the expiry of the period of forty five days. 3421: The respondent company in this appeal was a private limited company. It had its Head Office at Bombay. The workmen were laid off in accordance with law with effect from 5th February, 1968. The lay off of the workmen whose names were mentioned in the notice was recalled by the management on the 22nd April, 1968. A dispute arose between the workmen and the management as to whether they should be paid compensation for the period of lay off or not. The Labour Court held that the workmen were not entitled to any lay off compensation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the workmen. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the lay off was illegal because the workmen were given employment only after the lay off had been sanctioned by the employer. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The layoff is an event which takes place when the workman is actually employed. [243E] 2. The lay Off is a permanent one. The lay down is permanent. The workmen are entitled to their full wages. [244F] 3. The lay out is permanent. [245A] 4. The lay of the workmen is temporary. The lay is permanent. There is no reason why the workmen should be denied the benefit of the lay off. [246B] 5. The lay has to be read in conjunction with the other provisions of the Act. [247C] 6. The lay should be read in harmony with the other relevant provisions of the statute. [248D]
2297: The appellant was a member of the Assam Judicial Service. He was appointed as a Judge of the High Court by the Governor of Assam on February 1, 1956. On March 31, 1957 he was transferred to Gauhati and was posted at Sibsagar. In September 1957 he was promoted as a District Judge. On October 3, 1958 he was transferred from Gauhati to Gauhati. On November 3, 1958 the appellant was transferred to Sibsagar and was relieved from his duties in Sibsagar on December 2, 1958. On January 25, 1959 he was again transferred to Sibasagar. On January 26, 1959 he resigned from the post of a District Judge and was appointed as an Additional District Judge. In September 1959 he was transferred back to Gauhati where he had been working as a Commission of Enquiry. On April 30, 1960 he was transferred as a District judge. On May 1, 1961 he was transferred and joined the High Court as a Judge. On July 10, 1961 he resigned. On August 16, 1961 he applied for leave to join the High Court but it was refused. On August 17, 1961 he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of transfer. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the High Court 'was not right when it held that Dutta J. could not act as a Judge; (ii) the High court was wrong in holding that Dutta was not a Judge of High Court within the meaning of article 222(1)(a); (iii) the High Courts were not competent to deal with the matter by virtue of the provisions of article 224(1)(b). HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the Chief Justice of the High Courts was not competent to hear the petition and pass the stay order. [617 G] (ii)The High Court was wrong in thinking that the Chief justice of the High court should be the Chief Justice or the Chief Justice. [618 A B] (iii)The High Courts are not competent to decide the question whether a particular High Court is or is not a High Court. It is only the Chief Justice who can decide the question. [619 C
3390: The appellants were the subscribers to a telephone exchange. They were in possession of telephones and telephones for the purpose of their business. He was competent in exercising his powers under rule 422 to issue directions to the appellants to disconnect the telephones. 6645: The Government of Jammu & Kashmir granted land in dispute to the Ziarat. The Ziarat was subsequently transferred by the Government in favour of the defendants father in his personal capacity. The Zikar was then given possession of the land in dispute and the defendants were put in possession of the same. The Zidar, who had been allotted the land in question, filed a suit against the Ziardar for an injunction restraining him from alienating, raising construction or recovering the rent from the Wakf land in dispute vested in the Ziarbari. The defendants claimed that the land in suit belonged to them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the two grants by the State Government were in fact made in favour of Mian Lal Din and not in favour of Ziarat; that the grant was in fact made by the Government and that the Ziard was in fact given to the defendants father. The High Court reversed the decree on appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the grant in favour of Yusuf was in fact in the nature of a gift and as such could not be treated as a property of the Ziawar. HELD: (1) The grant in favour Yusuff is not a property of Ziawar but it is a sort of a bargain between the Ziars and the Ziirds. [257 H] (2) The grant was in favour of a Ziarat and not in the nature and character of a gift. The grant in the instant case was in favour Yousuf and not in his individual capacity. [258 A B] (3) The grant did not create any interest in the property in favour of any Ziarat nor did it confer any title on Yusuft. The grant was only in respect of the land which was given to Yusufe. The grant itself was in favour and not in respect of any other land. [259 C D] (4) The grant being in favour of an Ziarat, the grant was not in the character of a grant. [260 E]
2618: The appellant was a Sales Tax Officer in the State of Bombay. He was appointed as a Sales Tax officer in the former State of Bombay after merger. In December 1962 he was served with a charge sheet containing allegations of attempt to obtain illegal gratification from certain cloth dealers. A departmental enquiry was held and on March 15, 1963 the Enquiry Officer made certain recommendations regarding the punishment which in his opinion should be inflicted on the first respondent. On March 15, he was dismissed from service. In May 1958 the City Civil Court decreed the suit holding that the order of dismissal was illegal. The High Court allowed the appeal filed by the first respondent and set aside the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the failure to send a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer containing his findings on the various charges against him which were found to have been proved did not amount to a failure to provide reasonable opportunity of making a representation against the penalty proposed within the meaning of article 311(2) of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The failure to supply copies of the reports of the Enquiry Officers containing his findings was not fatal to the proceedings. [254 G] (2) The Enquiry Officer had also made some recommendations regarding the punishments which may be imposed on the first Respondent. The first respondent was given an opportunity to make a representation against his penalty. The first Respondent having failed to do so, the enquiry was vitiated. [255 C D] (3) The Enquiry Report contained the findings on the charges against the first respondent but the Enquiry Officer had only made certain recommendations about the punishment which was to be imposed on him. The first and second respondents were entitled to know the reasons why they had come to the conclusion that the first respondent was guilty of the charges. [256 E F] (4) The first respondent could not be said to have been prejudiced because he was not supplied with the report of Enquiry Officer. The first respondents were not entitled to make any representations against the findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer. [257 B] (5) The first respondents had no right to ask for a copy of any report of the enquiry officer or the report of any other authority. The first two respondents
2435: The petitioner was detained under section 3(3) of the Bombay Police Act, 1951. He challenged his detention on the ground that he had been deprived of his right to make a representation against his detention and that there was no provision in the Act for such an approval. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the delay in sending the report could not be avoided by the Commissioner and (ii) the delay was due to causes beyond the control of the detaining authority. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) The delay in sending a report to the State Government is due to causes not of his making, but to causes to which the activities of the petitioner were contributing. [10A B] (2) The delay was not explained satisfactorily. The reasons given are sufficient to justify the delay. [10C D] (3) The delay must be explained. The delay was due not to any fault of the petitioner but to some other cause. [10D E]
1748: The petitioners, who were members of a joint Hindu family governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law, filed a suit in the Court of the Chief Commissioner for the State of Tripura against the Ruler of an Indian State. The petitioners contended that they and respondent No. 2, their representatives, had no authority to file a suit against the Ruler and that the provisions of section 87B(1) were ultra vires the Constitution. The petitioners also alleged that the Ruler was not competent to file a civil suit against the Rulers of an Indian States. The petitioners further alleged that the respondent No. 1, the Ruler, had acted arbitrarily in refusing to grant sanction under section 87B C.P.C., as he was not a member of the Indian State. They also alleged that respondent No. I, the Ruler had acted arbitrly in refusing to make any increase in the total expenditure on the allowances to the maintenance holders. The petitioners claimed that they and the respondent No, 2, their representative, had no power or authority to file suits against the Ruler. The petitioners therefore prayed for a declaration that the provisions contained in section 87B, C.P,.C., are ultra vires, because it contravenes article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the petitioners have failed to establish that the impugned provision is violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(f). The petitioners have failed in proving that the impugned section is ultra vires. The petitioners have not established that the impugned provisions are ultra vires.
3489: The respondent, a displaced person from West Pakistan, filed an application under section 7 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 for fixation of standard rent. The Estate Officer passed an order on September 28, 1960 under section 7(1) of the Act directing the respondent to pay the amount in arrears within one month from that date. The appellant 's appeal to the Additional District Judge from the said order was dismissed by the Circuit Bench of the Punjab High Court at Delhi as not maintainable. The respondent then filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order against him. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since section 7 did not put a time limit for taking steps under that section and as the limitation prescribed for a suit to recover the amount had expired, the High Court was in error in holding that the amount in question could not be recovered under section 7 because the time for instituting a suit to recovery the amount had already expired. HELD: (i) The expression "payable" in section 7 means "the amount payable in respect of any public premises." [839 E] (ii) The word "payable' is quite comprehensive enough to include all payments which are made by the Government or the statutory authority to the person who has given the public premises. The word "payment" in its ordinary signification must mean "to make payment". It does not mean to make payment to the person making the payment. It may be paid either in cash or in bonds or partly in cash and partly in bonds. It may also be paid in bonds or both. It may well be paid out of the funds of the Government or of the statutory authority. [840 G H; 841 A B] (iii) The word 'payable ' in section 7 does not necessarily mean 'to make payment '. It only means to make payment in cash or by way of bonds or both and not to make payment of money otherwise. [842 C] (iv) The word `payable ' is very comprehensive enough to cover all payments which have been made by the government or the statutory authorities to the person paying the rent. [843 D] (v) The word pay '
4072: The appellants, who were the highest bidders for the sale of jewellery belonging to H.E.H. the Nizam 's Jewellery Trust, effected by the Board of Trustees in exercise of their discretionary power of sale under cl. 13 of the trust deed in favour of the appellants and other successful tenderers for Rs. 14.43 crores, and accepting instead the offer of the eighth respondent, Peter Jansin Fernandez for Rs. 20.25 crores made during the lifetime of his eldest son Prince Azam Jah (if and so long as the Dynasty of the Settlor continues and Prince Azm Jah) sold the said jewels and other articles to the appellants and others successful tenderers on March 9, 1978. The appellants and other unsuccessful tenderers filed a suit against the trustees for recovery of the said jewelleries and other articles mentioned in the first schedule to the trust deed. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the sale was not vitiated by fraud or undue influence but only because the appellants had failed to prove that they had any knowledge about the transaction between the appellants and the other successful tenderer. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree passed by the trial court. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sale of 37 items of jewellery belonging exclusively to the appellants was invalid inasmuch as the appellants had no notice of the transactions between them and the other contesting tenderers and that the sale could be set aside on the ground that the appellants had not been served with any notice of the proceedings before the trustees. [8A B] 1.2 The sale of the jewellery belonging to a third party is not vitiated merely because the appellant has not been served at all. [8C] 1.3 The sale of an item of jewellery belonging solely to the appellants cannot be challenged on the ground of fraud or undue influences. [8D] 1.4 The sale of a jewellery belonging to an individual is not vitiated by any fraud or undue pressure or coercion. [8F] 1.5 The sale
5027: The appellant was granted a quarry lease for the period ending with 31st March, 1984. The appellant challenged the grant of the quarry lease by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed and the appellant was directed to be granted a quarry licence for the period commencing from 1st April, 1984. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the grant of quarry lease and that the appellant could not have been denied the right to carry on mining operations without complying with the provisions of the Act and Rules. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the appellant was entitled to the grant of a quarry lease. [547C] 1.2 The High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant had participated in the auction and was not given any opportunity to make a representation against the grant of lease. [553E] 2.1 The appellant was not entitled to the concession made by the State Government under the Act and the Rules. [554F] 2.2 The appellant was entitled only to the concession as he had participated in a bid for the grant of mining lease. [561G H] 3.1 The State Government did not confirm the auction held on February 20, 1981. The appellant was bound to give the highest bid. The appellant had not given any such offer. The appellant could not be said to have been prejudiced because of the fact that the matter was disposed of by the High Court. [556A B] 3.2 The State Government had no power to grant a quarry lease in favour of a person who had participated in an auction. The High Court erred in holding that there was no violation of Article 14 of the Constitution. [558B C] 3.3 The High Court should have considered the question whether the appellant had been discriminated against or not. [559D]
1145: The appellant was a registered union of the employees of the Mill owners. The appellant was an employee of the Mill owner and was paid bonus for the years 1952 and 1953. The appellant claimed that it had been paying bonus to its workmen for the years 1951 and 1953, and also for the years 1954 to 1957. The appellant contended that the award made by the Industrial Court in respect of bonus for the year 1952 and 1953 was not enforceable as an award by the Industrial court against the appellant. The Industrial Court held that the award was not enforceable under section 114(2) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The award made by a Labour Court is binding on the employer and the employee. The Labour Appellate Tribunal has no jurisdiction to interfere with the award of the Industrial Court. [111 B] (ii) The award of the Labour Court was not enforceable because it was not a settlement between the parties. The award was not a decree by the Industrial Tribunal but only an award by a Labour court. [111 C D] (iii) The award was made by the Labour Court in exercise of its powers vested in it by section 114(1)(a) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The award therefore did not become enforceable. [111 E F] (iv) The award in respect of the year 1952 was not a 'settlement ' within the meaning of section 114(6) of the Indian Evidence Act. The award in regard to the year 1952 could not be said to be a settlement or settlement between the appellant and the respondent. [110 A B] (v) The award does not create any right in favour of the appellant. It merely declares the award as one which is binding upon the appellant. [110 G H]
5346: The appellant landlord filed a petition under section 10(3)(c) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that he required the premises bona fide for his personal use and occupation. The Rent Controller held that the respondent was not entitled to recover possession of non residential premises for his residential requirements and dismissed the petition for eviction. On appeal by the appellant, the Appellate Authority reversed the findings of the Rent Controller and also held that the appellant was not entitled for eviction of respondent under Section 10(3) (a)(i) of the Act. The High Court in revision set aside the order of the Appellate Authority and restored the order of eviction passed by the Rent Controller. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The High court was in error in interfering with the finding of fact rendered by the Appellate Authority while exercising its revisional jurisdiction under Section 25 of the Act, since the grounds floor constitute a building by itself within the meaning of Section 2(2) of the Madras Buildings (Leasing, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1960. [5B] 2. The High Courts ' interference with the concurrent findings of fact is permissible only if they are perverse or based on no evidence. [6C] 3. In any event the factors of relative hardship be tween the parties weigh more in favour of the appellant than the respondent. [6D] 4. The High courts ' interference with concurrent findings of facts is permissible only when there is an element of perversity involved in it. [6E] 5. The High has rightly exercised its revisional powers under Section 25. [6F] 6. The High would have been justified in interfering with this finding but the High Court did not interfere with the same. [7A] 7. The High does not appear to have taken into consideration the relevant factors of comparative hardship. [7B] 8. The High should not have interfered with the concurrent finding of fact unless it is shown that the High had misread or misconstrued the relevant materials. [8C] 9. The High could not have interfered in the exercise of its revisional power under Section 25 because the High Court was not right in interfering
1091: The respondent company was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1954 55. The Income tax Officer, by an order dated January 25, 1954 rectified this error and imposed a penalty of Rs. 5,000 on the respondent company. The respondent company filed a revision petition before the Commissioner of Income tax but the revision petition was dismissed. Thereafter the respondent company filed another petition in the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the orders made by the Income tax Officer. The High Court held that the orders were without jurisdiction and therefore quashed the orders. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the order was without jurisdiction as the proviso (ii) of Part B of the First Schedule of the Finance Act did not apply; (ii) the order could be corrected only if there was an apparent mistake which had crept into the order or some other extraneous matter had been overlooked; and (iii) the order being a mistake apparent on the face of the record, the High Court should have set aside the order. HELD: (1) The proviso (ii), Part B of First Schedule of Finance Act does not apply because the order is without jurisdiction. [560 C] (2) The proviso applies only where a mistake has occurred in the order and not where the mistake is apparent from an accidental slip or omission. [566 D] (3) The proviso does not apply when the mistake is patent on the face. It merely provides that the amendment shall come into force on such date as may be specified in the order. The proviso does no more than provide that the amendment will come into force after the date of the order. [565 E F] (4) The proviso is not intended to confer any new right. It merely clarifies the position. It is not intended as a rule of evidence to support a claim for rectification. [567 A B] (5) The proviso cannot be construed as giving retrospective effect to the main provision. [568 G H]
6912: The appellant landlord filed a suit for possession of the suit premises on the ground that the respondent tenant had failed to pay rent from 1.1.1980 to 31.3.1981 and thereafter made regular payment of Rs. 600 every month. The trial court decreed the suit for possession. The appellate court reversed the decree holding that the service of notice dated 7.8.1980 was not proved. The High Court in second appeal held that the evidence of the plaintiff showed that the copy of the notice was sent to all the defendants by registered post, but the same was not served on the defendant company. In this view of the matter, the High Court set aside the finding of the trial court and held that the service was proved. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts judgment is based on misreading of the provisions of Section 12(3)(b) of the Act. [10B] 2. The presumption under Section 114 of the Evidence Act can be drawn only if the person who has received the notice has put his signature or thumb impression on it. [10C] 3. The presumption of service of notice is rebuttable. It is also important to note that the notice was served on the company and in the facts and circumstances of the case, the burden of proof was upon the tenant to prove that the postal acknowledgment was not correct. [10D] 4. The High court was wrong in drawing presumption of service on the defendant. [11E] 5. The High courts judgment is based upon misreading and misappreciation of the provisions contained in Section 114 of Evidence Act. [11F] 6. The Highs Court erred in holding that the evidence was not rebutted by the defendant. The defendant admitted that he had paid Rs. 55,800 on 16.1.1984 and thereafter made a regular payment of the said amount. The defendant did make regular payment of rent. The defendant admits that he had sent the notice on 7.880. He denies having received any notice. The defendant has not led any evidence to show that the notice dated 7th August 1980 was served on him. [11G H]

6184: The appellants were tenants of certain intermediary landlords known as Girasdars. Respondents Nos. 1 to 3 were tenants of some of the appellants. Respondent No. 9 was a Girasdar who was represented by the Assistant Custodian of Evacuee Property and the rest of the respondents were the other tenants from whom the appellants held lands on leases. The appellants filed an application before the Deputy Collector for allotment of land to them under section 4(1) of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951. The Deputy Collector rejected the said application holding that the appellants had no interest in the result of these appeals and that they were not entitled to separate allotments. The appellants then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of the Deputy Collector. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order of Deputy Collector. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the appellants were not entitled under section 4 to separate allotment of land from the Girasdari tenants; (ii) the appellants had acquired interest in the land held by them jointly and the separate allotments made in respect of the land held jointly by them were not in excess of the permissible area of the Girasdar and (iii) the appellants could not be treated as tenants of the Girasadars. HELD: (i) The appellants were not tenants of the land in question. They were not entitled either to separate allotment or to separate allotment in respect of their land held by the Girasdas. [563 D] (iv) The appellants did not acquire any interest in the lands held by them. They were therefore not entitled to any separate allotment. The appellants were therefore not liable to ejectment. [564 E]

1277: The respondent was appointed as a clerk in the Southern Railway. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Station Master in the scale of Rs. 260 400 and his pay was fixed at Rs. 330 400. In the year 1967, he was posted as a Senior Clerk in the scale Rs. 330 700. On the question whether the circular dated December 18, 1966 issued by the General Manager, Southern Railway, was applicable to the respondent, HELD: (i) The circular did not provide for reservation of selection posts in Class III of the service but only provided that the reservation would be made in the case of initial appointment and promotion. [617 D] (ii) The circular does not say that it is applicable only to initial appointments and promotions. It merely provides that the seniority of the employees in the grade shall be determined on the basis of length of service put in by them in the grade. [618 E F] (iii) The circular cannot be construed as an executive instruction or order which can be given effect to retrospectively. [619 G H] (iv) The circular has no statutory force and therefore could not have been given retrospective operation. [620 B C] (v) The circular is not intended to give any benefit to the respondent who had already been promoted to the higher grades. [621 A] (vi) The circular was not meant to apply to the respondent 's case because he was not selected and put in the panel. [622 A B]
2660: The appellant firm was assessed to income tax for the year 1946 47, the appellant firm purchased 50,000 ordinary shares of Raymond Woollen Mills Ltd. In appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the transaction was one to facilitate acquisition of a capital asset being a capital investment, and since the firm had entered into a well planned scheme for earning profit and that in furtherance and execution of that profit making scheme they sold the shares at the instance of the firm, the profits realised by sale of the said shares were not liable to be assessed to income-tax. The Tribunal affirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner. In further appeal to this Court, the question for consideration was whether the transaction was a "sale" within the meaning of section 2(1) (a) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. Held, that the transaction did not involve any commercial activity but was one to assist the assessee in carrying on his business. The word 'sale ' is not defined in the Act and has been used in the sense of an agreement between two or more persons to do a certain thing which the parties themselves may enter into. It is not necessary that there should be actual delivery of goods or passing of title thereto. The word "sale" in the context in which it occurs must mean a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer property in any goods to the buyer for a price. The word is used in the context of a transaction of sale of goods. The word sale is not confined to a mere contract of sale or purchase. The word `sale ' means a transfer of property in goods from one person to another. A transfer of property takes place when the ownership of the property changes hands. But a transfer of the property does not involve any element of transfer of property. The word transfer is used in contradistinction to transfer of property and
1910: The appellant was a local board of Barpeta in Assam. He had been granted licence under section 62 of the Assam Local Boards Act, 1948 for holding a market on his land since the year 1936. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The impost is not a tax but only a fee. It is a compulsory exaction of money by public authorities for public purposes enforceable in court. [567 C D] (3) The rule is not applicable where the impost imposes a tax which is not a fee. [568 E F] (4) The rule does not offend article 14 of Constitution. [569 A] (5) The rule cannot be said to be arbitrary or unreasonable. It is well settled that if a statute imposes a tax it must be strictly construed. [570 G]

710: The U. P. Transport Service (Development) Act, 1955 was passed by the Parliament in 1956 and it came into force on January 1, 1956. The Act was amended by the Amending Act of 1956 with effect from April 1, 1956, and the provisions of the Amending Act were made applicable to the U.P. Transport Service. The appellants challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that it violated their fundamental rights guaranteed under article 31(2). Held, that the Act did not infringe the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 31(1), but merely provided for the imposition of a ceiling on the exercise of the right to carry on business. The Act did not offend the provisions of article 31(l) as it stood before the Constitution (Sixth Amendment) Act, 1956, which was passed by Parliament. The Act had been enacted in order to provide for the acquisition of property for public purposes and for giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing the principles specified in clause (b) of article 39 of the Constitution. The Act could not be said to have infringed the fundamental rights of the appellants. The Act does not contravene articles 14, 19 or 31 of the Constitution; it is only a piece of legislation which can be struck down on the ground of infringement of any of the fundamental rights.
2966: The appellant was a dealer in cloth. It manufactured cloth by means of powerlooms. The question for decision was whether the cloth manufactured by the appellant was "mill" within the meaning of the notification issued under section 3A of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. The High Court held that the cloth manufactured was "cloth manufactured by hand or by power". In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word "mills" had not been defined either by the Act or by the notification mentioned before the meaning of 'mean cloth ' and therefore the cloth manufactured could not fall within the definition of "mill". Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The word "mill", as used in the notification, must be understood according to its dictionary meaning. "Mill" is a machine which manufactures goods for sale. [639 B] (2) The word 'mill ' has not been defined in the Act nor in the notification. According to the dictionary meaning, the word "ma chin" would mean a machine which is used for the purpose of storage. [640 C] (3) The word milch ' is a word of a very wide import and it includes all kinds of cloth including cloth made from cotton. [641 A] (4) The word Mill ' is a machine capable of being used for the purposes of storing cloth. The word "Mill ' does not include cloth made from cloth. [642 D] (5) The word `mill ' is not defined in the notification but it may be said that it is used in the sense of a factory. [643 E] (6) The word used in the Notification must be understood in the context in which it is used. [644 G]

In July, 1953, a group of persons who were appointed as managing agents of the company filed an application before the Central Government under section 326 of the , for extension of the managing agency of the company for five years with effect from August 15, 1960. The Central Government granted extension for five years under section 326, but the extension was not approved by the Central Government. The company then moved a petition in the High Court of Delhi on June 10, 1967, for quashing the decision of the Board and for an order directing the Central Government to approve the extension of the Managing Agency till March 31, 1970. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the company had no locus standi to file the petition. The company appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The company was a subsidiary and a subsidiary company. The company was formed in 1946 and it was constituted in 1950. The company has been functioning since then. [639 E] (2) The company had been working as a managing agent of the company since its incorporation. 2971: The appellant company was incorporated in the year of account, and its managing agency business was acquired by the respondent company. The Income tax Officer disallowed an amount of Rs.11,88,000/ out of this loss on the ground that it relates to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the company in Elphinsstone Mill Ltd. In appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Income Tax Officer but reduced the amount of Rs 11,88, 000/ from the claim made by the appellant company. The Tribunal, however, allowed the appeal of the respondent company and set aside the order of Income Tax Officer. The High Court dismissed the appeal of Revenue. In appeal to this Court, it was contended: (i) that the Tribunal erred in holding that the appellant company had suffered a losses in the previous year; (ii) that the appellant should be directed to pay interest at the rate of 15% per annum on the amount of loss incurred by it; and (iii) that the amount of income tax payable by the appellant should have been deducted from the sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ which was due to the appellant on account of the loss sustained by it in the previous years. [311 A B] (iv) The condition relating to the use of the goods for producing any new or different goods is not satisfied because the condition is satisfied. 1892: The appellant Corporation was constituted by the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, an Act passed by the Legislature of the State of West Bengal. In 1948 the Corporation had fixed the scale of fees on the basis of annual valuation of the cinema houses made by a method which does not appear on the record. The respondent moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the resolution. His submissions in support of the validity of the levy were : (1) that the levy was not a fee but a tax; and (2) that the imposition was not a tax as it did not impose any burden on the licensee. Held, that the levy imposed by the impugned resolution was not a levy of tax within the meaning of article 110(2). The word "fee" is used in a wide sense to denote a charge or charge levied by statute. It is not a mere charge or a charge for a special benefit or privilege. It is a payment for services rendered. A fee may be charged for a privilege or a duty. But the fact that the grant of a privilege or the like is dependent upon the performance or fulfilment of some particular object cannot be said to render the grant a wholly illusory or merely an illusory exercise of the power. The word "tax" has been defined in section 2(6) of the Act to mean a tax on the entry of goods into a local area for consumption, use or sale therein. The word 'tax ' means a tax on goods and not on the entry or exit from a local area. The word tax is not used in the Act to connote a tax on land or building. The word is used in the context of a tax on property. The word has been used in the widest possible sense to denotes a tax on a capital value of assets. The word must be construed in its popular sense and in the sense in which it is understood in common parlance. The word may also include a tax on income. The word can also mean a tax or a fee. The word itself indicates that the tax is a tax on something else. The word taxes is not used to connote taxes. The word taxation is a concept well known in commercial circles. 4851: The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of paper and paper products. The respondent company paid a sum of Rs. 1,000 to the appellant for the supply of raw materials. The appellant claimed that it had paid Rs. 1.5 lakhs as incentive bonus on account of the fact that the respondent had been paying the same amount as wages to its employees. The appellant contended that the respondent was not liable to pay any additional amount under the terms of the contract of employment because the respondent had not paid the said amount. The respondent contended that the appellant had not paid any extra amount to the respondent. The Labour Court held that the respondent 's claim was not justified. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The definition of 'wages ' is an inclusive definition and does not include any contribution paid by the employer to any pension fund or provident fund or under the Act any travelling allowance or the value of any travelling concession, by whatever name called. [717 B] (2) The definition is wide enough to cover all payments made to the employee by way of salary, wages, leave salary, bonus etc., which are not included in the definition. [718 C D] (3) The definition has to be read with the definition of 'salary ' in section 2(14) of the Act. [719 E F] (4) The definition does not exclude any payment made to the employees by way of bonus but only excludes any payment made in respect of any period of leave, lock out, strike which is not illegal or lay off. [720 A] (5) The definition includes remuneration paid to an employee by wayof commission for services rendered. [721 B] (6) The definition covers even the basic wage plus dearness allowance including the additional remuneration payable at intervals not exceeding two months. [722 C]

1696: The Bhopal Reclamation and Development of Lands (Eradication of Kans) Act, 1954 was enacted to provide for the rehabilitating and reclamation of land in the State of Madhya Pradesh. 2165: The respondents, claiming to be the khatedars of an extent of 57.07 acres of land in Mauza Bhanpur, Tahsil Huzur, Bhopal, filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of possession of the said land on the ground that they were his shikmi tenants and that the latter was in illegal possession thereof. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondents had title to the property and that the appellant was entitled to retain possession of the same. The appellate court confirmed the decree. In second appeal the High Court held that the suit was not barred by limitation. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision of the revenue court on the question of title to the suit land barring section 96(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, was erroneous and that the suit should have been dismissed as barred by limitation under section 96(2). HELD: (i) The decision of the Tahsildar on the question whether the suit was barred by limitation is final and conclusive. [623 E] (ii) The decision given by the Tahsildar on a question of title cannot be challenged in a civil court. The decision of a Tahsildar is binding on the parties to the suit and the decision of a civil court binds the parties to it. [624 F G] (iii) The decision rendered by the Tahsildar in regard to the title of the respondents to the land in dispute is final and binding on the respondents. [625 A B] (iv) The decision in regard to title of the respondent to the land is final and cannot be questioned in a civil suit. [626 C D]
435: The Company was a private limited company. It had two branches in Calcutta, one of which was the branch of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce and the other was the branch at Calcutta. In the year 1947, the Company passed an award fixing dearness allowance for the workmen of the Company at Rs. 7/8/ per month. The Tribunal increased the dearness allowance by Rs. 7 /8/ for workmen in the pay ranges below Rs. 50 and up to the pay range of Rs. 250 and by a flat rate of Rs. 5 in the higher pay range. The Tribunal also awarded dearness allowance on the basis of the recommendation of the Bengal Chambers of Commerce as accepted by the Bengal Chamber. The Company appealed to this Court against the award of the Tribunal. Held, that the Tribunal had not adopted any principle or acted in violation of any statute and the Industrial Tribunal had rightly come to the conclusion that the dearness allowance should be on the same rates as decided upon by the Bengal Chamters of Commerce. The Tribunal had correctly applied the principle laid down by the Bengal High Court in the case of the Company. The Tribunal has not committed any error in coming to the conclusion it did. The Tribunal was right in holding that the dearness allowances should be on a different scale as decided upon in the Bengal Chamber and that the Tribunal was right when it came to the conclusion.
6500: The appellant was the second son of Raja Padam Singh, who had purchased the lands in question from the erstwhile ruler of the State. He died on 8th October, 1942 leaving behind his widow and two sons. The appellant 's father executed a deed of lease dated 14th Maghar 1999 in favour of the respondent for a period of 20 years. The lease deed provided that the land would be used by the appellant for the purpose of cultivation of his own land. The appellant applied to the Government for permission to use the land for the purpose for which it was leased out. The Government granted the permission subject to certain conditions. The appellant continued to enjoy the land till the year 1976 when he made an application under section 27 of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953. The appellant filed a suit for declaration of title and possession against the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the grant was in respect of revenue yielding lands only admeasuring about 263.4 bighas and not in respect of the forest lands. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the grant in favour of respondent was in respect only of the forest land and not in relation to the forest lands and that the High Court erred in holding that the land was not a forest land. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The grant in favour the respondent was in relation to a forest land and the High Court committed error in holding that it was in respect to the forest land. [515E] 1.2 The grant in respect of a forest land is not a mere grant but is a grant of a right of user in the forest land itself. It is a grant in respect to a forest. [516F G] 2.1 The High Court was wrong in holding that after the execution of the lease deed dated 25th September 1942, the Raja granted the rights in favour of a third party. The grant was in relation of a forest. The grant in the instant case was in respect thereof. [517G H] 3.1 The appellant could not have been held to be a tenant of the respondent. [518A]

The respondents filed an application under section 10(2) of the Jammu & Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) for eviction of the appellants from the suit premises on the ground that they required the building for their personal occupation. The trial court dismissed the plaintiffs ' suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the appellants had not proved their personal requirement. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the finding of the trial court that the appellants were entitled to occupy the premises was based on no evidence and that the High Court should have interfered with the said finding. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Court has taken an erroneous view of law on the nature of the need of the appellants as also on the question of comparative advantages or disadvantages of the landlord and the tenant if a decree for eviction followed. [801 B] 1.2. The High Courts are right in holding that the landlord is entitled to evict the appellants from their premises if they require them for their personal necessity. [802 C D] 2.1. It is well settled that the landlord must be able to prove his personal requirement by leading cogent evidence. [803 A] 2.2. In the instant case, the appellants did not merely have a desire to occupy the building but they actually needed the same and their need was both genuine and reasonable. [804 E F] 2.3. The High court was wrong in its conclusion that the appellants could not be evicted unless they were given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed eviction. [805 G H] 2.4. The High courts were right in holding the appellants entitled to evict them from the premises in question. [806 A B] 2.5. The Highs Court was right in holding, that the appellants would be entitled to evict from the premises if they were evicted without giving them an opportunity to put forward their case. [807 B] 2:6.
