3930: The appellant was the owner of certain lands in Hyderabad City. He sold them to the respondent who was a revenue agent. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of possession of the lands and the appellant contended that he had no title to the lands and that the respondent was not entitled to any relief. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the respondent being the owner of the lands could not sell the same without the consent of the appellant and that the appellant was not the owner of those lands. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The respondent was not the lull and absolute owner of the suit lands but was a benamidar. [285 G] (2) The respondent did not acquire any title to the land nor did he have any right to the lands. The respondent was merely a benamidars. The appellant was not a benamdar. [286 A B] (3) The respondent being the purchaser from the appellant, his vendor had no authority to sell the lands. [287 C D] (4) The respondent having entered into an agreement with the appellant for sale of the lands, the appellant was the real owner of the property. [288 E F] (5) The respondent had no right to sell the land. [289 H] (6) The respondent could not be said to be the owner of any land unless the appellant was a benami owner. [280 A B]
5488: The appellant was a tenant in respect of a room bearing No. 1 in a building belonging to the respondent. The respondent filed a petition for eviction against the appellant on the ground that he had become liable to be evicted from the premises in question under clause (d) of sub section (1) of Section 11 of Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947. The appellant pleaded inter alia in his written statement that at the time of the inception of the tenancy it had paid the respondent a sum of Rs.140 as advance rent with an understanding that the amount of advance could be set off against the rent whenever necessary or required. The appellant denied the said contention and stated that he had paid the amount of Rs. 140 as advance rent in advance on the ground of non payment of the rent in advance. The Additional Subordinate Judge held that the appellant had failed to pay the rent for the months of September and October, 1972 which was the date of the filing of the suit and that the appellant was entitled to claim adjustment if it was necessary or required and that since the receipt under which the said advance was received did not state that the amount received was liable to be adjusted towards arrears of rent only on the appellant informing the respondent orally or otherwise, the appellant could not be considered as a defaulter in payment of rent for purposes of clause (d). The High Court confirmed the order of the Additional Subordinate Judge. In appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant having failed to pay rent for the month of September and 10th October, 1972, the respondent became liable to be ejected from the premises taken on lease. [817 B] 2. The appellant had failed in paying the rent for September and October 1972 though it accepted the plea of the appellant that he had made payment of the amount of rent in advance as well as the amount of the rent payable in advance. It is true that if the parties are in pari delicto court will not come in rescue of either party. The receipt under which advance was received does not state that it was liable to adjustment towards the arrears of rent. [818 C D] 3. The appellant has failed to prove that the amount paid by him was liable to adjust towards the arrears. [
2728: The appellant was a tenant in respect of a shop. He filed a suit for ejectment on the plea that he had sub let the shop to one Gokal Chand who was a tenant under him. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The order of the District Magistrate under section 3A of the Act is not final as it does not determine any question of title or any other right whatsoever. [367 D] (2) The order passed by the District Magistrate is not final because the District Magistrate has no power to pass an order under section 3 A of the Act. [368 E] (3) The order made by the District magistrate under section 3(4) of the Act cannot be challenged in a civil suit. [369 F] (4) The order under section 7A of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 is not final since it is not open to the landlord to challenge it before the Civil Court. [366 B] (5) The order is not final and the landlord can challenge it only after the decision of the Civil Court under section 5(4). [367 C] (6) The order does not decide any question of law which may arise in the case. It merely decides whether the premises are required by the landlord for his own occupation. [361 H]
2302: The petitioners, who were citizens of India, challenged the validity of the Taxation Laws (Extension to Union Territories) Regulation No. 3 of 1963, on the ground that the President had no power to promulgate the Regulation under article 240 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the power conferred by the Regulation was not a legislative power but only an enabling one and that the power could be exercised in respect of the territory which was included within the Union Territory. Held, that the power to make laws extends to the whole of India and is not confined to the territories of the States. The power to legislate in respect of a territory is a legislative power and it cannot extend to the territory of India. The power of making laws extends to a territory which is part of the territory of the State. The power can be exercised in relation to a territory only if it is a part of the State or is a part or parts of the territory. The power is not limited to the territories which are part of the territories of India.
3266: The appellant was a private limited company carrying on business in jute. For the first time in its history entered into certain transactions in jute, the bulk of its income was from selling commission on tea. In fact the bulk of the income was from buying and selling of shares and securities. The assessee had contracted to purchase bales of B Twill and 2500 bales of corn sacks. The sale price was fixed at Rs. 1,000 per share. The assessee entered into contracts with two parties, M/s. The goods were in the godown of the mills and only the delivery orders addressed to the mills changed hands. The assessee claimed that the loss could be set off against speculation profits, and as there were no speculation profits in that year he held that the loss would be carried forward and set off against the speculation profits. The Income tax officer held that the transactions involving mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods were of a speculative character as contemplated in explanation to sec. 24(1) and the loss could not be set off under the proviso to sec.24(1). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. On further appeal the Tribunal held that the transaction involving mere transfer and delivery of the commodity was of a speculation profit and as there was no speculation profit in that year, the loss could have been set off against profits made by the assessee 's non speculation profits and as there are no speculation losses in that year it was not a speculation profits but a loss arising out of the contract for the sale of the goods. The High Court dismissed the reference holding that the sales in question were speculative and consequently the losses suffered by the assessee in these transactions could not be allowed to be set off. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the transactions involved in the present case were speculative transactions within the meaning of Explanation 2 to section 24(1), and the loss suffered by the appellant in these transactions should be set off as against the profits made by it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The transaction involving mere sale of goods is a speculative transaction. It is not a speculative transactions. [780G]

The High court further held that the Director General could not have made any appointment to the post of Deputy Mankac hries without the concurrence of the Ministry of Defence. The High Cou rt further held that since the appellant was holding the post of Assistant Mankachari ly Service, he could be considered for promotion to the post. The appellant contended that the Director, Military Lands and Enterprises had no authority to issue the impugned orders. The High Co urt further held: "The Director General has no power to appoint a person who is not
4772: The first respondent secured more votes than the appellant. He was declared elected to the Assembly seat by the Election Commission of India. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the Commission had no power to make any law in respect of the conduct of elections to Parliament and State Legislatures, and that the Commission being a creature of the Constitution itself, its plenary powers flowing directly from article 324 must prevail over any Act passed by the Parliament or the Rules made thereunder. Held, that the Commission having been invested with the power to make laws in respect of matters relating to or in connection with the elections to the Parliament and State Legislature, it is not competent to the Commission to make any legislation in respect of such matters. The Commission being a constitutional body has to act within the limits of its authority and the Court cannot interfere with it merely because it can do so. The Commission is a creature either of the Constitution or of an Act of Parliament. It is not necessary for the Commission to be a party to the proceedings before the Commission. The Commission has to function within the limits set down in the Constitution and it cannot encroach into the domain of the Executive or the Legislature. The Commission exercises its functions under the Constitution and the Rules framed thereunder. The Commission does not have the power to issue directions to the Commission as to how they should proceed. The Commission may also issue directions to other Election Commissioners to perform their functions under the Act.
5384: The appellant was appointed as Chairman of the Board on 10 12 1985. On his appointment as Chairman of Board he resigned his post as Professor Director and took over as Chairman of Haryana Board of School Education, in place of Shri Anil Razdan, I.A.S., with immediate effect for the period of two years. He resigned his office as Chairman of State Board of School Educa tion, in place o f Shri Anil R.R. Razdan. His resignation letter dated 24 3 1986 was accepted by the Government. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of termination of his service. The High Court dismissed the same holding that the appellant had not been able to show any material to show that he had been removed from the post of Chairman of the State Board of school Education, in view of the provisions contained in section 4 A of the Act. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant has no right to continue as Chairman of a Board after expiry of his term of office. [817B] 1.2 The appellant was holding the office of Chairman of a State Board of Secondary Education, which is a statutory body constituted under the Haryana Board of Secondary Ed ucation Act, 1969. The terms and conditions of his appointment were notified later on. The appellant having resigned his duties as Chairman of that Board, there was no question of his being appointed as Chairman. [818C D] 2.1 The High Court erred in holding that the order of appointment of the appellant was made without the approval of the State Government. [819E] 2.2 The High Court failed to consider the relevant facts and circumstances of the case. It did not consider the fact that the appellant was holding an office of Chairman and the order of removal was passed without the approval or sanction of the State Govern ment. [820F G]
3992: The appellant company was incorporated under the Rampur State and its registered office was at Rampur. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948. The agreements provided that the Rampur company should grant to the company leases of the agricultural lands with adequate irrigation facilities suitable for cultivation of sugar cane. The agreement provided that the Razas would be entitled to the agricultural income from the agricultural produce of the company during the period of the lease. The agreement also provided that the income derived by the company from the sale of sugarcane could be utilised for the purpose of the factory. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment order dated 29th June, 1962 made by the Assessing Authority against the Razads. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Assessing Authority committed an error of law in assessing the two partners of the Agricultural Company and not assessing the firm as such. The High court held that in the absence of notice to the partnership firm proceedings cannot be taken against the two companies for assessment of the tax. The High. Court further held that in view of the provisions of section 18(1) of the U. P. Agricultural Income tax Act, 1948, it is open to the authorities while proceeding with the assessment of the firm to determine the agricultural income of each member of the fir. The High 'Court accordingly set aside the assessment order and directed the Assessing Authority to proceed with the assessment in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that in the present case the Assessing Authority had no jurisdiction to assess the two partners in respect of their agricultural income. [424 E] (ii) The High Courts have been consistent in their approach in dealing with the question whether the Assessing Authority has jurisdiction to assess a firm or a company. The High Courts are not bound by the decision of the
150: The petitioner was detained in a case under section 344 of the Criminal Procedure Code on the allegation that he had been found to be in possession of certain contraband articles. He was produced before the Magistrate and remanded to judicial custody. On the 9th March, the Magistrate passed an order directing him to be kept in judicial lock up until further orders. The petitioner challenged this order by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution which was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioner: (i) that the order of remand dated 6th March, 1951, was not made by the trying Magistrate on the 9th of March, but with reference to the institution of the proceedings; (ii) that the Magistrate could not have ordered the production of the petitioner in court without his being called upon to do so; and (iii) that the petitioner should have been allowed to remain at large in jail till the 11th March, and that the order was not passed as a lawful one. HELD : (i) The order of remand is not a mere formality or routine order and does not amount to a direction for the release of the person concerned. It merely directs the release of a person from detention pending trial. [912 D] (ii)The order of remand was not a mere direction for the return of the petitioner to custody. The order of the Magistrate was not a direction for his release from custody. The only direction which the Magistrate could give was to direct the release of any person from detention. [913 E F] (iii)The order dated 6th of March 1951, was a valid order and did not require any interference. The order was not a substantive order. It was not a final order. It merely directed the release of some persons from detention. The order did not require the release of persons from detention, but only required the release of those who were already in detention. [991 G H]
1018: The respondent was appointed a constable in the U.P. Police Force on December 1, 1945. On November 17, 1952, he was posted as officer incharge of Police Station Intiathok, District Gonda. The High court was wrong in its view that the respondent could not have been dismissed from service without complying with any of the requirements of the said sub para. 2643: The Income tax Officer, Meerut, issued a notice under section 132(1) of the Income tax Act, 1961 to the appellant firm requiring it to produce certain documents. The appellant filed an application before the Income tax Officer for a direction that the documents be produced and the Income tax officer was directed to examine them. The Income tax officer examined the documents and gave his report. The Income Tax Officer also gave a certificate that the documents were not relevant for the purpose of any proceeding under the Act. The appellant 's case was that the documents seized by the Income tax Officers were irrelevant for the purpose Of any proceedings under the Act; that besides the documents seized they were not relevant as they were not in the possession of the Income Tax Officer at the time when the search was made; that the documents which were seized were not relevant because they were not the subject matter of the search; that the Income tax officers had no authority to seize the documents or to make copies thereof; that the police force employed during the raid was excessive; that the records showed that the appellant had been carrying on business in the name of M/s Seth Brothers and the income tax authorities had no power to seize the books of account or other documents seized from the appellant; that the appellant was entitled to inspect the premises of the firm and to take extracts therefrom; that the books of accounts and other documents seized were not liable to be destroyed under section 27 of the Indian Income tax Act; that the income tax officers had failed to comply with the provisions of section 27 of that Act; that there was no reason to believe that the said documents were forged or fabricated; that the statements contained in the affidavits filed by the appellant were false and that the appellant could not have been prosecuted without a charge against him. (ii) The Income Tax Officers had no jurisdiction to investigate the facts of the case. (iii) The Income 'tax Officers had no power under the Act to require production of the documents seized from him. 5431: The appellants were the owners of a property in Delhi. They had been inducted as tenants by the respondent. The respondent was paying rent to the appellants. The appellants claimed interest on the amount awarded by the High Court. The respondent contended that the appellants were entitled to interest only from the date of the judgment of the High Court and not from the date when the possession of the premises was taken over. The High Court held that the appellants are entitled to interest from the date they took possession of the property till the date of payment of the amount. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the appellants would be entitled to interest for the period from March 7, 1975 to 31st July, 1987 when principal amount of compensation had been paid and or when the premises in question had been de requisitioned and handed back to the owner, on the amount payable from the respective dates. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants are entitled for interest on the amounts awarded by the courts below from the date the amount became due till the date the same is actually paid. [990B] 1.2 Interest will be payable only on the balance amount which remained to be payable to the appellants i.e. the amount due minus what has been paid from the respective date. [991C] 2.1 The High Court was right in holding that interest would accrue from the date on which the possession of premises was taken by the appellants. [992D]
927: The appellant was a Sub Inspector of Police in the State of Pepsu. He was dismissed from service by an order dated August 16, 1950, passed by the Chief Secretary of the State. The appellant challenged his dismissal on the ground that he had been removed from service and that it was not necessary to hold a departmental enquiry against him under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, that the order of compulsory retirement did not amount to removal from service within the meaning of article 311 of the Constitution and as the requirement of that Article had not been complied with it was void in law. The order of compulsory retrial was not one of punishment but only of reduction in rank and therefore the order was not invalid. The order was not one which could be said to have been made in the exercise of the power conferred by article 311 of Constitution. The order being one of punishment, it was not one for removal from service. The order did not amount either to removal or dismissal from service. It was not one such punishment as was contemplated by article 311(2) of the Constitution.
3306: The appellant was convicted under section 379 read with section 34 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. He preferred an appeal against the order of conviction and sentence to the High Court but the High Court dismissed his appeal. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended that the provisions of section 6 were not applicable to the case because the appellant had not done anything since the date of the offence to deserve the mercy of the Court and it did not, therefore, see any reason to interfere with the sentence of imprisonment imposed on him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 6 is intended for the benefit of juvenile delinquents who are found guilty of the offence under section 379 and section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. [639 B] (2) The expression 'punishment which may be imposed ' in sub section (1) means 'simple imprisonment ' or 'torture ' or 'duty ' or 'punishments '. It does not mean 'simility ' or 'conviction '. [640 C D]
5056: The plaintiffs, a company incorporated in the United States of America, filed a suit for infringement of two patents (Numbers 104120 and 125381) by the defendant, an Indian Private Limited Company. The plaintiffs claimed that they had acquired patented pharmaceutical products from the defendant and that the defendant was using them as a drug for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals. The defendant contended that the plaintiffs were not entitled to any relief on the ground that the patent was not in accordance with the specifications of the patents. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that the patent in question was in contravention of the provisions of the Act or that it infringed the patent. The appeal preferred by the defendant before the High Court was unsuccessful. In the appeal by special leave to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the plaintiffs were entitled to relief on the basis of the patent having been granted by the defendant; (ii) the plaintiffs could not be said to have contravened the provisions of section 3(3)(b) of the Act; (iii) the plaintiffs had no locus standi to file the suit because the patent was granted by the respondent company which is a public limited company and not a private limited company. The plaintiffs were entitled under the Act to get the patent revoked if they found that the patent has been obtained by fraud or misrepresentation. [914A] 4. The plaintiffs had not made out a case that the patent had been granted by a public limited Company. The plaintiff had not pleaded that the patent did not contain any preservative or other material which would make the product marketable. [915B C] 5. The plaintiffs do not fall within the definition of "public" as defined in section 2(d) of the . [9
3921: The appellant was convicted for offences under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 18 months on each could and a fine of Rs. 2000/ . He was also convicted for an offence under section 161 IPC and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. The appellant 's appeal against his conviction and sentence was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the sanction is not valid in law; (ii) the order of the President refusing sanction is bad in law; and (iii) the appellant had been acquitted by the trial court and the High Court without any reason. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The sanction is a condition precedent to the validity of the prosecution. [877 C] 2. The question whether the sanction is valid or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The authority competent to remove the appellant from service is the appointing authority. The power conferred by sub rule (2) of rule 11 and clause (b) of sub rule (1) of rule 23 of the Central Civil Services Classification Control and Appeal Rules, 1957, is not absolute but can be exercised only when there are reasonable grounds for doing so. It is open to the authority competent to dismiss the appellant from the service. [878 E F] 3. The order of the Governor refusing sanction is not final as it does not affect the rights of the appellant. [879 G H] 4. The order passed by the Governor is not subject to judicial review. The order is not subject either to judicial review or to judicial review, as the case may be. [880 A B] 5. The order cannot be challenged on the ground that it is not in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution or the Act. [881 D] 6. The order does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality before the law and equal protection of laws enshrined in Article 14 of the Constitution. [882 C] 7. The order has to be set aside because it is not made in conformity with the provisions contained in the Act and the rules framed thereunder. [883 D]
2950: The appellant, a firm of which the respondent was the Managing Partner, was prosecuted for having committed offences under section 120B read with section 420 I.P.C. and section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted the accused but the High Court confirmed the acquittal. 1984: The appellant, a registered dealer in respect of the assessment year 1956 62, claimed exemption under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947. The assessing authority disallowed the claim on the ground that the declaration forms were not signed by the registered dealers and that they had been issued to them by the purchasing dealers themselves. The revision filed by the appellant before the Revenue Board was also dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the rule was only directory and not mandatory and that the requirement of the rule was not complied with. HELD: (i) The rule is merely directory and not imperative. It is well settled that if a statute provides for a thing to be done in a particular manner it can be done in that manner alone and no other. [560 B] (ii) The rule does not require that the form should be filled up or signed by the person making the declaration. It is open to the person making a declaration to fill up the form and to give notice thereof to the other party concerned. If he fails to do so, his right to make a representation would be defeated. [561 C D] (iii) The rule was intended to prevent evasion of tax and to provide for the levy of additional tax on the sales effected by the dealer to the purchasing dealer. The rule was enacted to avoid evasion of tax. [562 E F] (iv) The rule made under the Orissa Sales tax Act, 1947, was a substantive provision which provided for the exemption of certain sales to a dealer who wishes to claim exemption thereunder. The rule did not contain any condition that the declaration must be signed by the purchasing dealer himself. The rule could have been easily read into the rule as a whole. But the rule was intended only to prevent evasion and to ensure that the dealer 's sales are not affected by the provisions of the Act. [563 A B]
3051: The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had a lease of certain flats in the building known as Himalaya House. The appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent company for the purpose of developing the said building and to construct a building thereon. The appellant also agreed to pay the rent at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. The respondent company paid the rent to the appellant company but did not execute the deed of assignment. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent company and its directors for recovery of possession of the flat. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the appellant company was entitled to recover possession of the said flat from the respondent company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court erred in holding that the consideration mentioned in the document was nil; (ii) the High court erred in holding otherwise than by way of a decree for specific performance of contract. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that "the consideration mentioned in document is nil". [887C] 2. The High court was wrong in holding that it was not necessary to mention the consideration in the document because the document was executed by the respondent company in favour of the appellant company. [888D E] 3. The High Courts decision in Bharpet Mohammad Hussain Sahib and Another vs District Registrar, Kurnool and Another, [1977] A.P.L.J. 769, followed.

3805: The appellant purchased the properties in village Devanoor and the appellant purchased the same from the decree holder. The sale was set aside as there was some delay in payment of the sale price. The Court proceeded to sell the properties in villages Devanoor, Gudipadu and Devanoor. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 12,500/ against the 5th respondent/decree holder. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the sale was not valid and that the appellant had failed to pay the amount mentioned in the sale proclamation within the time specified therein. The High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sale of the properties in the village Devano was sufficient to satisfy the decretal amount mentioned in sale proclamation but a few days after the sale had already taken place, the Court should have stopped the sale as required by 0.21 r. 64 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The sale of the property in village Devana was sufficient to meet the claim of the decree holder in O.S. 19 of 1953 and he also applied for a certificate to the appellant to file an appeal in this Court. [511 B] (2) The sale was held on October 12, 1952 at which the lands situated in villages Devana and Gudipad were put to sale. But this sale was set off against the decreta amount of Rs.12,500/ and the appellant was entitled to be paid the balance of the sale money. The appellant could not therefore be said to have been prejudiced by the failure of the decree holders to pay the balance of sale price. [513 C D] (3) The sale in favour of the appellant was not vitiated merely because the decree holder did not take steps to bring the decree into execution. The sale in his favour was set aside and the sale was restored. [514 E F] (4) The sale is not vitiated merely on account of the fact that the decree holder has obtained a decree for specific performance of contract for sale of the land in dispute. [515 A B]
1187: The petitioners who were the legal representatives of their father, who was an evacuee, applied to the Custodian for declaring them evacuee property. The Custodian rejected their application on the ground that they had become evacuees and their shares in the properties could be properly declared evacuee property. They challenged the order of the Custodian by a petition under article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the order was not a nullity as it did not affect the petitioners ' rights under the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The order dated August 14, 1952, is a nullity as the notice under section 7 of the Act on which it was based, was bad for the reason that it was issued to Abdul Hai and his six children who were dead. [535 C] (ii) The order of August 14, 1951, was a nullity as no notice under section 8(2) of the Act was given to the petitioners. The petitioners had not been served with any notice under section 9 of the Act. The petitioners therefore could not have any right to challenge the validity of the order dated August 4, 1952, made under section 11 of the Act, because the notice under Section 7 of the said Act was not a notice under section 6 of the Act but was only a notice under sections 9 and 10 of the Act and the petitioners had no locus standi to question the validity of such notice. [536 D E; 537 A B] (iii) The order passed by the Custodian under section 11 is a nullity since it does not affect the rights of the petitioners. It also provides that the order shall contain the particulars of the property which is subject matter of the order. [539 F G] (iv) The order was a nullity because it was passed without giving notice to the petitioners under section 7. [540 A B]
862: The respondents were the Apollo Mills, a textile mill, and other companies owning cotton textile mills specified in the annexure to the Special Leave Petition. The respondents claimed compensation for loss of wages due to the short working or closure of the Textile Mills on certain days during the period between November 1, 1951, and July 13, 1952, but the appellant contended that the Industrial Court had jurisdiction to decide the dispute under section 40(1) of the Bombay Electricity (Special Powers) Act, 1946. Held, that the decision of the Bombay High Court in Digambar Ramachandra 's case (1), was not applicable to the present case because the provisions of section 40(2) and the addition of Sch. 111 item 7 in the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, did not find place in the Bombay (1) (2) ; and the decision of this Court in Digamber Ramachandra vs Khandesh Mills (1) applied. The decision in Digambeer Ramachandra v Khandesh Mills, (supra) was given by the Bombay High court in view of the provisions of the Bombay (I) (2). The decision in the Digambeers ' case (1) was given in view of section 40 of the Bombay Act which provided that the provisions of that Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force.
